item.title: Doing Social Media in the AI Era, Your Boss Is More Hopeless Than the Algorithm
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-oddlots-ai-时代做社媒-老板比算法更让人绝望/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-oddlots-ai-时代做社媒-老板比算法更让人绝望/
item.description: The real AI shock to marketing teams comes from the boss: outsourcing intuition to Claude, approving only what Copilot generates, so employees disguise their own ideas as Copilot screenshots to sneak them past approval.
item.content:encoded:
The real AI shock to marketing teams comes from the boss: outsourcing intuition to Claude, approving only what Copilot generates, so employees disguise their own ideas as Copilot screenshots to sneak them past approval.

Medium information density, but Rachel's first-hand interviews about "boss AI brain" and the Threads algorithm mechanics are industry details you won't hear anywhere else.

4:06 Bosses have outsourced their intuition to Claude
Rachel interviewed roughly a hundred marketers and found that the main path AI takes into a team isn't tool procurement, it's the boss. A social media manager carefully makes a funny meme, sends it to the boss, and the boss drops it into Claude to ask "is this funny." More absurd still, some marketers discovered their boss only approves ideas that come from Copilot, so they first mock their own ideas up to look like the Copilot interface, then send that to the boss for approval. Rachel says what's behind this is the boss outsourcing their entire intuitive judgment to AI, while the team has no training or guardrails at all on how to use AI — she contrasts it with her own experience spending months at Condé Nast learning Asana.

7:14 Consumers don't hate AI, they hate being fooled
Taylor points out an overlooked fact: plenty of YouTubers now read AI-generated scripts straight to camera, and the comments still praise the "brilliant analysis, well-written script." In other words, when people don't know they're consuming AI content, they actually like it. What triggers real anger isn't AI itself, it's the feeling of having been played. Rachel adds the explanation for this double standard: an AI fruit romance meme like Fruit Love Island is a low-stakes meme, and nobody cares about the craft of a meme; but when a brand you pay money to uses AI to generate a menu, you wonder how much else it's cutting corners on in the product. The same person can curse brands for using AI while forwarding an AI fruit meme to a friend.

9:16 How-to creators are the first to be replaced by AI
Rachel splits creators into two categories. The ones who built their following on how-to content are most at risk — from the earliest YouTube beauty tutorials onward, the democratization of media ran along this path, but for questions like "how do I fix the dishwasher," AI is the better authority and people will just ask it. Taylor gives the example of her own mother, who recently fixed a toilet with ChatGPT and was very proud of it, something that would have been unthinkable before. The other category of creator is actually safe: people doing deep parasocial content, doing commentary, doing things that aren't easy to replicate can use these tools to make better content. The test is whether the content itself is replicable.

11:28 Anti-data-center and anti-extinction people never allied
Taylor observes that the people opposing data centers and the people worried AI will exterminate humanity are two groups with completely different motivations, and they have yet to form any coherent alliance; she even half-jokes that they should team up, but their interests diverge too much. Her own position is clear: AI won't kill us, "it's actually very hard to kill all humans on Earth, even if we wanted to." What she thinks genuinely deserves scrutiny is how people anthropomorphize AI and grant these products agency — especially dangerous in policy debates about assigning responsibility, because they are computer programs, not living things. She also quotes a former FTC commissioner: we survived the Black Death, and that only killed 50% of people.

19:35 AI accounts are pulling Instagram's slot machine
Taylor thinks Meta is in a hard spot, because it is essentially a 2010s social network whose influence peaked in the 2010s, while Google is better positioned than Meta. In the short term, AI's impact on platforms is about scale and speed: one AI account can post 50 times a day, which is like constantly pulling Instagram's slot machine — eventually one will hit. She looked at the 20 most-viewed reels at the time, and two or three of them were AI-generated, and all were very new. One used a "behind-the-scenes reveal" framing to show how a crew films ocean waves and how the waves wash away a house, essentially using "proof of authenticity" as a shell to manufacture confusion. Her judgment: this is monetizing confusion, with short-term gains and a very bad long-term outcome.

21:35 Threads is the most toxic social platform
Taylor says she recently posted hot takes calling Threads the most toxic social platform to date, far more toxic than Twitter — "Twitter compared to Threads is a beautiful wonderland." The mechanism is that the algorithm prioritizes replies extremely heavily, so you get dropped straight into someone's angry reply about something, which in turn feeds the algorithm and rapidly escalates into a groupthink pile-on. She also points out that Threads' AI-generated news summaries "are just lying, making things up outright." Asked who uses Threads, her answer is her mom.

22:36 The growth secret is turning your account into a series
Asked how to grow an audience in the AI era, Rachel says the accounts growing now all have a clear through-line of familiarity in their content, like they're making their own TV show. Her example is a restaurant chef filming himself cooking while wearing Meta glasses, who grew to about 500,000 followers in two or three months under the account name Gil Holy Cooks, posting one episode a day. Taylor adds that content is becoming serialized across the board, and you really have to think about how to entertain people; the era of "share your life" is clearly declining, and in 2026 you should not become a lifestyle influencer — there is a lot of anger toward those people.

24:42 Instagram handed out an official division-of-labor chart for formats
Rachel says Instagram once shared a very useful chart with her readers explaining what each content format is for: carousels and reels are for reaching new audiences and get pushed to non-followers, and what the current algorithm really feeds on is non-follower views — if only your own audience can understand the content, the platform judges it "not entertaining enough" and withholds main-feed traffic. Single-image posts only serve your existing audience. Stories and DMs are treated by the platform as where community happens. She also quotes Adam Mosseri on Bloomberg Screen Time: the "social" in social media is no longer about sharing family photos, but about DMing friends the things that remind you of them. She finds this quite sad, but it does clarify what "social" now means on social media.

item.title: AI makes starting a company easier than getting a job, but solo founders have no fallback
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-solofounders-ai-让开公司比找工作容易-但单人创始人没有退路/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-solofounders-ai-让开公司比找工作容易-但单人创始人没有退路/
item.description: Durable hit a million users in three months, but its founder says he took a detour: website generation wasn't the endgame — handing the entire back office of the services industry to AI is. Being a solo founder isn't more freedom; it's carrying every decision yourself.
item.content:encoded:
Durable hit a million users in three months, but its founder says he took a detour: website generation wasn't the endgame — handing the entire back office of the services industry to AI is. Being a solo founder isn't more freedom; it's carrying every decision yourself.

The first half is founder backstory and fundraising, with average information density; the second half — on product judgment, the death of UI, and the pros and cons of solo founding — is worth listening to.

10:19 3.5 million sign-ups, and over half are brand-new businesses
About 3.5 million people have signed up on Durable to start a business, and more than half of them are net new — not existing businesses coming online, but people starting a company for the first time. These people aren't in the brainstorming phase; they already have an idea and possibly a little revenue. The first thing they do on Durable is build an online presence, do SEO and GEO, get found on ChatGPT and Google, and start running ads and following up with customers. Clift says this showed him a mass of businesses he "could never have dreamed existed," like decorating porches for Halloween, which can do several hundred thousand dollars a year.

24:37 The AI website generator was a detour, not the endgame
Durable's original vision was "Shopify for the services industry," close to a franchise model: franchisees pay $100,000, Durable takes $10,000, and gives them the same leads, website and marketing system. After GPT-2.5 appeared, they ran a one-week internal hack week, built an AI website generator, launched it in 2022, and it went viral, going from zero to about a million users in three months and bringing in meaningful revenue. But they spent a year and a half on that product, and Clift now calls it an "interesting distraction" — a good business, but not the market they wanted to be in. Four years later they're back to the original vision: an AI version of a "business in a box" for service business owners.

31:50 Users don't want buttons, they want outcomes
Clift deliberately avoids the UI details in customer feedback: everyone says they want to change this button, add this component, customize that, but what they actually want is a better-looking, better-performing website. Likewise, appointment scheduling can fall down a rabbit hole of time zones and multiple calendars, but what people really want is "jobs getting booked." His conclusion: building UI is now extremely low-value, first because AI makes UI easy to build, and second because nobody wants to click through a pile of things anymore — if users never log into Durable and just get one text message a day, that's a better experience. The product should be input and output: describe the problem you want solved, and it gets solved.

36:01 You should now deliberately pick harder problems
Clift says that since models will keep getting stronger and will make your product obsolete ("it may already be obsolete, and it'll be obsolete again at least once within six months"), you should deliberately choose harder problems. Durable has millions of people actively starting new businesses, and making them succeed is an extremely hard problem, but once solved it corresponds to trillions of dollars in GMV and economic value. He also mentions team size: still only six engineers, but "six engineers are roughly equivalent to sixty agents," so adding features is no longer scary, and the real risk becomes "are you building the right thing for the right customer."

44:24 Going solo was about shedding responsibility for other people
Clift says he didn't deliberately choose to be a solo founder; rather, his first two partnerships with co-founders both got stuck on the same thing: mismatched runway and risk. He couldn't help calculating the other person's opportunity cost — "how much they could make at Amazon, how much they could make consulting" — and by rational calculation you should never start a software company. More importantly, there's the psychological burden: with even one co-founder, he felt he had to keep that person happy and take care of them, effectively carrying that person's family's livelihood on his shoulders. Going solo removed that pressure — "now it's all on me alone" — and he can think only about the business, be freer to do creative work, and if he fails, only he is affected.

48:30 Built in Vancouver, funded in San Francisco
Clift's judgment: to win a venture-backed, outsized outcome, you probably still have to be in San Francisco; but Vancouver is a great place to build, and San Francisco is a great place to raise money and get inspired. Every time he goes to San Francisco he thinks "we should work harder, faster, be more ambitious," but that energy also often gets in the way of actually building product and understanding customers, producing that lost founder who is "caffeinated, trying a million things, gripping the handlebars for dear life without knowing what they're doing." His approach: the company DNA, ambition and fundraising are Silicon Valley-style, but the customers aren't in Silicon Valley — they're in the middle of America, internationally, and they're solo owners.

54:33 Door-to-door sales taught him rejection
In college, Clift cleaned windows and gutters and sold door to door. He learned two things: first, desensitization to rejection — nobody yells at you for knocking and offering to help, and they won't remember you two days, or even two minutes, later; second, volume. Knock on enough doors and you'll close, and then a neighborhood "flips": one house does it, puts up a sign, and the neighbors all follow. He draws a direct analogy to fundraising and cold outreach emails: the worst outcome is that they don't read it, and that's probably what will happen. He also says that if building gets easier because of AI, then sales becomes more valuable.

1:03:49 Earning your first dollar is a worldview unlock
Clift thinks one of the most interesting parts of the human experience is "earning money yourself," and not even in a financial sense. The world is designed around employment, and profit flows to business owners; yet earning a dollar yourself is still outside the norm for most people — "I had an idea, and someone paid for it." He says it's like opening a small door, and you become more ambitious, going from twenty or thirty dollars to tens of millions in revenue. He also admits you might try it and find you don't like it, but everyone should try it once, and most people are better at it than they think.

item.title: Good ayis are always on the job: what a domestic-help consultant really sells isn't information
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-bizthisway-好阿姨永远在户上-家政顾问卖的不是信息/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-bizthisway-好阿姨永远在户上-家政顾问卖的不是信息/
item.description: Domestic help is a supply-led industry: good ayis never reach the open market, and the hard part of a consultant's job isn't closing the deal but handling replacements after the sale. Both employers and ayis are just pass-throughs for their wages.
item.content:encoded:
Domestic help is a supply-led industry: good ayis never reach the open market, and the hard part of a consultant's job isn't closing the deal but handling replacements after the sale. Both employers and ayis are just pass-throughs for their wages.

A frontline post-00s domestic-help consultant lays out an overlooked essential-need industry: matching mechanics, pricing, off-platform deals, boundaries. High information density, and the second half is worth more.

18:44 Good ayis are always on the job
This market has a circulation paradox: ayis with good reviews never reach the open market. She works for one family for two or three years, and the moment she leaves she's referred straight to the next one. The ones actually circulating on the market are usually the ones nobody could settle on. So the industry's core contradiction is supply — where good ayis come from and how they get discovered. A domestic-help company is essentially a human resources company: it has to recruit, train and re-match.

19:37 Every woman in this business has a story
The ayi profile clusters in third- and fourth-tier cities and even poor villages, aged 30 to 45, many divorced or single. Live-in sisters spend little time with their own families, giving their time to another household. Two clear traits define why they choose this work: they like children, and they want to earn — not a comfortable life back home farming and drinking tea, but packing everything they own, buying a green-skin train ticket and squeezing into Shanghai.

26:00 This time you're the boss
There has to be a sense of boundaries and proportion between ayi and employer — not just for the ayi, but for the employer too. Some people spoil the ayi past the line, but people always push for more. More subtly, a live-in ayi is together with the family 24 hours a day and may know more about the household's private life than relatives do — the pressure is heavy. Some moms are raising kids effectively widowed, with the dad absent, and it's the ayi who keeps the mom company longer; the two become teammates.

37:24 Employers and ayis are both pass-throughs for wages
For the employer it's like being a pass-through for wages, and the same goes for the ayi: every month the WeChat transfer comes in, and immediately two kids' tuition goes out, then the household living expenses, transferred straight away. Many yuesao and yuer sao earn the most important — sometimes the only — income in their family, which is why their role as wife carries so much weight in the family structure. That also explains why employers care about the ayi's family background: you're not hiring a company employee, and her stability is directly tied to her family situation.

41:09 How ten pages of job requirements don't scare the ayi off
The longest yuesao job requirement I've seen ran a full ten pages, at a price that was only the market average. The employer thinks that if every minute is spelled out, the ayi will execute like a robot — but people are emotional. The consultant doesn't forward it directly; she calls first to set the ground: asks about luggage, navigation route, tells her the client says just arrive at this time, then explains that company rules require the employer to list requirements, and she can come to the consultant with any question. That way the ayi feels she's been handed a guidebook, not interrogated.

49:47 Closing the deal is easy; replacing someone is the test
Yuesao bookings are made in advance; yuer sao jobs are mostly urgent — an ayi only enters the market once she leaves her previous family, so demand is pressing. Many employers assume that whoever is available urgently must be bad, when often it's the booked one who's the fake. Closing isn't hard for a consultant: as long as the employer has a need and a budget, someone can always be found. The real difficulty is long-term after-sales — the interview can be thrilling, and afterwards there's a real chance of disappointment. Replacing someone is what truly tests a consultant's level.

56:17 The hardest case requires reading the family's core relationship
The hardest case: a single mother who is a female executive, wanting a daytime child development companion, but also expecting that person to do housework to cleaning-level standards — while the companion's hourly rate is twice a cleaner's. The consultant dealt with the assistant, while the core need was shaped by the executive mother. The compromise was cleaners clean, companions companion, but the mother still had to be won over. The person finally found was the polar opposite of the original spec — originally under 35 with a bilingual kindergarten teaching background; in the end, a sister approaching 50 with an education background and live-in experience.

1:03:36 Yuesao start at 15,000; yuer sao depends on age
In first-tier cities a yuesao's 26-day contract price is generally 15,000 to 16,000 or more; for one with two or three years' experience who has genuinely cared for newborns, it's basically 15,000 to 20,000. Shanghai rates for yuer sao: beginners from 7,000, experienced hands depending on age, skills and work history, basically 8,000-plus; stack on English, bilingual, early education, driving and it's 10,000-plus. Prices have risen in recent years partly because more highly educated people are entering the work, and partly because supply still falls short of demand.

item.title: After the 10,000-worker factory vanished, he had 20 years of snapshots of migrant life
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-cn907a40-万人工厂消失后-他用-20-年拍下打工者的日常/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-cn907a40-万人工厂消失后-他用-20-年拍下打工者的日常/
item.description: Others photographed the era's anomalies; he insisted on its ordinary days — meals, punch-ins, English classes. When the giant factory finally disappeared, almost no one else had kept the archive.
item.content:encoded:
Others photographed the era's anomalies; he insisted on its ordinary days — meals, punch-ins, English classes. When the giant factory finally disappeared, almost no one else had kept the archive.

Not an industry analysis — a migrant worker using a camera to write a biography of himself and his generation. The back half, on ‘density’ and ‘autoethnography’, is the most valuable part.

2:09 The logic of the assembly line is to make a person's value irrelevant
After the Foxconn suicides, Zhan Youbing was asked what he thought. He said he had seriously considered it: every assembly-line method works by subdividing the process so that manufacturing is more stable and people are more replaceable. Translated, those two sentences mean — anyone can do it, and anyone will do it just as well. The machines had not yet replaced the workers, but the person's value already barely mattered. That was the underlying motive for him later picking up a camera and aiming it at his fellow workers: inside a system deliberately flattening individual difference, to record specific people.

6:11 Riding the green-skin train felt like climbing into a bandits' den
In 1995, after leaving the army, he went south. The car was already full at the Wuchang origin station — people above the seats, people below, people sleeping on the luggage racks, people everywhere in the toilets and the gangways between cars. At Chenzhou someone smashed a window with a brick and shoved people onto the train like livestock. For more than thirty hours he could not sit and could not drink water; after getting off, his belly was badly swollen. At Guangzhou railway station he was then cheated by touts into being ‘sold like a piglet’ — first they took twenty-odd yuan saying it was for Dongguan, then on the highway they demanded another ten for the expressway toll, and if you refused someone would come up and slap you, and in the end you were dumped in a wasteland with no village ahead and no shop behind to change vehicles. He says he used the term for years before he understood what it meant last year.

11:48 He did 102 push-ups for a security guard job
In 1995 it was hard to find work; men had a far harder time than women, and factory recruitment notices stated outright that they only hired female workers aged 18 to 25. He saw a hiring notice by National Highway 107, and the security captain had all the applicants lie down in the parking lot and do push-ups to screen their stamina. The count was drawn out; by 20 people began dropping, by 40 only eight or ten were left, by 50-something only he was left. The captain said you're bragging, go ahead, and he did 102. Then he was told to spar with someone; the other man did a split, and he turned sideways, caught the leg and flipped him. That was how he got his first job: gate security at a hotel, 450 yuan a month.

17:16 An 1,800-yuan camera and 48-yuan rolls of film
In 2002 he agonised for a long time before buying his own camera: his wage was only around 1,500, he already had a child, and his wife was still back home. He called to discuss it, and his wife said, if you like it, buy it. The camera was 1,800 yuan; film, even bought ten rolls at a time wholesale, was 48 each, plus 5 for developing and another ten or twenty for prints — a huge drain on him in that era. At first he shot factory events, visiting guests, employee tug-of-war, assuming that photography was just a technical problem of getting things sharp. Later, reading Chinese photography magazines, he found there was so much learning in photography and he had no standard to measure by, so he bought the New York Institute of Photography textbook, whose first lesson is the three criteria of a good photograph.

24:00 A model-contest photo passed ten million clicks, then he was told to delete it
In 2007 the factory began holding a model contest; the women went on stage in swimsuits, evening gowns and uniforms, and there was pole dancing. In 2008 he changed position, went to the stage backdrop and shot downward — models in front, a dense black mass of audience behind — and sent it to Tencent in time; it went up on the portal and got tens of millions of clicks in a morning. But online comments said this was picking a mistress for the boss and a lover for the factory manager; the framing was distorted, the boss came under enormous pressure, and he was told to delete it. Tencent said it could only be hidden, other sites' viral reposting could not be stopped, and in the end he was served a notice reserving the right to pursue the matter.

25:23 The photo of the woman worker looking up — he had not planned to use it
On 5 January 2011, as a senior supervisor, he entered the clean room to inspect fire safety, and because the work required it he openly brought his camera. Clean-room work allows a four-minute break after two hours; the changing area was hung with unworn clean-room suits, and two people sat in front, one of them a fellow Hubei native. He pressed the shutter once or twice, and his fellow townsman heard the sound and looked up at him. He says the advice he was given when learning photography was that ‘a photo where the subject looks at the lens is not a good photo’, so he never used this one. Later Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China, organised the Off-Pix award; he submitted it, and it was unexpectedly made the lead image. Looking at it seriously afterwards, he admitted it has its own pull — different readers will have different inner responses, so a photographer should interpret his own photos as little as possible.

31:26 One set of ID papers lent to many people; after social security went online, his years of service were zeroed out
When he came out to find work in 1995, Hubei people were not wanted, Henan people were not wanted, Anhui people were acceptable, so he borrowed an Anhui man's ID card. At the time factories' information was separate, there was no networked computer system, and the social security system did not require contributions, so that set of papers was lent to many people and entered many factories. But after 2000 social security began to be networked, and the system would not accept it — same ID number, same name, same household registration address — and the enterprises decided you were dishonest and zeroed out your years of service. He says this won't do: our generation is about to reach retirement age, and those years of service are real. When even present-day life has no security, it is impossible to think about retirement twenty or fifty years away.

36:30 Density: he shot for 20 years before discovering it was everywhere
In 2019 he curated a set of photographs around the density of migrant working life, which won the Excellence Award and the Alpa Award at the third Hard Instant Image Awards. Workers' gatherings shot from high above, heads packed with almost no gaps; collective dormitories hung with clothes, from a distance airtight; workshop switches, key cabinets, lockers holding bowls and chopsticks — neatly divided structures producing a visual sense of density. He says at first it was unconscious: shooting with his phone every day, shooting security training, shooting any fellow worker he happened to see on the road, accumulating day by day, on and off for almost 20 years. When there were so many eras in so many factories, he had not observed in that way, and once he discovered it, it was terrifying — even the switches looked spectacular.

item.title: Companies That Treat Service as a Cost Center Are Giving Away Their Moat
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-twist-把服务当成本中心的公司-正在把护城河让出去/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-twist-把服务当成本中心的公司-正在把护城河让出去/
item.description: Products get replaced by better products, brands by stronger brands; the only durable competitive advantage is hospitality — the continuous, generous investment in relationships.
item.content:encoded:
Products get replaced by better products, brands by stronger brands; the only durable competitive advantage is hospitality — the continuous, generous investment in relationships.

This is Will Guidara talking about Unreasonable Hospitality. No AI, no fundraising tactics, but it nails "service as moat" — worth listening to as an operating philosophy.

4:05 Product moats get filled in sooner or later
Guidara's argument: most companies are looking for their moat, and the traditional answer is to build the best product, the strongest brand. But he thinks those only work to a degree, because time has repeatedly shown that sooner or later someone builds a better product, a stronger brand — the other side may be better capitalized, more creative, have new ideas, or simply be better than you. So he thinks the only competitive advantage that exists long term comes from hospitality, from continuously and generously investing in relationships. This isn't saying product doesn't matter; it's saying don't save your best effort only for the product — also invest in how people feel.

7:09 The front line has information and no power; leadership has power and no information
Guidara quotes retired Navy captain David Marquet: in most organizations, leadership has all the power and no information, while the front line has all the information and no power. His inference: you cannot deliver unreasonable hospitality without empowering the front line, because only the people on the front line know the guest well enough to know what would make this particular service "unreasonable." In his book he covers feedback methods, the daily 30-minute meeting, how to celebrate and create traditions the team looks forward to — but he says the greatest unreasonable hospitality you can give your colleagues is to genuinely give them agency.

17:16 Hospitality can be systematized, not just a flash of inspiration
One-off gestures like the hot dog or the first dance are hard to scale — they need someone to come up with them in the moment, and forcing them looks contrived. But Guidara says these are exactly what proves hospitality can be systematized: do pattern recognition, find the recurring moments, then write "how we respond when this moment happens" into the process. For example, guests used to constantly need to feed the parking meter, so the rule became: every time it comes up, go top it up for the guest. His key observation: once hospitality is written into the system, it actually makes the team want to be hospitable more — because every time you see the look on a guest's face when they're taken care of, that feeling is addictive.

24:18 A crying baby on a plane is a hundred-dollar bill nobody picks up
Guidara gives an example he considers "criminal": flying across the US with a one-year-old is excruciating, and it happens every single day, yet no airline has ever done anything about it — never handed out earplugs to the surrounding passengers, never offered help to the parent trying to soothe the baby, and milk is always somehow unavailable. He says this is a pattern-recognition opportunity sitting right there, "a hundred-dollar bill on the ground you don't pick up." Jason then adds the mechanism: top leadership needs to give the budget, say $250 a month per flight attendant to spend at their discretion to do something for the guest — that way employees love their jobs and guests become loyal customers.

26:20 Hospitality shouldn't be an "extra," it should be standard
Guidara says the top not only has to give the budget for people to exceed expectations, it also has to create a culture where this is no longer treated as "exceeding expectations" but as normal. His analogy: when you buy a car, everyone assumes it comes with tires — nobody thinks of that as an extra service; phones now don't come with a charging brick, and that was someone deciding that step went too far. So why can't an airline decide "this flight just includes these things"? His conclusion: if you run a company, hospitality should be in the table stakes, not an option.

34:24 Refund a bag of dog food when the pet dies, win a customer for life
Guidara gives the Chewy example: dog food is an auto-subscription, and after a dog dies, the owner's first thought usually isn't to cancel — they only remember when the next bag arrives, which is cruel. You call Chewy to cancel and send the bag back, and the response is always the same: we can't take the food back, but we'll refund you, just donate it. Then within a day or two, flowers arrive at that home. Guidara's inference: this person will get another dog, and where they buy dog food goes without saying — and they'll never consider anywhere else. He calls this "pattern recognition, recurring moments, systematizing kindness."

53:31 Killing tipping requires a business good enough to absorb it
Guidara eliminated tipping at Eleven Madison Park. He says it was the most successful no-tipping implementation, but after he sold the restaurant it was reinstated, because the restaurant wasn't performing as well. His judgment: eliminating tipping requires you to run the business extremely well, otherwise it backfires. Two preconditions must hold — first, demand must be high enough that guests don't mind higher prices covering the absence of tips, because the public will still compare your chicken to another restaurant's chicken without adding in the tip they'd pay elsewhere; second, you must stay consistently full, because you're covering the team's tips, and one slow night means you eat the loss directly. His approach wasn't a service charge — he built service directly into the fixed tasting-menu price.

1:03:36 Commuter rail hides a minute of grace
Guidara shares a discovery he recently wrote up in his newsletter: commuter rail systems like Metro-North and Amtrak have a built-in "minute of grace" — the timetable says 11:45 departure, but it always actually leaves at 11:46, precisely to leave time for the person sprinting through the doors at the last second. He says he used to think sliding through the doors just in time was luck; once he knew it was deliberate design, he started looking for places to add a "minute of grace" in his own work with other companies. He treats it as a takeaway operating principle: where can you add a little more grace?

item.title: America's Wealthiest Aren't CEOs — They Own Car Washes and HVAC Companies
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-mastersinbiz-美国最富的一群人-不是ceo而是开洗车店和暖通公司的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-mastersinbiz-美国最富的一群人-不是ceo而是开洗车店和暖通公司的/
item.description: Three million private business owners in the US hold net worths above $5 million, and their combined wealth is more than ten times that of the Forbes 400 — they run car washes, HVAC companies and car dealerships, and they got rich by owning, not by earning a salary.
item.content:encoded:
Three million private business owners in the US hold net worths above $5 million, and their combined wealth is more than ten times that of the Forbes 400 — they run car washes, HVAC companies and car dealerships, and they got rich by owning, not by earning a salary.

The data comes from IRS and Treasury tax records, which are more granular than Fed surveys. The core conclusion: to reach the top 0.1%, you get there by owning a business, not by earning a high salary.

1:03 The IRS pulled them in to audit taxes and they accidentally built a wealth database
Both authors had just finished graduate school when they were recruited by the Treasury Department and the Office of Tax Analysis to solve a tax-policy puzzle: pass-through businesses don't pay tax themselves, so you have to link the business back to its individual owner to compute the tax burden. The project accidentally produced a panel database that tracks every business along with its owners and employees — far richer than the Fed's Survey of Consumer Finances, which is large in scale but nowhere near as granular as tax records.

3:08 Wealth isn't in Silicon Valley or Wall Street — the whole map lights up
The authors assumed wealth was concentrated in tech and finance, and the data overturned that bias. When they plotted the "everywhere millionaire" on a map, the entire country lit up. These wealthy people are spread across a large number of unsexy industries — car dealerships, HVAC, dental practices, restaurants, distribution, sanitation. It isn't only the Forbes 400 getting richer; it's millions of people.

4:08 Three million private business owners hold ten times the wealth of the Forbes 400
The authors counted roughly 3 million "everywhere millionaires" — private business owners with a net worth of at least $5 million. Their combined wealth is more than ten times the total of the Forbes 400. That number changes the inequality narrative: what drives inequality statistics isn't a few hundred billionaires but millions of unknown business owners.

8:10 The higher the income, the smaller the wage share and the bigger the business-income share
Break open the top 10% of earners: people at the 90th percentile live mainly on wages. But moving up the curve, the lines cross — by the top 0.1%, most income comes from business income. The authors say the main typical way to get rich in America is to own something, not to earn a wage. That is both a tax advantage (owning is taxed more lightly than earning a wage) and the actual path of wealth accumulation.

10:15 The 1986 tax reform turned pass-through from a disadvantage into an advantage
The 1986 tax reform (Reagan as president, Democrats controlling Congress, a bipartisan effort) lowered personal income tax rates below the corporate rate for the first time. Before that, pass-through was unattractive because of the tax disadvantage; after, being a pass-through became cheaper. Later Bush tax cuts lowered personal rates further, and the 2017 tax reform added a 20% deduction for certain pass-through categories. The result: more than half of business income is pass-through income, nearly half of employment is at pass-through businesses, and almost all small businesses are pass-throughs.

13:18 Half of the top 1%'s income growth came from pass-through
The authors ran a counterfactual: if you held fixed the importance of pass-through business income as it stood in 1985 (before the 1986 tax reform) and let it evolve as it was, roughly half of the top 1%'s income growth would disappear. Looking at wealth growth, from 1989 to the latest SCF data, two-thirds of the top 0.1%'s wealth growth came from private businesses. This shows pass-through is accounting-wise central to the growth of wealth and top-end income.

14:20 Entrepreneurship pays only about 10% more on average, but failure isn't the end
Using data tracking roughly 10 million entrepreneurship events since 2000, the authors found founders' average income is about 10% higher than similar workers who didn't start a business — and that's before counting unrealized capital gains from selling the business, and the average already includes a large number of failures. About 20% of founders are serial entrepreneurs — it takes a second or third venture to actually make yacht money. After a failure you can return to the labor market or start again and fix what went wrong last time.

19:27 Every congressional district has a millionaire business owner
The authors say "every congressional district has an everywhere millionaire." Unlike Silicon Valley and Wall Street, which are concentrated in specific geographies, almost every district has a car dealer. These business owners employ many people, pay a lot of sales tax and are prominent in their local communities, which gives them outsized influence — their approval ratings are higher than the military's, the Supreme Court's and Congress's. About a quarter of members of Congress are private business owners; add law-firm partners and that share can reach 40% to 50%. At the state and local level, because positions are part-time and low-paid, business owners make up an even larger share — mayors especially.

item.title: AI can now build a virus; the defense side is still stuck on sequence alignment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-latentspace-ai-能造出病毒了-防御方还停在序列比对/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-latentspace-ai-能造出病毒了-防御方还停在序列比对/
item.description: The models that generate pathogenic sequences and the models that tell whether a sequence is pathogenic are essentially the same models, so the teams doing design are best positioned to do defense — but the defense side is far behind, with a baseline still stuck at sequence matching.
item.content:encoded:
The models that generate pathogenic sequences and the models that tell whether a sequence is pathogenic are essentially the same models, so the teams doing design are best positioned to do defense — but the defense side is far behind, with a baseline still stuck at sequence matching.

High information density; the middle and later sections on the four layers of biodefense, the DNA synthesis pipeline, and "you can't patch a human" are the most valuable.

0:00 The teams doing design are best positioned to do defense
The dual mission Eric set for Radical Numerics is not a PR gesture but a technical judgment: the models that can generate pathogenic sequences and the models that can tell whether a sequence is pathogenic are essentially the same models. So the teams doing design are naturally best positioned to do defense, rather than outsourcing defense to a different group. He acknowledges there is an arms-race dynamic here, and that the defense side has always been far behind; what the company wants to do is pull the defense side up to the same level.

8:12 AI built the first genome from scratch
Evo's work generating CRISPR-Cas systems landed in Science, and Eric later gave a TED Talk. More important is what scientists showed last year: using a generative DNA model to generate the first genome from scratch. Humans had previously only been able to copy and paste fragments of known function, never build from scratch at the genome level. What Evo generated was a functional bacteriophage, that is, a virus. Eric calls this a turning point for the scientific community and the company — it means being able to build complete organisms that do not exist in nature, and with that, the corresponding potential for harm.

12:16 Omni's breakthrough came from alignment, not pretraining
Evo showed the potential of pretraining, but on human genetics it still lost to specialized DNA models, and the community questioned why you would use a large model at all. Omni's difference is mid-training and post-training: presenting tasks in the question-and-answer form scientists actually want, for example, given a wild-type and a mutant sequence, help me find the causal variant. Eric says this kind of form does not emerge naturally from pretraining. The results surprised them — Omni was not just competitive across many tasks the way Evo was, it began pushing the frontier in every subfield, especially variant effect prediction.

23:50 Most real disease variants sit in non-coding regions
Traditional bioinformatics tools and statistical methods mostly focus on coding regions, and coding regions make up only about 1.5% to 2% of the genome. Eric says many, perhaps most, diseases actually fall in non-coding regulatory regions, where variants are harder to judge as pathogenic or not. This is exactly where Omni is strong: it can distinguish pathogenic mutations in non-coding regions, especially long-range ones. This is precisely what geneticists who have long been unable to use traditional tools want.

45:44 The biology of the experiment is doing the filtering
The mechanism of the SOLEX experiment is worth remembering: generate a large number of random sequences, turn them into aptamer switches, and read them out at high throughput with NGS — the more binding, the more reads, the higher the fitness; then mutate the winning sequences again and iterate. This experiment explored on the order of 10 to the 11th power sequences in parallel. The key is that "the biology of the experiment is actually doing the filtering" — the wet lab does the filtering, and the model reproduces that process in silico. This paradigm can be generalized to any biological experiment of "progressive refinement," as long as you can capture the intermediate states.

58:15 Stanford scientists said generating DNA was a stupid idea
Eric spent six months at Stanford on the idea of Evo "generating DNA," and almost every scientist he talked to thought it was a stupid idea. The objections were specific: humans themselves do not understand the rules of DNA, so why expect AI to learn them; you cannot even tell whether the generation is correct, so how do you give the model feedback; DNA has too many repetitive sequences, too noisy a distribution, no real rules, all junk. He admits he was just stubborn, felt "it just feels right," but at the time could not say what the use case was. The first time they trained Evo, they had no idea whether it would work.

1:12:48 The four pillars of biodefense
They break biodefense into four layers: detection and surveillance (detecting pathogen sequences from environmental samples such as airport nasal swabs and wastewater systems), attribution (judging whether the source is natural, foreign, or engineered in some country's lab), countermeasures (making antivirals or antibacterials), and deterrence (at the government level). They focus on the first three. The core criticism is this: the existing biodefense community relies mainly on sequence matching — aligning sequences against databases of known pathogens. This does not stop two things: new things that are not in the database, and designs that have been deliberately obfuscated, that do not match in sequence space but have the same function.

1:25:15 You can't patch a human
The host points out the key difference between biosecurity and cybersecurity: in cybersecurity, a sufficiently strong model can in principle find every vulnerability and patch it, and as long as people keep updating, they are safe; but the genome is fixed, "you can't patch a human," so the defense surface is harder. Conversely there are two buffers: the intensity of motivation to launch an attack may be much lower, and the threshold from printing arbitrary DNA to building a successful virus — especially one that does not first kill the designer — is actually quite high.

item.title: Whose Homes Did His Roads Tear Down: Robert Moses's New York Legacy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-stuffmissed-他修的路拆了谁的房-罗伯特-摩西的纽约遗产/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-stuffmissed-他修的路拆了谁的房-罗伯特-摩西的纽约遗产/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Moses used federal Title I money to demolish 26 blocks, pushing the poor from one slum to another, yet claimed 98% of relocatees were better housed — his legacy remains unresolved to this day.
item.content:encoded:
Moses used federal Title I money to demolish 26 blocks, pushing the poor from one slum to another, yet claimed 98% of relocatees were better housed — his legacy remains unresolved to this day.

This episode has medium information density, but the second half — on how power operates, media manipulation, and the mechanics of urban renewal — is worth hearing; the first half can be fast-forwarded.

2:03 The more power, the less explanation required
After LaGuardia retired in 1946, William O'Dwyer appointed Moses as New York City Construction Coordinator, a position that gave him jurisdiction over every public construction project in the city and a direct line to Washington. By 1959, critics pointed out that he simultaneously held multiple government positions and his power was unchecked: consultant fees were not public, staff salaries were not public, trust meetings were held behind closed doors, and he could seize land at will. Reporter Bob Baum noted that private companies could do these things, but as part of a government entity, the public had a right to know. Moses was therefore often called the "Construction Czar" or "Urban Planning Czar."

3:07 Roads first, and whole neighborhoods paid the price
In 1948, Moses began building the Cross Bronx Expressway, a seven-mile road cutting through the already heavily developed Bronx. Dozens of apartment buildings were demolished, hundreds of families were displaced, and many streets were severed into dead ends. This community fragmentation was later cited as one reason for rising local crime rates. Those affected were mostly the least resourced, predominantly non-white communities. In a 1945 Atlantic Monthly article, Moses wrote that arterial improvements were "not merely a strip of pavement laid in a gasoline ditch, but a real improvement of the entire area," and he genuinely believed he was making the best choices for New York, but his methods were often ruthless.

7:12 26 brochures, one act of visual persuasion
In 1949, Congress passed the American Housing Act Title I, providing $1 billion in loans and $100 million in annual grants for slum clearance. Moses realized New York could get a large share of federal money, so in the 1950s he had his team produce 26 brochures, each targeting a neighborhood he thought needed redevelopment. The brochures contained problem descriptions, photographs, and statistics, and were sent to the New York City Board of Estimate, the City Planning Commission, the Title I federal administrator, and the Housing and Home Finance Agency. In 2014, researcher Temis Kronopoulos analyzed the photographs and found: vacant lots were shown 22 times, the most common image of urban decay; 20 photos showed back-alley garbage and clotheslines; almost no people appeared in the photos. Kronopoulos wrote: "In this context, slum clearance was also a tool of social engineering."

10:18 Media praise first, scandal exposed later
On June 29, 1959, New York Times reporter Wayne Phillips began publishing a four-part series exposing problems in Moses's Title I slum clearance projects: associations with people he shouldn't have been involved with, unregulated funds, and information not shared. But as early as June 14, columns by George Sokolski began appearing in newspapers nationwide, distributed by King Features Syndicate, with titles like "Robert Moses Is a Selfless Man" and nearly identical content praising him for "constantly building and beautifying, his work never touched by corruption." These articles appeared two weeks before the New York Times critical series. Looking back, Sokolski appears to have been asked to preemptively cover for the coming scandal.

13:22 Mayor's ban and a public tantrum
After the scandal broke, Mayor Wagner did two things: first, he investigated Louis Pokras's role in a Harlem slum clearance project, and because Pokras had organized crime connections, Wagner publicly stated he would never allow him to sponsor any New York development project; second, he banned the city from working with Moses's favored architect Melvin E. Kessler, whose earlier Upper West Side redevelopment involved developer Manhattan Town Incorporated taking Title I funds but building no buildings and demolishing none, just collecting rents while the buildings decayed. Moses publicly responded that the mayor's "devastating charges and misstatements" scared off venture capital, and said "Title I is a dead duck." Other officials said Title I would continue and praised Moses. In media coverage, Moses looked like he was throwing a public tantrum.

15:26 "Moses Must Go": an open letter
In December 1959, the Metropolitan Housing Council began distributing leaflets in New York addressed to Mayor Robert Wagner. At the top, in bold, it read: "For New York's development, Moses must go." The leaflet listed ongoing problems with slum clearance projects: tenants were sold along with the land; indecent relocation practices continued; luxury housing was built at the people's expense while those who needed housing most were pushed from one slum to another; and as former rent administrator Charles Abrams pointed out, slum clearance had become "Negro and Puerto Rican removal." The leaflet demanded: more low-rent housing, an end to subsidizing luxury housing, and building new housing before demolishing old. It compared the situation to cancer and repeated: "Moses must go."

21:32 Fire Island showdown: Rockefeller accepts the resignation
In 1962, Moses clashed with New York Governor Nelson Rockefeller over a Fire Island road plan. Moses wanted to build a road spanning the entire island, and after a 1962 storm destroyed most houses, he thought his chance had come. But environmental groups and islanders opposed it, and residents proposed an alternative: making Fire Island a national seashore, which gained federal support. Public pressure gave the governor an opportunity to halt the road project and suggest Moses reduce his government roles to focus on the 1964 World's Fair. Moses submitted his resignation; he had previously threatened resignation with other governors, but they always refused because many public projects would collapse without him. Rockefeller accepted, triggering a media storm. Moses claimed the governor had demanded he immediately resign as chairman of the State Parks Commission so his brother Lawrence could take over; Rockefeller said a transition had been discussed for over a year.

26:38 World's Fair: 50 million vs. projected 70 million
The 1964 New York World's Fair drew about 50 million visitors, but Moses had projected 70 million. The New York Times reported that only 85% of the grounds were ready at opening, 15 of 139 pavilions were unfinished, and many completed pavilions had no exhibits. Some exhibitors arrived with nowhere to put their displays. A fair spokesman told the media that seeing all the other options would take over a week, and the unfinished pavilions would be completed before then. Some attractions were finished within weeks of opening; others were abandoned entirely. After the fair, Moses was no longer New York City Construction Coordinator. In September 1966, his wife Mary died after a long illness, and less than a month later Moses remarried Mary Grady, who worked as a secretary at the Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority. In 1968, Rockefeller merged Triborough into another transportation agency and removed Moses, his last New York government position.

item.title: The quantum scheme Google hid was overtaken by a group of amateur researchers
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-zeroknowledge-google-藏起来的量子方案-被一群业余研究者反超了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-zeroknowledge-google-藏起来的量子方案-被一群业余研究者反超了/
item.description: Google used a zero-knowledge proof to show it had found a more resource-efficient quantum attack, but wouldn't publish the circuit. Yukon turned the problem into an open competition, letting agents build on other people's submissions — and ended up beating Google's result by more than 60%.
item.content:encoded:
Google used a zero-knowledge proof to show it had found a more resource-efficient quantum attack, but wouldn't publish the circuit. Yukon turned the problem into an open competition, letting agents build on other people's submissions — and ended up beating Google's result by more than 60%.

High information density: it explains the mechanics of automated research competitions, the verifier design, and several real breakthrough cases. Worth a listen for anyone following AI for science, ZK and open innovation.

4:07 Google gave only the proof, not the circuit
Google published a paper claiming it had found a quantum scheme more resource-efficient than the previous state of the art for breaking the secp256k1 elliptic curve — the basis of Bitcoin's and Ethereum's public-key cryptography. But Google did not publish the scheme; it used a zero-knowledge proof to demonstrate that it did in fact possess such a scheme. Soubhik points out the consequence: if you want to prepare for Q-day, you have to know what schemes will appear, how to harden your systems, what the defences are; if you don't understand any of that, you are not prepared for Q-day. Not publishing the quantum circuit is the main consequence here.

8:08 The competition isn't everyone for themselves, it's a relay
The way you take part in ecdsa.fail is not to do the work locally and then submit. The platform's backend runs the same verifier Google used; through a command-line interface you have your agent read the competition details and other people's submissions, then build directly on top of someone else's scheme. Soubhik says this is how research actually works: you build on each other's experience, not like an Olympic event where everyone submits independently. Anna says she had assumed it was PvP, everyone finishing on their own machine and then submitting to compete; Soubhik confirms it isn't. This multi-user automated research framework produced enormous acceleration, because you don't have to rediscover everything yourself.

11:08 Three breakthroughs: externalising, mining, starting over
Soubhik sees three big breakthroughs. The first was externalising the environment and letting people outside the company take part — one team member who wasn't in the internal testing spent roughly $5,000 on a codex subscription the day before internal testing and made a huge leap the lead engineer couldn't understand. The second was mining French's work, building on it, and surpassing Google's result within two weeks. After that the chart was almost a plateau for two months. The third came in mid-August: Teddy, from Starkware, went back to the starting point of the competition, summarised all the techniques into a knowledge review, and then built from scratch rather than on other people's ideas, ultimately proposing the NSD ping-pong technique, which pushed the scheme from 49% better than Google to 57% better, and now past 60%.

27:15 If the question isn't asked right, you can't run a competition
Soubhik says many problems are posed incorrectly — that is, badly formulated. He gives the example: ‘Build me a quantum computer’ — that problem is too big, we don't know what it is. But if you break it down, you find that the problem state of ecdsa.fail is one of its subproblems. You need to split the big problem into a series of well-formulated subtasks, then run automated research on each subtask. Another example is the proximity gap conjecture: EF committed a $1 million prize, but the original statement is binary — you either prove it or you don't — and it's hard to write a verifier for it. Later Alexander Hicks and Gako wrote a simple verifier for one specific instance of the conjecture, and only then did it become the better.codes competition.

39:15 An algebraic geometer broke 64 bits in a few hours
better.codes has two bounds: the lower bound is the soundness bound, the upper bound is the attack bound. The lower bound had been stuck at the Johnson bound for years. On 21 August the competition was stuck at 63.99 bits, and 64 bits is the Johnson bound for this specific instance. Then there was no progress for 6 days; the chart was a straight line. Until 28 August, when the team contacted Bartosz from ECDSA — a Polish mathematician specialising in algebraic geometry, not a cryptographer at all, who had never heard of the problem. Within a few hours of joining he pushed the result from 63.99 to 64.0101 bits, breaking the Johnson bound for the first time. The technique he used was some combination of algebraic geometry, because he was already using his own codex subscription to do algebraic geometry work, and probably applied algebraic geometry methods to this problem.

41:15 One breakthrough set off a 30-year open problem
After Bartosz broke 64.01 bits, the whole circle erupted, with Ariel Gabizon, Kobi and others discussing it on Twitter. The story didn't end there: a few days later, some cryptographers had a bigger problem in coding theory that had been open for 30 years — proving a certain soundness bound. Within days three papers appeared claiming inspiration from the method used to break the Johnson bound. Soubhik says nobody could have predicted this; this is open innovation and collaborative research, and it still looks very early-stage: people are starting to realise that problems they thought couldn't be solved for a long time can at least be pushed forward, improved.

45:18 Domain experts point the agents the way on GitHub
On the hish tiling problem, Yukon piloted a discussion-format feature. The whole process is in the CLI; you don't even need to think or prompt your agent. While the agent does research it searches for information in the hills, formulates strategies locally, and uploads discussions to a GitHub forum. Other agents read those discussions, and domain experts like Bartosz answer by hand, and the agents read those answers — so the domain experts are effectively steering the automated research network. Soubhik says this is exactly what they want to achieve: a domain expert should be able to see where the automated research network has got to on his problem statement, then use his best intuition to steer it and leave clues about what to explore.

52:20 Yukon wants to be an AI-native research institution
Soubhik says Yukon's vision is to grow into an AI-based research institution, imitating three features of traditional research institutions: research means building at a higher level on each other's ideas; the originators of ideas must be credited; and even failed ideas should be recognised, because one success may come out of a thousand failures. What AI changes is that the whole research lifecycle accelerates from months or years to days. They are implementing a partial credit system that lets people give each other credit for ideas, including negative credit — failed ideas also earn credit. They also want a system that helps you decompose a badly formulated problem into a series of well-formulated subproblems.

item.title: Information Has Never Been More Plentiful, and We Choose Not to Know
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-iq2-信息从未如此充裕-我们却选择不知道/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-iq2-信息从未如此充裕-我们却选择不知道/
item.description: Lyse Doucet has reported from war zones for forty years, and her judgment is this: not knowing is not because there isn't enough information, but because we don't want to know. And this Iran war is a war of choice, and it has made everything worse.
item.content:encoded:
Lyse Doucet has reported from war zones for forty years, and her judgment is this: not knowing is not because there isn't enough information, but because we don't want to know. And this Iran war is a war of choice, and it has made everything worse.

The first half is instant judgment on Iran and Hormuz; the second half is a rare post-mortem on whether twenty years of intervention in Afghanistan was worth it. High information density, but it demands patience.

3:13 Not knowing is because we don't want to know
Doucet calls this "a really jarring time": information has never been more plentiful, but "If we don't know about something, it's because we don't want to know about something. We choose not to know." She traces the cause to being bombarded every day by statements from the American president — yesterday it was "we don't need guardrails on AI," even though some of the leading founders of AI are asking for regulation; today it's rolling back some environmental regulations. She reminds us: a president who said he wouldn't get into "forever wars" still ended up leading the country into these wars.

5:15 This is a war of choice, and it keeps getting worse
Doucet rarely offers a personal judgment: this war has put her under great strain, because it is "a war of choice" rather than "a war of necessity," and "it just seems to have made everything worse in every way." She acknowledges that the US and Israel together have done enormous damage to Iran's military and navy, and that Iran's economy is suffering, but strategically "this is a war where President Trump doesn't know how to end it." Iran has not collapsed, the regime is harder than before, the promises made to the demonstrators have not been kept, and their lives have gotten worse instead.

6:16 Daily market life under 82% inflation
Doucet uses inflation to illustrate Iran's predicament: Britons worry about single-digit inflation, "Oh, 4%, oh my God, it's 5%," while Iran is at 82%. She quotes an Iranian woman: I come to the market every day just to watch the prices go up, that's how I pass the time. She then places Iran alongside Ukraine — both are "war of choice" and miscalculation; Trump thought he could drive straight through Iran, Putin thought he could drive straight through Ukraine, and both found that people's resistance is both creative and determined.

8:16 Iran has weaponized Hormuz
Doucet gives the specific mechanism: the Houthis control the western shore of the Red Sea and the islands in between, claiming they don't affect maritime traffic, but the war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, which had been de-escalating, has reignited; oil has risen past $108 a barrel; the Strait of Hormuz is completely frozen. The Iranians will not let go — they don't treat it merely as a bargaining chip but as a long-term chip. "They've weaponized the Strait of Hormuz." She points out that Trump repeatedly says "I didn't expect them to do this," but anyone who has done war-gaming will tell you the games always quickly move toward Iran controlling Hormuz.

40:12 A "traditional Afghanistan" denied by exiles
When the Taliban required Afghan women to wear a burqa that leaves only the eyes exposed, Afghan women abroad pushed back, saying this is not traditional Afghanistan. Doucet points out that the burqa is locally called a chadili, with an embroidered mesh; but in the same period women were also being educated at Kabul University. While writing her book she dug out a large number of old photographs and decided she had to tell this history well, so she tracked down a person living in the United States — whose first reaction was "the Intercontinental Hotel, I love that hotel." Their first call lasted four hours, and the person drew the hotel's ground-floor plan from memory, pointing out which room belonged to the German wife of the mayor of Kabul and which to an Indian.

41:12 Four hours of oral history, six months of silence
The second call lasted three hours, and then the person disappeared for about six months. The reason lay in Afghanistan's political upheavals: in '73 the kingdom was ended by the first coup, and hotel employees were taken away for questioning — "Why do you work for an American hotel? Are you working for the CIA?" In '78 came the communist coup, people were thrown into prison, and she could only flee. Happy memories thus turned up sadness and pain. In the end Doucet called to ask for permission, and the person said: I can't appear in your book, it's too sad and too painful for me. Doucet's conclusion: a person writing a book can only get up the next day and find someone else to tell the story, and it will never be told as well.

1:03:14 Two trillion dollars bought a generation that knows its rights
Faced with the challenge of "what was it all for," Doucet acknowledges that both sides made mistakes, that this should be a humbling lesson for all NATO allies, and that there will be a formal reckoning in the future. But she insists it was not all for nothing: twenty years of international involvement created the space for the most educated and most connected generation in Afghanistan's history to grow up. She quotes Malala Yousafzai — even reading a book is an act of resistance — and says these girls know their rights, know that Islam gave them the right to education, know that girls around the world go to school while they cannot. "Not enough, but not zero."

1:14:42 The difference between hope and optimism is agency
Doucet says she could never quite distinguish hope from optimism until she read Gordon Brown's "The Future Starts With Us": optimism is wishful thinking, whereas hope is different because hope carries agency — you don't just make a wish, you actually work to bring it about. She says she doesn't have the privilege of "not needing to have hope"; the agency she has is fighting for an Afghan visa, listening to stories there, and telling those stories as well as she can; and everyone has their own bit of agency — some donate money, some help girls take online classes, some teach girls in Africa, some help South Sudan and Nicaragua, and some help struggling areas in Britain itself.

item.title: Russia Won't Invade NATO, but It Is Testing Whether NATO Holds Together
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-goodfight-俄罗斯不会入侵北约-但正在测试它会不会散架/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-goodfight-俄罗斯不会入侵北约-但正在测试它会不会散架/
item.description: Russia has no capacity for a ground offensive; its real goal is to corrode NATO's political cohesion — using drones, parcel bombs and grey zones to force the US to expose its divisions in a crisis.
item.content:encoded:
Russia has no capacity for a ground offensive; its real goal is to corrode NATO's political cohesion — using drones, parcel bombs and grey zones to force the US to expose its divisions in a crisis.

The first half, on Russian hybrid warfare and NATO cohesion, is very dense; the Middle East section in the second half is relatively diffuse, but the detail about Houthis using Claude to improve their missiles is worth hearing.

4:30 No ground-invasion risk, but hybrid escalation is rising
Joshi says it plainly: there is no risk of a Russian conventional ground offensive against NATO, this is not the kind of alarm it was in January 2022. The entire security apparatus of Estonia and Finland exists to detect exactly that kind of movement, and every port, naval base and forest route in western Russia is saturated with intelligence and technical sensors. But another risk is rising: Russia's tolerance for hybrid operations below the Article V threshold is increasing. They have already used drones against Ukrainian cargo planes that might be carrying supplies to Ukraine, put explosives in DHL parcels in Leipzig, and sabotaged power plants and railways across Europe. The question is: would they actually fire missiles at Polish facilities? Joshi thinks Russia is still quite cautious and wants to avoid dragging NATO into a broader conflict, but that debate is not settled in Europe.

10:15 Poland is sounding the loudest alarm; the Baltics say things are fine
The most alarming signal this week came from Poland. Tusk said intelligence indicated Russia might attack Poland and other NATO allies — not a conventional ground attack, but drones and missiles landing on NATO territory that Russia could portray as accidents. But Latvia's leadership, including the defence minister and the president, said there is no reason to panic and no elevated operational risk. Estonia also said it sees no risk of Russia aggressing in that way. Joshi says he has spoken to intelligence officials in multiple countries and there is no reason to fear a ground offensive. The disagreement is itself the information: Poland is raising the alarm, the Baltic states are cooling things down, and Russia is watching who believes whom.

14:20 Russia's real goal is to corrode NATO cohesion
Joshi lays out Russia's political objective: not to conquer NATO territory or occupy Western Europe, but to weaken and break apart NATO's unity. The mechanism works like this: if a drone lands on Polish territory and blows up a warehouse, Russia says it was an accident, and then Trump says ‘I talked to Putin and he assured me it was an accident’ — and that lays the alliance's internal divisions bare. Under the Biden administration, Jake Sullivan would call the Russians and say that if this continues you are risking us joining the war on Ukraine's side, and we will retaliate. But under a Trump administration, does Russia really believe Trump would step into a crisis the same way? So Russia has an opportunity not only to push back against attacks on Russia, but to test NATO's cohesion and its boundaries.

19:40 On Ukraine, Trump criticises in public and supplies intelligence in private
Joshi says Trump's support for Ukraine is quite limited, far below the Biden era. The US has effectively let weapons aid lapse; Ukraine desperately needs Patriot interceptor missiles, but the US has used up so much on the Iran war that it has given Ukraine almost no interceptors recently. Diplomatically, the administration leans toward Russia and expects Ukraine to make concessions. But there are two exceptions: first, the new Graham bill, which the president has agreed to, would impose new sanctions on Russian entities and force Trump to levy tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil and do not reduce their purchases — in practice China and India, and possibly Central European countries. Second, Trump is quietly, not publicly, providing intelligence to Ukraine to help it strike Russian energy facilities. That is the strange reversal: Trump criticises Ukraine overall, but secret assistance is still happening.

26:10 The Strait of Hormuz is still half-closed
The Trump administration insists this is not a war; Trump calls it an ‘excursion’. But the Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed, and oil traffic is far below pre-war levels. There is no deal with Iran, no resolution. Iran's nuclear programme has no formal limits, and there is no formal commitment to reopen Hormuz. Trump faces the midterms in a month and desperately needs to avoid a sharp escalation of the war that would send oil prices soaring. But politically he cannot make the concessions to Iran that a deal would require, because that would be too humiliating, too obviously equivalent to defeat, and would look catastrophic before an election. So it is a stalemate: Iran has considerable control over the strait, with occasional clashes — the US bombs Iranian coastal missile bases, Iran strikes tankers trying to pass through Hormuz.

31:45 Houthis used Claude to improve their ballistic missiles
Joshi tells a striking detail: when Anthropic published its report on harmful uses of Claude, one of the examples was Houthis using Claude to improve their ballistic missile programme. This group, widely seen as technologically primitive, is using the most advanced AI on Earth to improve the guidance systems of the ballistic missiles they fire at shipping in the Middle East. Mounk adds that being able — at least until being cut off — to access the most advanced American technology to strike America and America's allies is itself a fascinating story. This connects the Ukraine and Russia discussion to the Houthi discussion: in modern war, defensive capability dominates on the ground, but offensive capability dominates in the air.

38:20 Perception is the primary problem on the battlefield
Joshi offers a unifying framework for why ground defence dominates while air strikes still work: it is all about perception. To hit something, you first need to perceive it — find it on the battlefield, and then fire at it. That is much harder than it sounds. Perception is the primary problem on the battlefield; actually firing is secondary. On the Ukrainian front line, this is a sensor-saturated environment: small drones everywhere, thermal cameras detecting movement at night, radar penetrating foliage, satellites targeting the area. Anything that moves gets hit — it is a kill zone. But you cannot perceive everywhere equally easily. Drones can see ten kilometres behind the battlefield, but fifty kilometres back, satellite coverage is patchy. It is like the fog of war in a real-time strategy game — you send units out and the fog rolls back, but where you have not been remains fog. That is why Iran can still launch ballistic missiles, and why Houthis can fire from the mountains of Yemen into the Red Sea.

item.title: The young are useful to society as heretics, not as good citizens
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-a16z-年轻人对社会的用处是当异端-不是当好公民/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-a16z-年轻人对社会的用处是当异端-不是当好公民/
item.description: Universities train young people to be good citizens, but what society actually needs is for them to question what everyone takes for granted; in the AI era every student can build their own projects — all they lack is permission.
item.content:encoded:
Universities train young people to be good citizens, but what society actually needs is for them to question what everyone takes for granted; in the AI era every student can build their own projects — all they lack is permission.

Medium information density, but Amjad's path from chess to training models to building new Replit products is very concrete, and useful for judging whether young people should start companies now.

4:07 The young are useful as heretics
Amjad uses the sci-fi novel The City and the Stars as an analogy: in that city governed by an AGI, everyone is repeatedly reborn from compressed memories, until the machine breaks down and a genuinely new person is born, who immediately starts asking ‘what is outside the walls’. Amjad says the use of young people is to ask exactly this kind of question, to be heretics. But today's universities do the opposite — they tell you ‘we have already figured everything out, just learn our way’, and train you into a good citizen: marry, have kids, buy a house, buy a car. The problem is that world no longer exists; you can perform brilliantly in college and still end up unemployed with a pile of debt.

5:11 Silicon Valley is itself a monoculture
Amjad says every society has blind spots, and Silicon Valley has many too — it is a monoculture with a fixed way of thinking, so many ideas simply will not grow out of Silicon Valley. Even the most radical culture is, at bottom, a monoculture. So you need young people to experiment, to attempt what is considered impossible, and occasionally someone breaks through: impossible yesterday, suddenly possible today because the technology changed. What universities should do is gather people with clear minds and first-principles thinking, and encourage them to question what is deeply believed.

15:33 Raising at 18 is an overused option
Gagan says young people today face a wildly unfair binary: either go to a four-year university and be governed by attendance, homework, exams and grades, or tomorrow someone hands you $50,000 to start a company. He thinks the investor path should be used far less, and only a very small number of teenagers should raise money. Most people at 17 or 18 know they want to enter the business world, but having two years to explore and learn without pressure is precious. He argues for a middle ground: two years to explore freely, with Silicon Valley actively sending information and resources your way, and more support if you have a good idea.
