17:35 Starting too early is premature optimization
Amjad borrows the programming phrase ‘premature optimization is the root of all evil’: a lot of founding is premature optimization. He sees many kids now inside a circle where friends are raising big rounds and some have become unicorns, so the motive becomes a negative one like envy, and then they pre-commit to an idea they are not even interested in, optimizing early for a path they have not yet reached. He says the real question is what your curiosity is driving you toward; once you find the idea you are willing to spend ten years, a lifetime on, it has enormous gravity and you cannot dodge it — he himself actively did not want to start a company, but the thing blew up into one on its own. He also says VCs now go to Stanford and give students a million dollars with no idea yet, so there is already a cap table before anything is built — a bit like the music industry signing young artists.

20:43 From chess all the way to training models
Amjad says he has always oscillated between ‘wanting to build things’ and ‘wanting to read and explore widely’, the two feeding each other in a recursive process. He gives his recent obsession with chess as an example: he started playing very late, does not know why he was interested, then started writing programs to solve chess and training models, and found that LLMs are terrible at chess and hallucinate moves that do not exist. To figure it out, he — who had never trained a model — spent a lot of time studying how to train one. He realized from this that AI can now do machine learning itself, just as in 2024 Replit's agent suddenly learned to write code and afterward coding changed completely; machine learning may be at that same moment — he calls it vibe research or auto research. He is now building products at Replit to let anyone become a machine learning researcher, or let a boss with data fine-tune a model to solve a specific problem.

23:46 Companies will become self-driving organizations
Amjad thinks the shape of companies will change. Silicon Valley has tried many experiments to remake companies — Holacracy, Medium tried it, GitHub tried a no-manager system, and all failed spectacularly, but he thinks that was a technology problem: now you can let agents act as the glue in an organization, turn bureaucratic processes into invisible things machines do in the background, give people real autonomy to work on what interests them most, and let AI judge your impact. He says he has already changed how management works at Replit, calls it a ‘self-driving company’, and that ultimately the company will run itself. He admits he does not have a fully formed idea, but is certain everything will change, and much faster than you think; if you do not natively understand this stuff, the transition will be hard.

28:51 Trust makes money land six weeks faster
Gagan says he volunteers in local politics in his spare time, and the biggest takeaway is understanding how valuable trust is. He gives a concrete comparison: in a nonprofit, after a donor verbally commits $50,000 to you, the probability that the money actually lands in your account is only about 20% to 50%; in Silicon Valley, that probability is about 75% to 100%. The difference is that if you are certain the money is coming, you can confidently push forward, and by the time the check actually arrives you have already advanced six weeks, which makes the check worth even more. Conversely, without trust you change your approach for fear of upsetting the donor, drift from your mission, and are left with only anxiety and stress. He thinks this can be transplanted to schools: trust students to do what they want to do.

32:01 No grades means no fulcrum to push against
Asked how to handle disruptive students — like Zuckerberg, who nearly got expelled for FaceMash — Gagan says there must of course be red lines, rules for things like sexual harassment and publicly humiliating others, and you need to build trust and a positive-sum atmosphere. But he says one core principle of the academy bypasses the problem entirely: with no grades and no exams, the resistance students have to push against is already far smaller. So if you want to build FaceMash, go build it, and he is willing to defend that right even if he personally finds the idea weird and does not like it. He thinks that as long as you create an environment of trust and keep students from developing an anti-authority mindset, you unlock a huge amount of creativity and opportunity. Amjad adds that this drive to test boundaries can be channeled in healthy directions: kids who learn to code and hack on Roblox — rather than sending them to prison, make it a sandbox, discover the talent, and steer it toward cybersecurity jobs or even into government.

item.title: Jensen Huang: Saying There's a 10% Chance AI Destroys Humanity Is Irresponsible
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-ezra-黄仁勋-说-ai-有-10-概率毁灭人类是不负责任的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-ezra-黄仁勋-说-ai-有-10-概率毁灭人类是不负责任的/
item.description: He concedes AI will change every job, but treats the risk of losing control as a solvable engineering problem: if a lab truly believed it was losing control, the right answer is not to ship, not to buy the most compute while asking to be slowed down.
item.content:encoded:
He concedes AI will change every job, but treats the risk of losing control as a solvable engineering problem: if a lab truly believed it was losing control, the right answer is not to ship, not to buy the most compute while asking to be slowed down.

Huang rarely engages the AI doomer case head-on; here he gives concrete positions on alignment, evals and the compute split, and concedes the cycle will eventually turn. The unit economics in the back half are worth more than the front half.

6:28 Reading scans got automated, and there are more radiologists
Huang uses radiology as his core case: over the past decade computer vision reached superhuman levels, AI has seeped into every radiology application, able to detect any abnormality and any disease. But reading scans is a task a radiologist does, not the purpose of the job — the purpose is to diagnose disease and help patients. Once reading is automated, doctors can handle more cases, hospital revenue rises, and more radiologists are needed. From this he draws the distinction between the purpose of a job and the tasks of a job.

9:32 For jobs like customer service, the task is the job
Huang concedes AI will change every job and automate a great many tasks, and he names one category that gets replaced wholesale: when the job and the task are one and the same, as with phone customer service, the job is the task. But he offers counter-evidence too: AI only became genuinely useful in the past six months, after 15 years of getting it to run at all, and in those six months $500 billion of venture capital went into AI-native companies.

22:01 Data from 26,000 Chinese students: homework faster, exams down
Ezra cites a study from China: 26,000 students in grades 7 through 12, with staggered AI adoption. Homework scores rose 18% and completion time fell 30%, but within six months monthly exam scores fell 20% and high-stakes entrance exam scores fell 18% to 24%, with the full penalty showing up about two years later. Huang's response: he agrees completely with that last part, just as nobody does long division anymore and the multiplication table is being forgotten, but he doesn't think it matters — ‘we'll discover new skills, just maybe not those.’

35:28 Cheating isn't malice, it's the cheapest path in compute
Huang unpacks the Hugging Face agent attack: software given an objective function optimizes toward the objective, that's just what the algorithm does. If you tell software ‘get a perfect score on this test,’ the most obvious move is to go find the answers; if it can't do that at all, the second most obvious move is to figure out who the smartest kid in class is and copy off him. Only the third approach is to decompose the problem, go learn the material, and grind it out — that consumes the most compute and the most energy, so unless you align it and tell it that's how it must solve the problem, software takes the most obvious path.

40:48 A company with agency can't say it needs saving
Ezra relays the labs' public position: they face a hybrid problem of engineering, alignment and operational excellence, and competition with each other and with China is pushing them too fast, so they feel they are losing control of what they're building and want outside help to slow down. Huang rejects the frame: these are companies with agency, CEOs with agency, and they're using that agency to say ‘we need help.’ His analogy: if a car company believed it was about to ship an unsafe product, it has the ability, the power and the responsibility not to ship it — and it already has the incentive not to.

59:49 Hinton's prediction has no scientific basis
Ezra brings up Jeffrey Hinton saying a 10% chance of societal destruction is not unreasonable; Huang answers directly: I'd tell Jeff that saying that is irresponsible, his predictions have consistently been wrong, and that 10% isn't grounded in science or in research — ‘just because it comes from a scientist doesn't make it science.’ He then brings up the old score: the advice that nobody should go into radiology, the claim that deep learning would surpass radiologists within five years, which didn't happen; if that scares young people out of college because they think they won't find work, that's harmful.

1:17:30 The R&D split has to flip from 80/20
Huang gives a concrete ratio: at NVIDIA roughly 10% to 20% of people do design and 80% do verification, while most labs today are understandably 80% on capability and 20% on safety, verification and evals. That ratio will flip, he says, and that's the transition he means. He asks labs not to ship him anything unevaluated: don't send NVIDIA any product that hasn't been evaluated with a human in the loop. Safety, alignment, evals, guardrails, sandboxes, containment, monitoring, telemetry, external AI monitoring — all of it is AI technology, he argues, and should be accelerated as hard as possible.

1:24:48 The math on a one-gigawatt AI factory
Huang gives the unit economics of the new computing era: building a one-gigawatt data center, a one-gigawatt AI factory, costs $50 billion, and it can be rented out for $40 to $50 billion a year. He describes the shift from retrieval based computing (retrieving files, hence data center) to generative computing, with compute per user rising sharply; add agents also using generative AI, and it isn't just a billion people using computers but hundreds of billions of agents plus people, with compute demand potentially rising a billionfold.

item.title: The UK Productivity Crisis Was a Statistical Error: 0.7% Became 1.3%
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-moreorless-英国生产率危机是统计错误-0-7-被改成-1-3/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-moreorless-英国生产率危机是统计错误-0-7-被改成-1-3/
item.description: Fifteen years of Britain being cast as the worst-performing developed economy on productivity may just be the ONS miscounting hours worked — treating people on holiday as if they worked 40 hours, inflating the denominator and pushing productivity down.
item.content:encoded:
Fifteen years of Britain being cast as the worst-performing developed economy on productivity may just be the ONS miscounting hours worked — treating people on holiday as if they worked 40 hours, inflating the denominator and pushing productivity down.

Medium information density, but the UK productivity revision alone is enough to change your read on the "British disease"; the other three segments are routine fact-checks you can take or leave.

1:05 The UK productivity crisis was a calculation
After the financial crisis, UK productivity growth was estimated at 0.7% a year, the worst among advanced economies, and it became the raw material for fifteen years of the "productivity puzzle." After the ONS changed how it measures hours worked, that number became 1.3%, nearly double. Output and GDP did not change; only the denominator did: Britons actually work far fewer hours than previously thought. Chris Giles says pre-crisis growth was 2%, and 2% means productivity doubles roughly every 35 years, while 0.7% means it takes a century to double; 1.3% falls in between. Britain is no longer an international outlier, but growth is still below its pre-crisis level.

4:16 Asking people how many hours they work cannot be trusted
The old method simply asked respondents how many hours they worked in a week and took the answer at face value. The problem was in follow-ups: if no one answered the door in August, the ONS carried over the 40 hours that person had reported three months earlier and plugged in a 40 — even though that person was probably on holiday and had not worked a single hour. The OECD recommended back in 2018 that countries stop doing this; the UK took eight years to change. Giles says that during those eight years people wrote a batch of "UK productivity crisis" articles that no longer hold up. He admits this is maddening, but the change is in the right direction.

11:38 One in ten Irish people as clergy is a misreading
The book said that in the 1960s one in every ten Irish children became a nun, priest or Christian Brother. The 1961 census showed 18,854 Catholic clergy and nuns, 2,125 Christian Brothers and other religious brothers, and 4,842 seminarians — 25,821 in total, or 1/104 of the population. The 1951 ratio was 1/127. The original source is research by Mary Daly, who looked only at students sitting the 1966 leaving certificate exam; at the time fewer than 20% of the school-age population sat that exam, about 12,000 people, of whom roughly one in ten entered religious life. That qualifier was lost in retelling and became "all children." The author has said subsequent editions will be corrected.

14:41 Grid queue numbers are inflated by applications
Between November 2024 and June 2025, cumulative electricity demand in the UK grid connection queue jumped from about 41 GW to 125 GW, tripling in six months, with data centres accounting for 73 GW. But queuing is cheap, like booking a table at a popular restaurant months ahead; many projects will never actually be built or will shrink. Ofgem estimates that if all this data centre demand materialised, the cost would be close to £700bn, nearly a quarter of UK annual GDP. A 2025 government report projected 6 GW would be needed by 2030, while another queue analysis reckoned about 20 GW has serious financial backing behind it. Johnny Gowdy of Regen says no one knows how much will ultimately be built.

17:45 The data centre emissions comparison counts only direct emissions
Foxglove's analysis said two planned data centres at full load would emit more carbon than ExxonMobil's UK operations. That comparison counts only ExxonMobil's own operational emissions, excluding the petrol and diesel it sells — which is the main source of emissions, something an ordinary reader may not spot. Foxglove also assumed the data centres run at 100% power year-round, while a scholar studying AI's carbon footprint used 65%. More important is the power source: the planning documents for these two projects say that initially, because they cannot connect to the grid, they will use on-site gas generation. The UK grid as a whole gets about half its power from renewables and only 30% from gas, so these data centres amount to stimulating demand for higher-carbon generation.

23:00 Vinyl's physical limits mattered less, not more
The 1950s story goes: the closer a record gets to the centre, the lower the linear speed, and the less bass and brightness a groove can hold, so you put the quiet song at the end of a side. Mitchell Sterling's database has 2,284 albums and 27,000 songs spanning 1953 to the present. Measured by relative loudness, before 1982 closing tracks averaged about 0.65 dB quieter than earlier tracks; after 1982, when cassette sales overtook vinyl in the US and the constraint disappeared, the gap widened to about 1.5 dB. In the streaming era after 2010, the gap is still twice what it was in the vinyl era. In other words, the less the physical limit mattered, the quieter closing tracks became.

26:02 The quiet ending went from constraint to artistic device
Sterling defines a quiet, acoustic closing track as a "typical quiet acoustic farewell." In the 1950s more than 60% of albums ended with a quiet, acoustic song; as recordings overall got louder, that absolute share slid all the way down to under one-sixth in the 1980s; by the 2000s and 2010s it had recovered to about a third. Sterling's analogy is the save icon on a floppy disk: the constraint is long gone, the habit remains. He also found in streaming data that an album's last track averages longer, more acoustic and sadder — but that is an average, and hip-hop, heavy metal and electronic music are full of loud exceptions.

item.description: The 2010 paper claiming growth halves once debt exceeds 90% of GDP was used by politicians as a red line for over a decade; now even the dove economist who argued for bold spending calls herself a hawk, but no one can say where that line is.
item.content:encoded:
The 2010 paper claiming growth halves once debt exceeds 90% of GDP was used by politicians as a red line for over a decade; now even the dove economist who argued for bold spending calls herself a hawk, but no one can say where that line is.

Medium information density, but the second half's reversal of positions and the interest rate data are worth it. For understanding how the US debt debate evolved from 2010 to today, this episode is a clear recap.

2:05 The real fuse on the debt snowball is interest
The textbook worry isn't the debt itself, but that interest costs feed on themselves: pay more interest, the deficit grows; a bigger deficit pushes debt higher; next period's interest is even bigger, and so on compounding worse and worse. The other path is investors losing their appetite for Treasuries, forcing the government to keep raising rates to attract buyers, and the snowball rolls faster. Neither of these dire outcomes happened after the financial crisis, and in hindsight the people who argued the government should spend more were on the right side of history — Karen Dynan even thinks it should have spent more and the recession could have been shorter.

8:21 The 90% line was read into the paper
The 2010 six-page paper by Reinhart and Rogoff, "Growth in a Time of Debt," studied decades of debt data across 20 advanced economies and concluded that when debt reaches 90% of GDP, growth is only half its normal level. But what the paper actually did was sort countries into four buckets — low, medium, high, and very high — with the very high bucket containing countries with debt far above 90%, and technically it said that this bucket, on average and over long periods, was associated with lower growth. Politicians and the media read it as a red line: "cross 90% and the economy crashes." The paper never said that.

11:28 An Excel error detonated the austerity fight
The debate the paper sparked raged across blogs and newspapers, with one side calling for austerity and belt-tightening and the other saying don't kill the recovery, you can't stop spending now. Later, more debt-friendly economists pointed out a major error in the Excel spreadsheet Reinhart and Rogoff used, and the paper's final sentence said that since their findings were wrong, the austerity agendas in Europe and the US should be reassessed. Correcting the error weakened the claim everyone had seized on, but did not overturn it — the updated paper still showed high debt generally associated with slower growth, just less steeply.

13:41 Low growth can also cause high debt
High debt being correlated with low growth does not mean high debt causes low growth. Andrea Presbitero points out the causality could run the other way: when the economy underperforms, policymakers want to stimulate it, which means public consumption and public investment, and one way to pay for that is borrowing — borrowing pushes debt up, so you see low growth and high debt in the data at the same time. He and his coauthors ultimately reached the same conclusion as most people: based on the empirical evidence, there is no definitive answer, and causality could run both ways. Moreover, the debt threshold varies by country — it could be 90%, 45%, or 100% — and depends on who the creditors are, whether they are domestic or foreign investors, and whether the debt is short-term or long-term.

17:50 Zero rates shelved the whole issue
What makes high debt destructive isn't the debt itself but the interest you pay on it. After the financial crisis, global rates fell to near zero and stayed there for years, so many macroeconomists thought maybe there was no need to worry much about debt at all, and attention drifted away from the topic. Then the world changed twice: the pandemic and the spending that followed pushed debt even higher, and more importantly, rates rose again. Today the cost of holding a lot of debt for the US and other countries is much higher than five or six years ago, and the shelved question has become relevant again.

19:57 Rogoff says 91% and you're doomed is a misreading
Ken Rogoff is still annoyed by how the paper was interpreted. He says 90% was just their highest bucket, they never said that at 91% you suddenly go to hell — that's like a 55 mph speed limit, you go 56 and you'll crash the next minute. He thinks that interpretation was used and distorted polemically. But he also stresses that you can't therefore say there is no threshold and any level of debt is fine — that's crazy too. His basic intuition hasn't changed: constantly leveraging up is playing with fire, and the US trajectory needs adjusting, not just debt but also Social Security and Medicare.

25:22 The dove who argued for spending has changed her tune
Two years later, debt has grown by more than $4 trillion, the large tax cuts Congress passed in 2025 further reduced revenue, and interest alone costs over $1 trillion a year, a record. Karen Dynan, who thought spending was worth the risk, now says "I'm a debt hawk now," because changes in financial markets, especially the interest rate on Treasury borrowing, make her think this is trickier than she thought two years ago. She describes it as walking on ice and comforting yourself that it hasn't cracked yet. Last week the 10-year Treasury rate hit its highest level since before the Great Recession, and the CBO projects debt will exceed 120% of GDP by 2036, higher than at any point in US history including World War II.

28:32 Rogoff puts the odds of a big problem above 50%
Rogoff thinks the biggest misconception is believing rates will stay low forever, and that if they're high for a while it's just a nightmare that will pass. He says he thinks the probability of something very serious happening is greater than 50% — not the end of the world, a debt crisis isn't the end of the world, but something very significant will happen and we are not prepared. He also says we need to reflect on how wrong everyone was and for how long, because that belief hasn't disappeared — mainstream opinion leaders think basically the same now as they did then. As for the red line, neither economist can draw it, but both agree the solution is spending cuts, tax increases, or both, and that looks politically impossible.

item.title: AI Debt Is Crowding Out Treasuries, and the US Economy Is Actually in Deflation
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-betteroffline-ai-债务正在和美元抢钱-美国经济其实在通缩/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-betteroffline-ai-债务正在和美元抢钱-美国经济其实在通缩/
item.description: AI capex has grown large enough to push into the Treasury market and distort global trade and inflation data; strip out the AI-related portion and the US economy is mildly deflationary, while the Fed is hiking for the wrong reasons.
item.content:encoded:
AI capex has grown large enough to push into the Treasury market and distort global trade and inflation data; strip out the AI-related portion and the US economy is mildly deflationary, while the Fed is hiking for the wrong reasons.

Paul Kedrosky strings AI capex's seepage into Treasuries, trade and inflation into a single causal chain, and the back half on an Anthropic IPO and OpenAI's valuation is especially dense with information.

1:06 AI capex can now move Treasury yields
Over the past 12 to 18 months, AI capex has consistently accounted for 30% to 70% of US GDP growth. More anomalous is that it has started to seep into the Treasury market: AI-related debt issuance is approaching $1 trillion, and debt's share of AI financing has risen from 15% to 20% a year ago to over 60%, making it the single largest block in both the investment-grade and high-yield markets. The result is that yield-sensitive investors would rather hold hyperscaler debt than Treasuries at the same duration, pushing the 10-year yield up. Kedrosky stresses this is not the market losing faith in America's ability to pay — the US can print money and will not default — it is competition at the margin.

6:10 More than half of global trade growth is AI
The WTO had forecast that global goods trade would fall noticeably because of US tariff policy; instead it grew about 4.5%, close to double the forecast. Digging into the data to find out why, the WTO found that over the past three quarters 19% of global goods trade was AI-related, and close to 55% of global trade growth was AI-related — mostly NVIDIA GPUs. Kedrosky's conclusion: AI capex is masking the real impact of Trump's tariffs, because it is so large it drowns out every other signal.

8:12 Both sources of US inflation point back to AI
US inflation is still above 3%, yet consumers are more stretched and more indebted than they have been in a long time. Break inflation apart and the two biggest pieces are: first, AI capex pushing up energy prices, which pushes up construction costs, materials and all kinds of services; second, the energy shock from the Iran war. Kedrosky counts the latter as AI-related too — he argues the Trump administration was emboldened by the success of the operation Anthropic organised in Venezuela, turned war into an app, and Iran is next. So both preconditions for inflation sit on top of AI.

19:30 Strip out AI and the US is in deflation
If you remove AI-capex-related inflation, plus the energy inflation from the AI-emboldened Iran war, from the US economy, Kedrosky calculates the US is actually running about 0.25% deflation. That means the Fed is hiking for the wrong reasons — it thinks it is suppressing demand-side inflation, when the actual inflation is exogenous. This resembles the path into the 1929 crash: high rates stacked on a weak consumer are the classic precursor to a long balance sheet recession. He cites Richard Koo's work on Japan's lost decade and argues all the conditions are now in place.

22:35 Balance sheet recession: a decade of deleveraging, no spending, no hiring
The hyperscalers will not go bankrupt, but they will spend a decade cleaning up their balance sheets — going from the least indebted companies in the market to the most indebted. A balance sheet recession is when companies, regardless of the level of rates, focus on deleveraging and getting debt off the books. The consequence: no investment in growth, no hiring, while simultaneously looking for ways to use AI to cut headcount. Companies like CoreWeave face a different order of problem — rolling over debt over the next five years may force them into some form of insolvency. Kedrosky says this will be the most underrated macro event of the next five years.

29:47 The system is screaming: data centre financing costs are rising on their own
The 10-year yield has risen about 100 basis points over the past few months, directly raising the financing cost of new data centres. But it goes further: when the system is under stress, the spread between issuance yields and the 10-year widens from 100 basis points to 150 or even 200. So every time you see rates rise, you should translate it as "data centres' ability to prove out their future cash flows just got a lot harder." Kedrosky judges that on financing costs alone, this breaks within 6 to 12 months — the most stressed end of the market is demanding an 11% to 12% return, and that is impossible to deliver.

37:58 Data centres need to earn 7%, but nobody can make the math work
The investment-grade market currently demands a median return of about 7.2% from data centres, and the junk market demands 10%. But Kedrosky stresses this is the threshold to attract creditors, not the threshold to get your capital back — that is a separate question, and he thinks it simply cannot be earned back. He coined the term EBBT — earnings before bad things — where you cut out everything that costs money and of course the cash flow looks great, but the premise is that hyperscalers stop burning money on frontier models, and nobody is doing that. If you only do industrial-grade inference, then it is fundamentally an energy problem: China adds roughly 3x the new energy capacity the US does each year, and is already ahead.

41:01 Anthropic's IPO slipped from October to November, and employees are borrowing millions to exercise
What Kedrosky has heard is that Anthropic originally planned to IPO on 1 October, and it is now reportedly pushed to November. His general rule: even in a good market, at least half the companies that say they will list by year-end do not list that year. Internally there is panic about what an IPO this year would look like. More concretely, the employees: many have already exercised their options, and if the IPO does not land they face the IRS's AMT, generating tax bills in the millions — he knows quite a few people who have borrowed millions of dollars for this. He also mentions a supplier close to the company saying Anthropic's Q3 came in below expectations, but stresses this is rumour, and consistent with the backdrop of customer concentration and token maxing fading.

item.title: Silicon Valley Makes Too Much Money, and That's Why California's Government Has No Incentive to Get Better
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-allin-硅谷太赚钱-反而让加州政府没有变好的动力/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-allin-硅谷太赚钱-反而让加州政府没有变好的动力/
item.description: California has been a one-party state for 16 years — not because voters want big government, but because Silicon Valley's tax payments are so generous that the government doesn't need to survive on performance. Gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton says the price is the highest poverty rate, unemployment rate and cost of living in the country.
item.content:encoded:
California has been a one-party state for 16 years — not because voters want big government, but because Silicon Valley's tax payments are so generous that the government doesn't need to survive on performance. Gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton says the price is the highest poverty rate, unemployment rate and cost of living in the country.

What's worth listening for is two verifiable causal chains: how Sacramento's bill assembly line has piled up 420,000 regulations, and how Silicon Valley's tax revenue lets the government skip improving.

5:04 The rules aren't written, they're piled up every year
Hilton gives a countable form to the consequences of one-party rule: Sacramento passed 1,118 bills last year, and when he printed them out, the stack was twice his height. "Nobody's reading this" — do you think Gavin Newsom reads them all before signing? The result is that California has accumulated more than 420,000 regulations, and he promises to cut that below 200,000 in his first term. Who are the bills written for? He says a narrow set of interest groups that control the process: unions, plaintiff's attorneys, and people who donate to politicians. That's why California is the highest litigation-risk place in the country, and why starting a company there has a 90% chance of ending up in court. Structurally, over those 16 years Democrats took all eight statewide elected offices, a two-thirds majority in the state legislature, every big county and big city, and a 6-to-1 majority on the state Supreme Court.

13:08 The key is that 26% of undecided voters
What he offers isn't a "Republicans flip it" story but an arithmetic problem: internal polling at the start of the campaign had 33% firmly for him, 41% firmly for Becerra, and 26% undecided. That 26% is the key — mostly people who have voted Democratic but aren't die-hards, overwhelmingly non-college-educated working people who are financially maxed out, and whose top concern is the cost of living. So the platform is all priceable line items: cancel high-speed rail, cut the government payroll by 10%, stop funding the nonprofits that make homelessness worse, and that adds up to "the first $150,000 free of state income tax"; gas goes from $6 toward $3, because the low carbon fuel standard and cap and invest add roughly 150 dollars to the price of gas, and cap and invest money is flowing to high-speed rail; cap the vehicle registration fee at 73 dollars by abolishing the DMV. The polling gap has narrowed from 30 points on primary night to 8 points recently.

19:14 Silicon Valley's money removes the pressure to perform
This is the most counterintuitive stretch of the whole piece. One host cites Peter Thiel's observation from years ago: Silicon Valley is like a resource curse for California — it generates so much wealth and tax revenue that the state doesn't need a good government, and that's also why one-party rule persists. Hilton adds the evidence: before the primary, Becerra was asked on CNN what policies he'd change given homelessness, the highest poverty rate, the highest unemployment rate and a terrible cost of living, and his answer was that this is the world's fourth-largest economy, people still love coming to Disneyland and the beaches, so things must be heading in the right direction. Hilton's rebuttal is that the fourth-largest economy figure includes the size of the government itself — which doubled in a decade — while net private-sector job creation in California since the pandemic is basically zero.

23:19 What works is the content, not the AI
Spencer Pratt is running for mayor of Los Angeles as an independent and got a mountain of free media off a batch of AI-generated videos. He breaks down the mechanism himself: what actually worked was what the videos said — he went on every platform and just told the truths he knew, and then creative people across the country started throwing ideas into this "machine." "I don't think it's the AI that worked; it's just one piece of a lot of puzzle pieces." He thinks there's evidence for this: most of the people who voted for him are Democrats. He also claims that if Los Angeles's 200,000 registered Republicans had actually turned out to vote, he would have won.

27:21 Taxpayers are paying for needles handed out in the park
Hilton and Spencer together describe MacArthur Park: last Tuesday at 10:30 in the morning, sunny in downtown Los Angeles, and in every direction you look people are smoking crack, injecting drugs, some bent over from fentanyl. The reason is that four nonprofits show up every day to hand out crack pipes, needles and drug supplies, and the money comes from taxpayers. Spencer adds the follow-up: one of the needle distributors was found to be selling drugs at the same time. Hilton stresses this isn't a case of nobody doing anything — Los Angeles has a new DA cracking down on drugs and crime, and there are federal prosecutors going after gangs and cartels — but the scene in the park is the same every Tuesday.

29:22 Do the right thing and you're punished; do the wrong thing and you're rewarded
A Latino couple in South Los Angeles ran a shoe store for 14 years. The shop was spotless, and they paid every tax, license, electricity bill and permit that got more expensive every year. They asked Hilton to step outside and look at the sidewalk two blocks down: it was entirely vendors selling shoes, clothing and T-shirts who pay no taxes, no electricity, no rent, no license. That's why the couple is closing. When did it start? In the last six or seven years — in 2018 Sacramento passed a bill legalizing street vending statewide, and cities and counties have no power to regulate it. His conclusion: here, doing the right thing is punished and doing the wrong thing is rewarded, and the whole situation is upside down. Spencer adds the numbers: 50,000 food vendors, a permit costs just 21 dollars, yet the city council allocated 500,000 dollars to buy them carts, while the unbuilt Palisades reservoir cover would have cost 200,000 dollars.

42:32 Ballot collection is legal, so it can't be audited
Spencer's claim is that it isn't fake ballots, it's ballot harvesting, which California law allows. The mechanism has three steps: a witness's signature can be a smiley face or an X; the same witness can witness 43,000 ballots, and there's no verification allowed; and once ballots reach the counting center they're separated from their envelopes, the signatures stay on the envelopes, and the chain of custody is broken — so even if you know who these people are, you can't audit it, and a recount just recounts the same batch. The other side's rebuttal: voter fraud is a felony and is prosecuted regularly; after Trump lost last time he filed 60 such lawsuits and lost them all. Asked directly whether he believes he lost because of fraud, Spencer's answer is "without evidence I'd say no," and he lists the 200,000 registered Republicans who didn't vote as one of the reasons.

47:35 The empty reservoir and the reconstruction lawsuit
Spencer's house, his parents' house and his neighbors' houses all burned. Reconstruction is stuck on two things. First, that empty reservoir is still empty — even the one across from his house, the one he was sure would never burn, is empty, and Palisades is now supplied by a hose run all the way from Tanga through regrown dry brush. Second, they're pursuing a mass tort suit with 10,000 victims, naming Gavin Newsom's state parks, the city and the city's water and power department as defendants. His chain of allegations: on New Year's Eve there was an 8-acre fire in Pacific Palisades, and state parks should have monitored it per the manual but didn't, letting embers smolder into the known high-wind weather of January 6 and 7; firefighter whistleblowers told him there were visibly smoldering coals on the hillside, and state parks employees produced photos in testimony showing the hillside smoking.

item.title: Individual productivity tripled, but company delivery only went from 20 days to 17
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-lightstar-个人提效三倍-公司交付只从20天缩到17天/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-lightstar-个人提效三倍-公司交付只从20天缩到17天/
item.description: AI armed everyone, but the organization didn't get faster — because the weakest link isn't people, it's process. The real dividing line is whether you can transform processes and the organization, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.
item.content:encoded:
AI armed everyone, but the organization didn't get faster — because the weakest link isn't people, it's process. The real dividing line is whether you can transform processes and the organization, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.

A frontline CEO talks about building his own CEO AI, canceling weekly meetings, and using token consumption to identify elite performers — the mechanisms and numbers are concrete, and the decision-making hub section in the second half is the most valuable.

16:07 Individual productivity tripled, but delivery only sped up by three days
NetEase did a study last year: a software requirement, from the product manager receiving it and producing a design draft to the feature going live, averaged 20 working days. After AI coding crossed the inflection point, many engineers doubled or even tripled to quintupled their personal efficiency, with some hitting tenfold. But for features of the same scope, the entire process only shrank from 20 days to 17. The reason is that a team completing a complex task is like a barrel: of its 20 staves, 10 are engineers, 3 are product, 3 are testing. The engineer and product manager staves shot up quickly, but some staves aren't people — they're process — and they didn't improve at all. So AI adoption has to clear three hurdles: cognition, applying it to individuals' short-range tasks, and transforming processes and the organization. The third is the hardest.

20:11 Cancel the weekly meeting: AI syncs information, humans only solve problems
Ruan Liang asked friends who run companies whether they still hold weekly meetings; 99% said yes. Weekly meetings usually serve three purposes: syncing information, discovering problems and opportunities, and making decisions. They used to run 2.5 hours a week, but the time spent on this meeting could be ten times 2.5 hours — every department prepares materials layer by layer, and the information sync itself wasn't done well, because no one listens attentively the whole time and may miss a sentence relevant to them. After the reform: the general manager and management agree on what information is needed, everyone fills in a template and stores it in the knowledge base, and AI scans and integrates it into a focused, interactive HTML report where people can leave comments and follow-up questions; an AI agent produces a preliminary list of problems and opportunities, which human brains confirm and supplement; problem-solving and decision-making move to dedicated meetings.

28:20 SaaS isn't dead, but ordinary SaaS will die
Ruan Liang doesn't think SaaS is dead: SaaS is essentially Service, and Service always exists, it just changes form — AI as a Service and Agent as a Service are themselves software. But ordinary SaaS may indeed die, while truly good SaaS that has already entered a company's critical processes will only get better, because it becomes internal infrastructure. In the past, humans used software, limited by time and energy; in the future, large numbers of Agents will call databases, APIs, security APIs, review APIs, HR APIs, CRM APIs — call volumes far exceeding the number and actions of humans, which will surge enormously, and the more it's called, the more entrenched it becomes. The premise is that the Service itself is critical enough within the company.

32:21 Distill top salespeople into skills and distribute them to everyone
Bosses have two headaches: the sales team has only one or two strong performers and the rest are mediocre; or a salesperson is too strong and what if they leave? There used to be no solution, but now you can distill or extract a good salesperson's actions, scripts, and behaviors into skills. Two uses: distribute them to other salespeople to use directly; and have AI turn elite salespeople into teachers to train ordinary salespeople. What training should distill isn't the salesperson — it's the customer: take the customer interaction data a salesperson has had — calls, WeChat, emails — and have AI simulate various customers to train salespeople. Online sales is purely digital and on record; for offline sales, it's recommended or even required to equip them with a recording card, and after a visit, while memory is fresh, record a two-to-three-minute voice note, because salespeople dislike CRM (they think CRM is for managing them) but don't mind a recording card, since it's also useful for their own customer review.

44:31 Fewer middle managers, strong individuals lead Agent legions back to the front line
Ruan Liang judges that middle managers will become fewer, but not necessarily be eliminated — rather, they'll go to the front line, and the front line can also lead a bunch of agents. Middle managers with management responsibilities will become fewer, while elite individuals with strong skills will become more numerous. He gives the example of an engineering team: previously, socialized division of labor split software development ever finer — frontend, backend, algorithm, test engineers; in the last half year, it has clearly reverted to full-stack, with everyone becoming full-end engineers. In the future, organizations will increasingly resemble a fractal structure, with countless highly capable engineers, one mother peak commanding some engineers, and countless agents fighting a battle. He envisions a future interview negotiation scenario: a candidate says I'm not one person, I bring an AI team, a summary of all my past experience and skills, and the premium the company has to pay might be some kind of OPC.

50:35 AI value formula: quality times time saved
Ruan Liang gives a formula referencing a paper: AI's value = the quality of AI completing the task (as a ratio of human quality) × time saved × the company's economic value per unit time. For example, a human makes a cup of coffee at eight out of ten, and AI also makes it at eight out of ten, so the quality coefficient is 1; a human takes 20 minutes, AI takes only 10 seconds, saving 14 minutes 50 seconds; multiply by the company's economic value per unit time, and you can calculate ROI. Prioritize four types of tasks for AI: time-consuming, high-frequency, unavoidable, and tasks where different people produce roughly the same result. Once calculated, you can immediately decide whether to use AI. He also suggests first using the most expensive AI (Cloud, GPT) to prove the task can be done, solidify the process, then switch to cheaper ones — if the most expensive can do it, within two months the cheaper ones can too.

59:40 Token consumption leads by a landslide, output also leads by a landslide
NetEase started a points system in 2024, trying to quantify engineers' work tasks into points with work value. By the AI era, they found a group of people whose token consumption was astonishing, and whose work output and work value were also astonishing, forming a statistical pattern: people whose token consumption leads by a landslide are most likely building systems for themselves, saving their own work time and increasing thinking time, so their work quality and work results also lead by a landslide. Many bosses worry about AI abuse causing waste; Ruan Liang's hot take is that truly excellent or elite people won't waste — the company has audits but doesn't tell colleagues, and through statistics they found elite colleagues don't waste. He also says small companies are more likely to fully embrace AI, because there are fewer organizational relationships, the boss uses it first, the hierarchy is shallow, and the chain is short.

1:11:50 The core of a decision hub is decision history, not the model
Building an AI decision hub essentially requires a high-quality knowledge base, and what truly matters is the historical decision-making process and decision basis. This year NetEase preserved historical decisions, incorporated them into the knowledge base, combined the two types of knowledge to train an agent or skill, then fed back the original hundreds of cases for the agent to judge, achieving over 90% accuracy. Ruan Liang also mentions that Bridgewater equipped researchers and analysts with its own agent, precipitating the decision-making process and decision history into a decision knowledge base; what Bridgewater did better was making the agent a learnable, evolvable part — after a human adjusts it, the confirmed adjustment actions enter the next round of reinforcement, keeping pace with the times, equivalent to human-machine collaborative self-evolution.

item.title: Mooncakes Sell for Only Two Months a Year, Yet They've Built a 28.2 Billion Yuan Business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-beiwanglu-月饼一年只卖两个月-却做成了282亿的生意/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-beiwanglu-月饼一年只卖两个月-却做成了282亿的生意/
item.description: Bound to Mid-Autumn Festival, mooncakes are trapped in a narrow sales window — but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from gifting scenarios and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.
item.content:encoded:
Bound to Mid-Autumn Festival, mooncakes are trapped in a narrow sales window — but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from gifting scenarios and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.

Worth listening to for food industry practitioners and anyone wanting to understand holiday consumption businesses, but information density is low — much of the runtime is spent on faction taxonomy and flavors, with the business mechanics concentrated in the middle-to-late sections.

6:06 Zongzi can sell year-round; mooncakes cannot
Zongzi is tied to Dragon Boat Festival, but once vacuum-sealed for long shelf life it can sell all four seasons — Wufangzhai even opened restaurants to put zongzi into everyday scenarios. Mooncakes' problem isn't that the craft can't achieve long shelf life; it's that they're defined as ‘traditional festival pastries mainly eaten during Mid-Autumn Festival,’ and the national standard GB19855 writes the season directly into the definition. So of two festival foods, zongzi can decouple from its holiday through shelf life and channels, while mooncakes cannot.

12:12 The national standard draws hard lines on fillings
Lotus seed paste mooncakes must contain no less than 60% lotus seeds, fruit mooncakes must contain no less than 25% fruit products, and five-kernel mooncakes must use exactly five nuts: walnut, almond, olive kernel, melon seed, and sesame. The purpose of these lines is to push up ingredient costs and prevent cheap candied winter melon, red-and-green shredded rind, and inferior nuts from being used as filler. For consumers, reading the ingredient list order tells you how much of what is actually in there.

26:30 Why custard lava mooncakes are made so small
Custard lava mooncakes are small not out of stinginess but because of structure. The outside is flaky pastry, the middle is a custard layer, and the innermost is the lava layer — the custard layer acts as a moisture barrier. Production requires two rounds of baking to keep the lava semi-solid, and the lava's melting point must be engineered: solid during transport, then a few seconds in the microwave turns it into flowing liquid. If overheated, the lava gets absorbed by the pastry shell and it reverts to an ordinary custard mooncake.

37:34 ‘Everything can be a mooncake’ has five preconditions
Not everything can be stuffed into a mooncake. First is water content — hot-and-sour soup mooncakes can't be made because there's too much water to contain. Second is safety — meat, egg, and dairy are also what microbes like, so processing temperatures and sterilization processes must be tested repeatedly. Third is particle size — too large and the shell can't contain it, too fine and you can't taste it. Fourth is flavor retention after high-temperature baking — some aromas simply disappear once baked. Fifth is whether the cost can be handled. So long-term stable flavors are ones confirmed by generation after generation.

44:40 Choosing an OEM isn't a matter of bigger is better
When big brands make branded mooncakes through OEM, there's a common misconception: you must pick the best OEM factory in the country. But a top-tier OEM's production scale actually doesn't match yours. Indicators you can screen on include registered capital, tax payment records, number of employees with social insurance contributions, and accumulated safe-production days. Also, the nine major factions correspond to different factories — you can't ask Guangzhou Restaurant to produce Shanxi egg-skin mooncakes; they don't have that capability or production line.

48:44 Flexible production lines can take orders of a few hundred boxes
Mooncake production is semi-automated and semi-manual — wrapping and forming machines can do their part, but brushing egg wash, pressing patterns, and stamping require human hands, which actually makes it favorable for OEM and customization. Flexible factories can go as small as a few hundred boxes, and can do thousands or tens of thousands of boxes too. If a company has only 50 employees, they can directly use the factory's existing mooncakes and only need to design the gift box. This small-batch, fast-response capability is the core of why mooncakes can do corporate custom business.

51:47 The 28.2 billion scale is propped up by gifting
In 2025, China's mooncake output was 518,000 tons and sales scale was 28.2 billion RMB, both down from the previous year. At 80 grams each that's about 6.4 billion pieces; at 100 grams, about 5.18 billion pieces — across a population of 1.4 billion, an average of three to four per person. For comparison, Dragon Boat Festival zongzi annual sales scale is about 10 to 11 billion, and instant noodles about 68 to 120 billion. That mooncakes sell for only two months a year yet reach 28.2 billion is fundamentally about the gifting attribute — brands prepare large amounts of PR gifts at the two annual nodes of Chinese New Year and Mid-Autumn Festival, and zongzi's gifting attribute is far weaker than mooncakes'.

58:55 499 yuan is a number forced out by the regulatory line
In 2022, the National Development and Reform Commission and three other departments jointly issued an announcement placing boxed mooncakes priced above 500 yuan per unit under key supervision. So the highest mooncake price on the market is 499. The calculation logic: a box of mooncakes costs about 70 yuan per box, and adding channel commissions and allocated expenses, it can't exceed 500 yuan. Back when the economy was good there were sky-high mooncakes with very expensive tea or liquor bundled in, even wooden gift boxes, with both cost and price very high.

item.title: AI for science is stuck on the last 0.001 points, not on compute
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-latentspace-ai-做科学卡在最后-0-001-分-不是卡在算力/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-latentspace-ai-做科学卡在最后-0-001-分-不是卡在算力/
item.description: ERA can churn out thousands of candidate notebooks, but it can't close the gap on the last 30 places — because the inner loop is a machine, and the outer loop still needs a human to judge ‘this paper, you got it wrong’.
item.content:encoded:
ERA can churn out thousands of candidate notebooks, but it can't close the gap on the last 30 places — because the inner loop is a machine, and the outer loop still needs a human to judge ‘this paper, you got it wrong’.

High information density, but it takes some patience: the first half covers ERA's mechanics, the second half covers contrails, wildfires and quantum computing, all first-hand detail.

9:24 ERA's input is a chat, its output is a scored notebook
ERA's product form isn't having people write config files — you just start chatting. Because mapping a scientific problem onto a scorable task is itself non-obvious, Michael Brenner wrote a dedicated agent to conversationally help you define which score to optimize. When the chat is done, it generates a Python notebook underneath, containing a function that produces a score, and then the system starts mutating that notebook in a ‘clever way’, continually proposing new code to push the score higher.

10:24 It doesn't always pick the best candidate
ERA runs Monte Carlo Tree Search internally, keeping hundreds or thousands of notebook candidates at once, with the candidate pool structured as a tree. Selection uses the upper confidence bound from reinforcement learning: it estimates the 95th percentile outcome of a mutation and picks the one with the highest optimistic upper bound. So it doesn't always greedily pick the currently best-performing notebook — sometimes it picks the fifth best, in order to explore more efficiently. It has also tried combining the ideas of two candidates to generate a third.

18:38 Evolutionary coding was stuck for decades because random mutation is useless
Platt says evolutionary coding has been tried since the 1970s — mutating Lisp code and the like — but it never took off, because random mutation in code space is basically worthless: just like DNA, the vast majority of mutations are harmful. ERA works because the inner loop is itself an AI that knows which direction to try, which amounts to having a meaningful gradient underneath. The price is that it also overfits, and it also goes off the rails in ‘genie wish’ fashion.

22:44 A predictive model and a descriptive model are two different things
John Platt splits scientific modeling into two kinds: a predictive model just seeks the lowest error rate on some dataset; a descriptive model is what science actually wants — it contains some internal description of reality, so it can extrapolate. His example is Newton: an apple falling can be fitted, but gravity isn't about apples, and if you take a model that only fits apples and ask it about planets, it has no planetary data and knows nothing. He admits the line is blurry, because the scientist themself also brings a pile of known facts and intuitions to constrain the model.

31:59 This is a power tool, and it will cut your fingers off
Faced with multiple hypothesis testing and overfitting, Platt's answer isn't a new method but a harsher old one: because ERA is a power tool, you have to be stricter than before, with a holdout hidden so deep you never look at it yourself. He states plainly that no system yet discovers entirely new physics or entirely new science, and that scientists are still responsible for judging whether a conclusion is descriptive.

39:18 AI is stuck on the last 0.001 points
Ira pushed the score very close, but it didn't close the gap on roughly the last 30 places, because nobody goes and scrapes off that last 0.001 points. This exposes the system's real structure: the inner layer is a machine running for hours to produce candidates, and the outer layer is a human making judgments like ‘this paper, you got it wrong’. Platt compares it to a graduate student who never sleeps and is extremely eager — you tell it a direction, it goes and tries, but when it gets stuck a human has to change the approach.

48:08 The counterfactual model stalled the team for two years
To judge which contrail to avoid, you need to know how much warming it actually causes, and that's a counterfactual problem: you can't enter the universe where that contrail never existed. The team produced a version of a counterfactual model that worked for outgoing longwave radiation, but they could never build one for the part that reflects sunlight, and it stalled them for two years. They even self-tested with a dataset where contrails were artificially injected, and their own attempt couldn't pass their own test. In the end ERA found a simple model that searches over all confounders, passed the test, and cracked the problem.

1:24:27 A wildfire is best put out before it's room-sized
Google has a crisis resilience direction, and one project in it is called Firesat: a wildfire is extremely easy to extinguish when it's only as big as ‘this room’, and once it reaches an acre it's far harder, and the growth from room size to an acre may be exponential. The plan is a low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation using mid-wave IR (which corresponds to blackbody radiation, exactly the temperature of fire) for detection; about 50 to 80 satellites could cover the globe, spot a fire about 5 meters across, and raise an alarm within 15 to 20 minutes. The partner is the nonprofit Earth Fire Alliance, the satellites are built by Muon Space, and one prototype has already launched.

item.title: Trump Invites Xi to a Show. What Did the US Get in Return?
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-特朗普请习近平看戏-美国换到了什么实质东西/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-特朗普请习近平看戏-美国换到了什么实质东西/
item.description: This state visit has almost no substantive agenda — it is pure symbolism and optics. The question is not whether something goes wrong, but what the US traded symbolism for in substance. So far: nothing.
item.content:encoded:
This state visit has almost no substantive agenda — it is pure symbolism and optics. The question is not whether something goes wrong, but what the US traded symbolism for in substance. So far: nothing.

The first half covers the summit and US-China relations; the middle and later sections on China after Xi and fifty years since Mao's death are denser with information and worth hearing.

6:06 This visit has no substantive agenda at all
Gewirtz's judgment is that this state visit has "there is not a very deep substantive agenda at all." Trump invited Xi mainly because he wants to put on a show, wants the pomp and the cameras, and wants to push issues like the Iran war out of the news. For Beijing, this actually makes them less nervous — because if it were a more confrontational meeting, they would be more anxious. But Gewirtz flags two things: Trump himself is extremely unpredictable, and Beijing has internalized that; and Beijing watches the chaos in Washington and sees the American president himself often in situations they would never want Xi to be in — going to the wrong place, being photographed in unflattering images, being pressed by reporters. So the real question is not whether someone deliberately sets a trap, but whether things slip into exactly the scenario they are desperate to avoid.

9:25 Symbolism for substance: where is the trade
Gewirtz characterizes this visit as "we are in a space of symbolism and optics." He says that in US-China relations, trading symbolism for substance is itself a reasonable play: give Beijing the pomp and cameras it craves, and get back something concretely useful to Americans and American interests. That was the model for US relations with the Soviets during the Cold War and after — the US gave symbolism, legitimacy and that handshake photo, and got a step back from the other side on Third World countries or nuclear issues. But the problem this time is that the Trump administration does not even seem to have attempted to design a set of "deliverables." Gewirtz says "it doesn't even seem like they're trying." So what to watch is not where things go wrong, but "where is the trade happening."

11:37 The direction of concessions has been completely flipped
Gewirtz points to a counterintuitive dynamic: concessions the US might once have given China are now flipped into "gifts" China gives the US. Pomp and cameras were what Beijing wanted, but in Washington they are treated as Xi's visit being a concession to the US. The same flip happens on advanced semiconductors: the US used to not sell these things, so opening up products like the H200 would have been a huge concession; now, if Beijing agrees to buy, many in Washington would see it as Beijing conceding to Trump. Gewirtz says this flip keeps recurring, and the reason it really matters is not to score points for the administration, but that it reflects what happens in superpower competition when the power gap narrows — very small differences, interpersonal dynamics, can produce much larger displacements in the overall strategic picture.

12:39 US-China relations are also K-shaped, held up by the upper leg
Gewirtz uses "K-shaped" to describe US-China relations: one upward leg is the leader-level channel —密集 mutual visits, friendship, cameras; one downward leg is the competitive reality and the actions certain parts of both governments keep taking. The system is currently held up by the upward leg, but it is very fragile. He stresses the metaphor is not just a parallel analogy: saying "truce" or "detente" sounds too static, like a state already reached, but US-China relations are actually quite dynamic, quite unstable, moving in two directions at once. He applies the same K-shaped logic to China's economy — manufacturing and AI are flying, real estate and consumer demand are struggling, the upward leg is pulling the whole system forward, and the question is whether it can keep holding as the K widens.

22:03 The bipartisan consensus on China policy has shattered
Gewirtz argues that Trump changed the tone of America's China discussion in the 2016 election and became the symbol and standard-bearer of that turn; but now, after helping create that turn, he has helped destroy or transform it. He cites David Feith's article in the Reagan Institute on "a new cold war in an age of doubt" — that great rethink on China was not as great as many assumed. Gewirtz's conclusion: if the political dynamics are more complicated than imagined and the bipartisan consensus some people talk about does not exist, then this is a moment of "incredible fluidity." He says he has no confidence in the direction of either Democratic or Republican China policy in the medium term, and Beijing has no confidence either.

31:24 Chinese officials cannot talk about risks they have no solution for
Gewirtz offers a different read on how the US should interpret Chen Yixin's article. On the surface, Americans are panicking about existential risk and China is panicking about regime security, and that is correct. But he says: heads of American AI model companies can talk at length about risks they have no solution for, and all of them do; China's minister of state security cannot. In China, when you point out a risk in public, you are simultaneously saying "we the Communist Party see it, we will handle it, we have a solution." So the real question is: should we treat what we can see from Beijing as everything, or acknowledge there is more in the system that we cannot see. He gives an example from 25 years ago — Americans then predicted the internet would cause regime change in China, Clinton said that was like nailing Jell-O to the wall, and Beijing did in fact nail the Jell-O to the wall, namely the firewall.

35:37 Beijing has not decided how to regulate open models
Gewirtz says that around Xi's speech and Chen Yixin's article, the outside world has already been through several cycles of excitement and interpretation, but Beijing has still not given the single most important thing: how it plans to regulate open-weight models spreading globally — models that carry both risk and strategic benefit for Beijing. He calls this "the trillion dollar question." Both speeches can be read as pointing in some direction, but the decision has not been made. His guess is that this is because Beijing itself has not decided, because things are changing too fast and the trade-offs are too large. He contrasts with the Trump administration: it did not make a decision until Mythos came out, and then made another when Fable came out.

41:55 What to prepare for is not China's decline but Xi's decline
Gewirtz says that a few years ago the "peak China" debate asked whether to start preparing for China's decline, and now most people think China's economy is at least temporarily on a relatively sustainable path. But he argues the real question is not that, but "do we need to prepare for Xi Jinping's decline" — because people die, and modern Chinese history tells us that leaders in power for a long time change with age, certain obsessions become more prominent, behavior changes. By "prepare" he does not mean the departure itself, but acknowledging uncertainty: the outside world has treated Xi's tenure as fairly predictable, because since taking power in 2012 and 2013 he laid out a set of goals and largely pursued them. But he stresses the change could absolutely be worse for the US — "That doesn't mean he's going to mellow."

item.title: Canada Wants Into the EU: This Is a Permanent Breakup With America, Not a Wait for Trump to Leave
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-wsjournal-加拿大想加入欧盟-这是对美国的永久分手-不是等特朗普下台/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-wsjournal-加拿大想加入欧盟-这是对美国的永久分手-不是等特朗普下台/
item.description: Canada wants to be the EU's first "associate member," but the EU has no such status. It's a generational pivot toward Europe and away from the US — and Europe's economy grows at half America's pace.
item.content:encoded:
Canada wants to be the EU's first "associate member," but the EU has no such status. It's a generational pivot toward Europe and away from the US — and Europe's economy grows at half America's pace.

Medium information density, but the nonexistent "associate member" status, Carney's European network and book club, and the EU's Brexit-driven red line are three judgments you won't hear elsewhere.

0:00 Canada wants to be the EU's first associate member, but the status doesn't exist
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Canada is negotiating to become an associate member of the EU. But the show says it plainly: the EU has no such thing as an "associate member" — you're either a member, paying into the budget, accepting free movement of people and seamless truck crossings, or you're not. The current 27 members are all in Europe, sharing borders, regulations, and mostly the euro. So what Canada gets will be a status invented for it, with details still under negotiation. What Carney wants isn't another buyer but a group of "like-minded" countries to build, together, the institutions and technological capabilities that America's "wrecking ball" can't reach.

3:01 Canada once saw itself as Europeans living in North America
This isn't a new idea; it's a return to an old identity. In the first half of the 20th century, some Canadians genuinely saw themselves as "Europeans living in North America" — today's oldest Canadians were born British subjects, and Canada didn't open an embassy in Washington until the 1920s. On the eve of World War II, Canada's trade with Britain still exceeded its trade with the US. After the war America became the center of gravity of the West, the auto industry integrated in the 1960s, NAFTA took effect in 1994, and Canadian elites switched from going to Oxford and Cambridge to going to Harvard and Yale. Trump's tensions reopened a forgotten historical question: where do Canadians belong in the world?

6:13 The 51st state isn't a trade negotiation, it's a sovereignty question
When Trump returned for a second term, he didn't just want to renegotiate a trade deal; he questioned the territorial integrity of allies like Canada and Denmark, and said openly he wanted Canada to become the 51st state. The show's judgment: if it were just renegotiating trade, you could negotiate; once it touches sovereignty, it hits something highly emotional, sensitive, electorally meaningful and bound up with a country's self-image. One Canadian official, after reading every Trump biography he could find, concluded that the 51st state talk was "price discovery" — throwing out an outrageous idea to test the reaction. Whatever the intent, the effect was real: Carney went from 25 points behind in the polls to winning overnight.

8:17 Carney defined the trade war as "we are being attacked"
Carney had two signature moments after taking office. One was the Davos speech, landing right in the middle of the Greenland crisis, with Trump due to speak the next day; Carney went first and delivered the clearest anti-Trumpist manifesto yet: Canadians' old comfortable assumption that geography and alliances automatically deliver prosperity and security no longer holds. The second came when the US imposed tariffs: instead of backing down he escalated, hitting back with tariffs of his own, and after the final round of trade talks collapsed he still wouldn't budge. Asked at a press conference why it felt like war was about to start today, his answer was "because we are being attacked." The show notes that a technocrat and centrist taking escalatory action is counterintuitive, and that this is exactly what makes him seen as a leader of the Western allies' anti-Trump movement — for better or worse.

11:22 Carney's European network matters more than his policies
A North American prime minister with an unusually large number of European friends: a doctorate in economics from Oxford, the first foreigner to run the Bank of England. Macron was a banker, German Chancellor Merz worked at BlackRock, Finnish President Stubb also came from finance — Carney knows them all. In Ottawa he also has a book club whose members are political heavyweights and industry leaders, with a Fight Club-style rule: "the first rule of book club is you don't talk about book club." Most of them were educated at Oxford or Cambridge, are familiar with Europe, and remain in touch with the prime minister, feeding him exactly the kinds of ideas about how to bring Canada closer to Europe. The show says interviewees were far more secretive about the book club than about Canada's plan to join the EU.

14:27 The talks aren't just trade — they're data cables and Erasmus
What the two sides are discussing goes far beyond tariffs: laying data cables connecting Europe and Canada; jointly building data centers, cloud storage and satellite networks placed beyond the reach of American tech giants; building new pipelines in Canada to ship natural gas to the East Coast and on to Europe; using icebreakers to open Arctic routes for fertilizer shipments. They also plan to entwine Canadian and EU research institutions to create a network of academic and scientific output that can rival the American system. Canada is even pushing to join the EU's Erasmus student exchange program — the show says this is a big deal in Europe, and has led to a lot of marriages. If a generation of Canadians goes to school in Paris, Spain and Italy, and a generation of Italians comes to Ottawa, Montreal and Vancouver, then what's being discussed isn't just economics but social ties deeper than the flow of natural gas and minerals.

17:45 The EU's red line: no one can think you can quit and still get the benefits
For Europe, Canada is a "shiny new toy": it has raw materials, critical minerals and energy Europe has long coveted, its values are close, and Carney speaking French and English and making his first trip to Paris and London rather than Washington means a lot to Europeans. But the risks are just as clear. The EU is haunted by Brexit, and its long-standing red line is that "no one can ever be allowed to think they can leave the club and keep enjoying the benefits" — if major countries start quitting and demanding a Canada-style deal, that would be fatal for the EU. So the puzzle Carney has to solve is: get Canada a large share of the trade and connectivity benefits without creating a precedent that lets a country like Italy say "we don't like these regulations, let's leave and become a Canada-style member — no rules but all the benefits."

19:54 The real pain hasn't arrived yet; the White House bets geography is destiny
There are concerns inside Canada: how much sovereignty would an associate membership with a vague identity require giving up, which regulations would it accept, what happens to immigration — conservative voters and mainstream newspaper columnists are all asking. But the bigger fear is the cost of decoupling from the US, because so far it's only a war of words and the real pain hasn't hit the Canadian economy: two-thirds of exports go to the US, and that's a lot of people's businesses and jobs. The White House's judgment is that geography is destiny, Canada is right there, decades of economic ties are real, and in the end Canada will be pulled back to the negotiating table — flirting with Europe won't change economic reality. You can't force Canadian businesses to do business in Europe when a few miles (or, as they'd say in Canada, a few kilometers) across the border sits an attractive market.

item.title: Ranking Psychology's Classic Experiments: Many Conclusions Don't Survive Replication
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-verybad-心理学经典实验排等级-很多结论撑不过复现/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-verybad-心理学经典实验排等级-很多结论撑不过复现/
item.description: Milgram's shock experiment still replicates, which is itself absurd; and the Good Samaritan experiment had only 40 subjects total, so even if they got it right, they got it right by accident.
item.content:encoded:
Milgram's shock experiment still replicates, which is itself absurd; and the Good Samaritan experiment had only 40 subjects total, so even if they got it right, they got it right by accident.

Two philosophers plus a psychologist rank classic studies from D to S, and along the way settle accounts with the replication crisis, Zimbardo's fraudulent original notes, and small samples.

10:08 Milgram still replicating is itself absurd
Milgram recruited New Haven workers in a Yale basement, led them to believe they were shocking another person, with the voltage labeled up to 300 volts and marked dangerous; the person being "shocked" was actually a trained actor, and about 65% of them pressed all the way to the end. He ran a large number of variants, manipulating whether the experimenter wore a white coat, the distance to the person being shocked, and which university's name was on the door. The study directly rewrote psychology's ethics review system; today this kind of experiment can no longer be done. Dave says that a social psychology study from the 50s and 60s that still replicates is itself "[ __ ] banana," which is why it goes in the S tier — he's using replication as the bar, not fame.

29:20 The Good Samaritan experiment had only 40 people
Darley and Batson had seminary students go to the other side of campus to deliver the parable of the Good Samaritan, with a visibly injured, groaning person asking for help placed along the way; the manipulated variable was the time pressure they were under. It turned out that time pressure predicted whether they stopped to help better than what topic they were going to speak on. But Dave points out that the entire experiment had only 40 subjects total, and once split into groups the samples were tiny. He lumps this kind of study together with the phone booth coin-drop experiment as a common disease of 60s and 70s social psychology: severely underpowered, "even if they were right, they were right by accident." Paul says it's great as material for making people reflect on human nature, but as a scientific finding he doesn't trust it, and gives it a D.

48:38 On the cloth mother experiment, mothers already knew
Harlow separated infant monkeys from their mothers and built two surrogate mothers: a wire frame with a bottle attached, and a soft, huggable cloth mother that provided no milk. Except when they had to nurse, the infants stayed on the cloth mother the rest of the time. This refuted the behaviorist explanation that "infants love their mothers because the mother provides food," and supported the role of contact comfort. The episode clarifies that Harlow did not actually shock the monkeys; what's hard to watch is the footage of frightened infants lunging at the cloth mother and clinging on for dear life. He also called the isolation apparatus the "pit of despair" and the restraint device the "rape rack" in published articles, and the reaction on the show was "he's just a psychopath." Tamler argues for giving it the lowest score, not because it was cruel, but because these studies didn't demonstrate anything any mother could have known by intuition if you'd just asked her.

1:10:52 The prison experiment's director was teaching guards to abuse
