The original notes and recordings dug up on the Stanford prison experiment show that Zimbardo himself was coaching the people randomly assigned to be guards to engage in abusive behavior. If the intended story of the study is "put people in this role and they spontaneously become sadists," then on the available evidence that conclusion is highly suspect — he never reported just how much he pushed them. David considers this close to scientific fraud, lumps it in with "dog torturers," and no longer teaches it. But David also cautions: across the Milgram and Asch series, people differ — some said "screw you, I'm not doing it" at the lowest shock level. Tamler adds that when he interviewed Zimbardo, the latter talked about Milgram, saying Milgram did no psychological screening and that some of the people who showed up might have been sociopaths, while Zimbardo claimed he did screen, using that to prove these were normal people.

1:15:59 Even adults fail the false belief task
The false belief task comes from Premack and Woodruff's paper "Does the Chimpanzee Have a Theory of Mind"; Dennett proposed this design in his commentary: Sally puts a toy in a box and leaves, Anne moves it to a basket, and you ask where Sally will look for it when she returns. Children before age three or four say the place where the toy actually is, and around age five they start getting it right; this shift from failure to success is one of the most robust findings in all of developmental psychology. But Paul and Susan Birch tested adults and found that adults find it hard too — there's an immediate intuition pointing at "where the thing actually is" that has to be inhibited; he demonstrates it live in his intro course, and about a third of the students get it wrong. Tamler's irritation is that once the paradigm got hot, the whole field shifted from that interesting question to the methodology itself, and the test became the construct.

1:24:06 To deny that the methods are all broken, you have to accept ESP
Daryl Bem published a paper in a top social psychology journal in 2011 claiming to have found precognition: subjects first rated their preference for unfamiliar Chinese characters, and only afterward were shown emotional images as primes; it turned out that the characters that were positively primed afterward had been rated higher beforehand. He made all his materials and data public, and Paul thinks he genuinely believed the result. Bem's defense is a dilemma: if you say my research isn't good research, then almost all research in social psychology isn't good research — so either admit your methods are reliable and accept ESP, or admit your methods are unreliable. Paul says he was furious at the time: this would overturn our entire understanding of space and time, and you want to accept it on a p less than 0.05. This is also the driving force behind the Bayesian countermovement in psychology: results should be compared against prior plausibility, not against 0.05.

1:29:09 Delayed gratification may measure trust, not self-control
Mischel and Ebbesen had preschoolers choose between taking a small reward immediately and waiting for two. What's more interesting in the original study is that some children spontaneously used strategies — thinking of the marshmallow as a white cloud, singing, distracting themselves; Tamler says they were "tying themselves to the mast." The problem comes later: following these children and claiming that waiting time predicts SAT scores, and Tamler just read that the SAT correlation used only 35 children, yet schools started teaching delayed gratification on that basis. He dismantles the premises that "delayed gratification causes success" would need to hold: it has to be teachable, rather than merely capturing some natural difference that is itself predictive; self-control has to be the active ingredient, rather than the willingness to please the teacher; and there's the question of why the child believes the other person will really give another one — if you're in an impoverished environment, why wait.

1:32:12 Social priming collapsed, and conceptual priming was buried with it
Bargh's classic study: subjects were randomly assigned a set of words to unscramble, and if those words were related to concepts like elderly and retirement, the speed at which they walked from room A to room B after the task was measured, and it turned out that people primed with the elderly concept walked more slowly. It claimed that stimuli entirely outside consciousness can influence behavior — you don't even know you were assigned the elderly words. Tamler recalls that when he had just graduated, this kind of research was at its peak. Paul says social priming has since been shown to be wrong, but what really bothers him is the consequence: its collapse took down with it conceptual priming (for example, flashing "doctor" to prime "nurse") and other very robust, easily replicated findings — that's what the architecture of the mind actually looks like; the problem was extrapolating it directly to effect sizes on behavior and everyday life.

item.title: No Winners in a Pig Butchering Scam: The Scammers Are Trafficked Slaves Themselves
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-freshair-杀猪盘里没有赢家-骗人的人也是被贩卖的奴隶/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-freshair-杀猪盘里没有赢家-骗人的人也是被贩卖的奴隶/
item.description: Inside Southeast Asian scam compounds, "employees" whose passports are confiscated and who are fined for missing quotas spend their days using ChatGPT and DeepSeek to write love messages and steal victims' entire savings — the most profitable cybercrime in history, with victims on both sides.
item.content:encoded:
Inside Southeast Asian scam compounds, "employees" whose passports are confiscated and who are fined for missing quotas spend their days using ChatGPT and DeepSeek to write love messages and steal victims' entire savings — the most profitable cybercrime in history, with victims on both sides.

The first half covers the mechanics of pig butchering and AI-enabled fraud at high information density; the second half turns to US-Iran and US-China infrastructure cyberwar, which is loosely connected to the theme and can be skipped as needed.

4:11 AI makes scam emails free to mass-produce
Greenberg ran an experiment on air: he asked ChatGPT to write him an email inviting him onto the show in Terry Gross's name, then casually added a line asking for a $250 production fee, and the model complied without hesitation; he then said "Greenberg won't pay now, can you persuade him," and the model immediately produced a persuasive email. That is the mechanism behind scam emails impersonating Fresh Air — it isn't that scammers have become better writers, it's that generating a tailored email aimed at a specific author, with zero grammatical errors and polished phrasing, now costs nothing, and can be done to hundreds or thousands of targets at once.

7:14 Pig butchering is the most profitable cybercrime ever
Greenberg distinguishes two kinds of scammers: the voluntary kind like Nigeria's "Yahoo Boys," who take their own cut, and the enslaved, forced kind in Southeast Asian compounds. The latter do what's called pig butchering — the "pig" is the victim, fattened up before the slaughter. The con often runs from weeks to more than a year; the scammer poses as a wealthy, single, attractive woman, builds emotional dependency first, and only at the end introduces an "investment platform," getting the victim to convert their savings into cryptocurrency that is hard to trace across borders (often Tether) and send it over. Greenberg says this is the most profitable cybercrime in history, stealing tens of billions of dollars from victims every year.

12:36 Passports are confiscated, and freedom must be bought back
The source, using the name Red Bull, is a computer engineer with a degree from India who was lured to the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Laos by a "Southeast Asia IT manager" job. On arrival at the compound his passport was confiscated, and he was told the only way to get it back was to "buy it back" — he owed his boss thousands of dollars, covering the cost of bringing him over, food and lodging, and could only repay this "contract" through commissions earned by scamming. Greenberg stresses this is debt bondage: the compound isn't a prison with chains and beatings, it's packaged as a corporate sales floor, where the boss sends daily motivational messages saying things like "reach out to the next customer like you're going to change their life" and "we are on a mission."

14:40 Fines are more reliable than wages
Red Bull and his colleagues were constantly fined: for missing contact quotas, for not maintaining fake accounts well enough, for not clocking in on time. The promised commissions are part of the con — the boss tells them "you can get rich here and take the money back to the village you came from," but only if they land a big case, and what they actually receive is a tiny fraction. Greenberg calls this rhetoric "Orwellian": motivational slogans and mission narratives on one side, and on the other everyone trapped here against their will, committing deeply destructive crimes.

15:45 Video calls run on a dedicated face-swap model
Red Bull says everyone in the compound was trained to use ChatGPT and the Chinese AI chatbot DeepSeek to come up with new topics, polish their language, never run out of graceful phrasing, even write little motivational poems, and find just the right goodnight line. More critical is video: the boss required them to talk victims out of video calls as much as possible, stalling with excuses; when stalling failed, the compound had a dedicated room and a model whose full-time job was video calls, using face-swap software to change the model's face into the photo originally sent to the victim. Greenberg says this kind of software isn't perfect, but by the video-call stage the victim wants so badly to believe it's real that they overlook the flaws.

18:54 The next step is fully autonomous AI pig butchering
Greenberg's judgment is that AI is currently just a tool for human scammers, but the next step — already starting to appear — is fully autonomous AI fraud. He cites a case from an Anthropic report the previous week: a Chinese group built 20 dating apps populated entirely by AI, where victims had to keep paying to continue the conversation, and "most" of the other side were fully autonomous large models. He also mentions a study showing that at most stages of the scam process, AI is better than a real person at building relationships — more responsive, more invested, more attentive — which is exactly what the con is doing for the vast majority of the time before it reaches the endgame of asking for money.

23:08 Thirty people, three months, only $2.2 million
Greenberg gives a concrete scale: Red Bull's group of about 30 people earned only about $2.2 million in total over the three months Red Bull recorded and leaked to Wired. This shows pig butchering is a game of probability — a single group's output is limited, but Laos alone has dozens of such compounds, and Cambodia and Myanmar have more, and together they add up to the billions of dollars a year. Greenberg also notes that Red Bull himself was a "very inefficient scammer," which is why he was penniless, eating rice from the compound canteen and vegetables that tasted of strange chemicals, constantly sick, and disgusted by what he was doing.

24:12 Forging a police letter to escape, then beaten when caught
Red Bull's escape attempt was to forge a letter from the police in his home state in India, saying he was under investigation and had to return home to deal with it, or his boss would be in trouble too. Greenberg advised him against it, but he went ahead, and the forgery was immediately spotted. The boss locked him in a room, beat him, kicked him, denied him food, interrogated him, and even gave him a glass of water with white powder dissolved in it and forced him to drink it — Greenberg guesses it was some kind of stimulant, making him talk more while his skin broke out in hives. They never found out he was in contact with a journalist; Greenberg says if they had, he would certainly have been killed.

item.title: Entropy Doesn't Mean Things Get Messier: Oil and Water Layering and Frost Crystals Are Spontaneous Order
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-intotheimpossi-熵增不等于变乱-油水分层-霜花结晶都是自发的秩序/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-intotheimpossi-熵增不等于变乱-油水分层-霜花结晶都是自发的秩序/
item.category: Into the Impossible With Brian Keating
item.description: The second law of thermodynamics is often told as "things tend toward disorder," yet oil and water separate, beaches sort themselves, and frost grows on windows — all spontaneous order. Carlo Rovelli says low entropy may not be in the universe but in how we look at it.
item.content:encoded:
The second law of thermodynamics is often told as "things tend toward disorder," yet oil and water separate, beaches sort themselves, and frost grows on windows — all spontaneous order. Carlo Rovelli says low entropy may not be in the universe but in how we look at it.

This episode has medium-to-high information density. The first half on entropy and time is the most valuable; the second half on AI and free will is more speculative. The ad segment can be skipped.

2:03 Oil and water separating isn't anti-entropy — it's entropy producing order
Rovelli uses a set of everyday images to dismantle the popular claim that "entropy = disorder": water and vinegar mix into a uniform blend, but water and oil separate into layers; fine sand and pebbles sort themselves on a beach; frost on a window grows regular structures on its own. He says that under a properly defined notion of "order," many things in nature become spontaneously ordered if you just leave them alone. This doesn't overturn the second law — it says popular science draws the correspondence between "order" and "entropy" too crudely. He points out in particular that the complexity of biology and the structure of Earth's surface are often misread as "anti-entropy," when in fact entropy growth itself constantly produces order.

7:12 Low entropy may not be in the universe but in how you coarse-grain
Rovelli proposes a hypothesis he has written into a paper but isn't sure is right: low entropy means "special," but what's special isn't the state of the universe — it's coarse graining itself. Coarse graining is a perspective: looking at only some variables, not all the details. If the hypothesis holds, the universe can be in a completely arbitrary state, yet from our perspective, which sees only some variables, it appears low-entropy in the direction we call "the past." This turns the "initial low-entropy boundary condition" from a fact about the universe into a question about how an observer slices up information.

12:16 You can be in two places at once — just not to yourself
Rovelli pushes quantum superposition onto people: if quantum mechanics is universal, Brian can be in a superposition of Los Angeles and San Francisco, and Carlo can measure that interference. But to Brian himself, quantum mechanics never tells you that you're in a superposition — you look around and see either San Diego or Los Angeles. So "where you are" is a different thing for you and for me. He compares this to Galileo discovering that velocity is relative: saying "velocity is zero" actually omits "relative to Earth." What quantum mechanics says is that all properties must be understood relative to something.

19:34 Galileo got the tides wrong by violating his own relativity principle
Rovelli uses Galileo's tidal model to show that "having an idea" and "pushing it to the end" are two different things. Galileo thought the combination of Earth's orbit around the sun and its rotation stirred the seas and produced the tides. But Rovelli points out that orbital motion is uniform straight-line motion to first order, and rotation alone can't produce an effect either, so the tides can't come from this — what actually explains the tides is Newton. Galileo himself precisely violated the relativity principle he had discovered. Rovelli says Einstein was the same: after writing general relativity in 1915, he later wrote a paper denying gravitational waves (and corrected it after a referee sent it back), and insisted the Schwarzschild singularity was the end of the world — an error he never corrected until he died.

31:06 Without dissipation you can't record anything
Rovelli says that already in classical mechanics he found a fact that made him "see the light": if you try to model a measuring device with classical mechanics — a barometer, say, or a device that records whether a ball is on the left or the right — you can't do it unless you introduce dissipation. A ball dropped into a box will bounce back up; it must dissipate to stop and leave a record. So measurement is essentially a statistical process requiring dissipation, and this was already true before quantum mechanics — it isn't unique to quantum mechanics. This directly answers the puzzle of "unitary evolution is reversible, so where does irreversibility come from": recording itself requires that something be thrown away.

33:45 A chess program deliberates, and so do you
Rovelli uses his chess computer to dismantle free will: the computer is deterministic, and given its internal state and the opponent's move, its output is necessarily predetermined. But why does it still spend time enumerating all possible moves and evaluating them one by one? Because the only way to reach that result is to go through this evaluation process, and that process is called deliberation. He says it's foolish to say it isn't deliberating, because deliberation is exactly this. Brian is the same: without going through this complex process, he wouldn't make the decision to start a project or choose a career. So-called freedom isn't violating the laws of nature — it is precisely the fact of "having gone through deliberation."

40:56 In principle yes, not now, and within two years he doubts it
Asked whether a machine could have Einstein's "happiest thought" (the equivalence principle in free fall), Rovelli answers in three layers: in principle yes, he doesn't think humans are so special as to be unreproducible; not now; and within two years he's skeptical, though he has no hard evidence that it's impossible. He mentions that last week he had Claude do something his PhD student hadn't finished in a month, and Claude did it in half an hour, so the capability is beyond doubt. But he says Claude didn't invent the equivalence principle, and within two years he thinks that's hard. At the same time he states plainly that there's a lot of hype in AI.

56:45 Ten years and unlimited funding, he'd build a roomful of Josephson junctions
Asked what he'd do with "ten years and unlimited funding," Rovelli's answer isn't a telescope or a collider but a large room full of Josephson junctions, plus an engineering team. The reason: loop quantum gravity predicts particles of Planck mass, possibly dark matter candidates, with a mass roughly equal to a small piece of hair or a flea egg. He says we already know the direction, mass, and interaction strength of dark matter clouds — though it's only an extremely feeble Newtonian gravity — and Josephson junctions could catch it through simple physics. He thinks it's technically feasible within ten years; what's missing is only the money.

item.title: Supersonic Passenger Flight Stalled for Fifty Years — the Engine, Not Aerodynamics, Was the Blocker
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-allin-超音速客机没落五十年-卡在发动机不在空气动力学/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-allin-超音速客机没落五十年-卡在发动机不在空气动力学/
item.description: Concorde wasn't banned because the technology failed; the sonic boom hit the ground. Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban goes away. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and it's now being sent to power data centers first.
item.content:encoded:
Concorde wasn't banned because the technology failed; the sonic boom hit the ground. Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban goes away. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and it's now being sent to power data centers first.

The founder's own account of the full path from being turned down by Bezos to building engines in-house and pivoting to data center power generation, with specific numbers and regulatory detail, at high information density.

5:12 Bend the sonic boom and the ban disappears
Boom's answer to the sonic boom isn't to make the aircraft quiet — it's to use the atmosphere's own refractive capacity to redirect the boom back up into the sky. Blake calls it boomless cruise; engineers call it Mach cutoff. The boom is still generated at the aircraft, at normal strength, but it bends sharply in the air and never reaches the ground. This works below Mach 1.3 — that is, 50% faster than today. So you can't go full speed over land, but a 9 a.m. departure from New York and a 9:30 a.m. arrival in San Francisco still holds. Over the ocean nobody is listening, so full speed is fine. Push the logic to its limit and you get the line: if there's no sonic boom at all, there's nothing to argue about.

5:12 From executive order to act of Congress, unanimous
The U.S. ban on supersonic flight over land, in place since 1973, ended last June 6. But Blake knew an executive order can in theory be overturned by the next person, so he turned to pushing legislation through Congress. The Supersonic Legalization Act passed the House unanimously, and recently cleared a Senate committee unanimously as well. He puts the significance plainly: supersonic isn't a partisan issue, which is the only way to get that kind of vote count. For a hardware company that has to span multiple administrations on a timeline measured in decades, upgrading regulation from executive order to law turns policy risk from a variable into a constant.

6:12 Getting stood up by a big company saved the company
Blake says one of the dumbest things he ever did was outsource engine development to an established large company; the plan failed, the split with Rolls-Royce was public, and everyone said Boom was finished. So they decided to do what everyone said was impossible: build the engine from scratch in-house — and not just design it, but manufacture even the hardest parts, like turbine blades, themselves. His judgment: engineering and manufacturing have to be done together, and if you want to reindustrialize America you have to invent the next generation of manufacturing technology here, not bring back what was offshored to China. That forced choice later became the source of the company's valuation — because an engine designed to run at full power for long periods at the high temperatures of Mach 1.7, with the fan removed from the front and a generator bolted on the back, is a power generation device.

8:13 The supersonic engine's first customer is a data center
Boom's engine's first application isn't in the sky, it's on the ground. Take off the fan, put a generator on the back, drop it into a few trailers, and you can do 42 megawatts of behind-the-meter generation — and because the engine core was designed to run at high temperature anyway, it needs no water. Blake pointedly notes that water is a common objection, so just make it disappear. The factory has already started producing the first parts, with a target of multiple gigawatts a year and more than 10 gigawatts added to the grid over the next five years. The financial significance of this path: before the supersonic airliner ever gets its airworthiness certificate, the company already has a product it can sell — and it's selling to the buyer that is least short of money right now.

10:14 Run on the ground first, then fly
Boom putting the engine to work in ground power generation first has an engineering side effect: it will be the most-tested new jet engine in history, because it will have run for enormous numbers of hours on the ground before ever being installed and flown. Blake admits many hard problems remain and success isn't guaranteed. The promise to passengers: twice as fast over water, 50% faster over land with no sonic boom. The sequencing itself is worth noting — normally an aviation engine's validation comes from accumulating flight hours; Boom has moved validation to the ground and to data center scenarios, effectively having another market pay the test bill for the aviation business.

10:38 Transatlantic round trip, breakeven fare $3,500
The numbers Blake gives: a Mach 1.7 transatlantic round trip in 3 hours, breakeven fare around $3,500, with the actual price most likely higher — and every extra dollar is United's profit. His assessment of Concorde: zero out of three on safe, comfortable and cheap; Boom intends to take all three. On timeline, the target is 4 years, but he states plainly that ‘faster matters more than predictable’, can't give a firm date, and only commits to delivering at the earliest moment physically possible — which from the outside looks like around 2030. There's a tradeoff worth noting here: a hardware company publicly admitting it can't be predicted, trading certainty for speed.

13:15 Data center demand is so big they'll auction it
Asked whether the data center business is a money printer, Blake's answer is ‘it's the most incredible money-printing business I've ever seen’, and he says his inbox holds tens of gigawatts of demand. The first engine fires up next month, and then they plan to auction off all of the capacity. Asked whether he's talked to Elon, or whether this is for Colossus, Blake only says ‘you should ask Elon’. The value of this segment is the anomalous supply-demand signal it gives off: for a power product that isn't in mass production yet, demand already far exceeds capacity, and the pricing mechanism has shifted from a quote to an auction.

16:19 Break the sound barrier Monday, model in the Oval Office Thursday
Blake walks through how fast this regulatory push moved: broke the sound barrier on a Monday, tweeted, Elon retweeted, flew to Washington that night to start lobbying for legalization, and by the time he landed had an invitation from the White House; into the West Wing on Tuesday, and by Thursday the aircraft model was in the Oval Office — and it's still there. From launch to signature, the executive order took 115 days, which he thinks is slow but concedes would be slower under a different administration. His assessment of this administration: ‘I like that it moves fast’. This is the most concrete sample of policy operation in the whole episode: how a single technical milestone gets converted directly into political attention.

item.title: Why renaming a charity is more dangerous than renaming a company
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-masterscale-慈善机构改名-为什么比企业改名更危险/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-masterscale-慈善机构改名-为什么比企业改名更危险/
item.description: Mercy Corps became Prosper Global not because the strategy changed, but because the old name could no longer hold what it already does — and in conflict zones, a rename can put staff more at risk.
item.content:encoded:
Mercy Corps became Prosper Global not because the strategy changed, but because the old name could no longer hold what it already does — and in conflict zones, a rename can put staff more at risk.

Medium information density. The first half is disaster response and the logic of the rename; the second half, on the erosion of international humanitarian law and AI entering aid work, is worth more.

4:21 The rename isn't a new strategy — the old name can't hold the new business
Jada says an organization's identity grows up like a person's. The name Mercy Corps described the starting point of aid — rushing in to save people, handing out food, casting itself as the merciful giver. But what she now discusses with potential donors is cash assistance, seed insurance, identity management on blockchain, and the response she gets is flatly "that has nothing to do with your name." The rename is not a change of mission; mission and values are the source of continuity, the name is not. Prosper Global wants to shorten the conversation and put the values up front: we believe every person has the capacity to prosper, not just to survive.

6:31 Renaming in a conflict zone puts safety on the line
Prosper Global operates in more than 30 countries, many of them remote sub-offices, often in conflict zones. Communities recognize Mercy Corps' colors and know who to look for. A rename means a phased rollout, one country at a time, with local people judging the timing and the context. Jada is blunt: they don't rate armed guards, they don't carry weapons, and their ability to work rests entirely on the trust of the communities they serve. So this is not an ordinary corporate logo swap — in the short term it may make frontline staff more vulnerable. The interesting part: 90% of staff live in the communities they serve, and many program staff were the first to understand the rename — they don't want to be treated as "charity cases."

8:37 Syria is the clearest case for the rename logic
Driving from Aleppo to Damascus, Jada saw rubble the whole way. Syria has just come out of 14 years of civil war and is one of the few countries in the world where the population is flowing back in rather than out, with millions returning home at the same time. But many are still living in camps, and the communities they return to have no working water systems and destroyed houses. She tells the story of a woman named Ola: her husband was injured in the war, she hadn't worked before the war, and her community wasn't used to women doing certain things, so she was forced to take over the farming and start cultivating. Prosper Global helped her set up drip irrigation and repair the local water system, and along the way she learned to ride a motorcycle and brought another group of women along with her. Jada says Syria may be one of the world's rare pieces of good news, and it has been forgotten.

10:44 Oil in Hormuz decides whether African farmers plant at all
Prosper Global published a report called From Hormuz to Hunger, tracking how conflict in the Strait of Hormuz ripples into six fragile countries: Sudan, Somalia, Ethiopia, Pakistan, Myanmar and Lebanon. The mechanism: these countries depend on Hormuz for basic fuel, and higher fuel prices hit fertilizer supply directly. When Jada was in Sudan, farmers had only a two-to-three-week window to get seeds in the ground, and fuel costs had already risen 60%. When farmers can't work out what to plant or which inputs they can afford, some decide to abandon the land. This isn't just a present problem — it cripples next season's food supply too. At the same time, aid organizations are paying higher fuel prices themselves, so the same money serves fewer people.

12:47 Ukraine's grain silos are being bombed on purpose
Prosper Global has just launched a grain storage project with the UN and the Ukrainian Red Cross. Jada says Ukraine actually had a good harvest this year, but Russia is increasingly targeting civilian and economic infrastructure, especially hitting grain silos and storage facilities with drones. The logic is simple: even with a good harvest, if the silos and storage are blown up, or the roads and ports are bombed so the grain can't move, that season's income is gone. This is a deliberate attack on that kind of infrastructure. What they do includes providing sleeved grain storage bags, helping farmers clear mines, and helping those who lost machinery rebuild or find alternatives. Ukraine was once the breadbasket for many countries, and it needs that grain to feed itself and its own economy.

14:47 Prevention costs about seven times less than response, and nobody wants to fund it
Jada says there is a tendency in the current relationship with the US government to fund only life-saving aid, which is in fact the least efficient way to do it. Her number: doing prevention, trying to avert a crisis before it happens, costs roughly seven times less than intervening afterward. She also notes they were ready to rename to Prosper Global before the Trump administration took office, but held off to see how things would shake out — the funding had already vanished and the whole sector was in a hard place. Instead they doubled down on helping Americans understand the nature of humanitarian need and what aid actually looks like today, correcting a lot of misinformation. She says the key to a leadership moment is intentionality: what are you letting go of, and what are you continuing to build on?

19:59 With USAID gone, the sector has to rebuild an architecture
Jada acknowledges they have to do more with less money, but stresses this isn't just about saving money — it's about rebuilding an architecture, in a sense. USAID's offices and missions around the world used to carry a huge amount of coordination and information-sharing, and now all of that is gone. So the question isn't just "can AI help," it's that the sector's entire coordination layer has been pulled out. She says AI can't physically deliver supplies for you and has limits in knowledge, but it's useful at the program level: accessing best practices, targeting more precisely what a community needs, anticipating certain needs. They haven't found the magic solution yet, but they're talking to AI companies, hoping to build something together that genuinely changes humanitarian aid.

23:02 International humanitarian law is eroding, starting with Ukraine
Jada says the checks on international humanitarian law are being tested and violated, and that this is a broader trend. She believes the first case seen as a deliberate pattern was Russia's invasion of Ukraine — attacks on ports, bridges and other civilian infrastructure traditionally treated as untouchable appeared very quickly. Then the pattern spread to the way the war is fought in Sudan, and they believe violations of international law are also occurring in Gaza. She notes it took the deaths and destruction of millions after World War II to bring these rules into being: no collective punishment, people must be able to go to school and have a hospital network, civilians shouldn't pay the price. Now those rules are being violated everywhere. She says even the phrase "international humanitarian law" sounds like Greek to a lot of people.

item.title: In the AI Era the Most Valuable Thing Isn't Intelligence, It's the Audit Trail
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ilt-ai-时代最值钱的不是智能-是审计轨迹/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ilt-ai-时代最值钱的不是智能-是审计轨迹/
item.description: Rogo founder Gabe Stengel says models are already smarter than anyone he knows, and what's left is all plumbing — whoever runs the pipes into banks' compliance and systems of record wins.
item.content:encoded:
Rogo founder Gabe Stengel says models are already smarter than anyone he knows, and what's left is all plumbing — whoever runs the pipes into banks' compliance and systems of record wins.

Worth hearing for vertical AI founders, investment banking/PE practitioners, and enterprise software investors. The first half's product history is only moderately dense with information; the pricing, audit and sales mechanics in the second half are worth more.

2:03 Model companies are refineries; vertical companies are chemical plants
Gabe reasons from Dario's line: if tomorrow a whole data center full of geniuses appeared at the door of Goldman, Millennium, Citadel, those institutions would still take a long time to figure out how to change the way they work and how to wire it into their systems. So he thinks the biggest challenge for every great investor over the next five years is not getting access to intelligence, but wiring AI into the investment lifecycle. It also explains why he isn't worried about Anthropic and OpenAI: finance is a collection of niches each with different data, definitions and regulatory requirements, and for Anthropic to stop and pick up this coin would be pulling over on the road from $100 billion in revenue to $1 trillion.

4:04 Applied AI companies have a first-mover disadvantage
Gabe says companies that did applied AI early were actually at a disadvantage: you think you know where the world is going, you build the product for that end state, but the models aren't there yet, and users try it and just say ‘this is garbage.’ Rogo went through that phase itself. His judgment is that if your read on the end state is right and you keep building toward it, the moment the models catch up is the magic moment. He ties Rogo's product eras directly to model eras: 01 Pro was the first version reliable enough to at least serve as a search tool; by Opus 4.5, and from late 2025 into early 2026, the models can basically do anything a junior investment or banking professional does, provided you give the right instructions and context.

6:06 The MD annotating on an iPad is the real last mile
Gabe gives an example as concrete as it gets: the typical workflow of an investment banking MD is to email deck comments to an analyst, and Rogo lets that MD email the comments to an AI analyst and get a revised draft back in 20 minutes instead of two days, while automatically notifying the junior analysts on the deal and showing a full audit trail of every small change. He points out the key: this finance professional hasn't logged into a computer in ten years, but he has an iPad, and he knows how to annotate on an iPad. That kind of product detail for a specific end user can only be built by someone with a spidey sense for the job.

16:57 The harness matters more than the model itself
Gabe compares Claude Code and Claude Cowork with ChatGPT: the models are actually similar, but Claude's harness and presentation are far better, letting the model exercise more long-horizon capability, and so usage and expansion took off. He extends the analogy to the brain: humans have high agency not just because of raw memory, IQ and knowledge, but because there are a bunch of microservices in the head — how knowledge is stored, how it's retrieved, how it's triggered, and emotion is one way of triggering a microservice. A great investor's judgment comes from seeing something in the market that triggers a memory of some event, producing a creative decision. Those microservices are what vertical companies have to build.

23:43 Skip seat-based pricing and go straight to outcome-based
Rogo today is classic enterprise software: priced per seat, because buyers are used to comparing it to Bloomberg, FactSet, Capital IQ, PitchBook, and every deal needs an AE plus a solutions architect to shake hands and explain the integration. Gabe says selling to them was easy for Anthropic, with spend rising exponentially and no human in the loop, because it's a token-consumption model; but many industries can't ride the token-consumption wave, and Rogo is one of them, so it has to build its GTM machine at five times the speed. His pricing judgment is that every company goes through two pricing revolutions: first to usage based, then to outcome based. He'd rather skip tokens and usage and ask clients directly: how much do you charge per good investment idea? Per quarterly LP report? Per investment banking CIM?

31:19 Auditability matters more than accuracy
Gabe says accuracy is of course still super important, but auditability matters more than accuracy, and the two are often conflated. The logic: if the answer is inaccurate and you don't know how to check it or see where it came from, then whether it's accurate or not you can't use it, because you don't trust it. Conversely, if it's right most of the time and even when it's wrong you can clearly see the assumptions and the data sources, it's still actionable and still saves time. As tools move from copilot to autopilot — not just retrieving information but having agency, actually making investment decisions or sending emails — you have to be able to look back at why it decided the way it did, because you need to debug it, just as when an individual investor makes a bad decision you check whether the data input was wrong or someone lied to him. In regulated capital markets, a decision you can't explain doesn't get past the gate.

34:48 The company brain is called Shrek, and every conversation is recorded
Every conversation inside Rogo is recorded, and new hires are told on day one ‘you are always being recorded’; the content is filtered into the company brain, named Shrek because the engineers thought that was funny. There's a dashboard showing the ‘swamp’ of what everyone is working on, connected to the company's various systems, with a very clear sense of company goals, values, what has to be delivered to clients, and the north star metric, so it can shape every answer and deliverable. It's both passive and active: you can go in and ask ‘how do I pitch the value proposition and savings of model routing to a large institution’ and it pulls the information out; it also proactively reminds you ‘Patrick, I see you're meeting this private credit firm on Thursday, here's what you should know, the use cases that will resonate, and the ROI metrics companies you've worked with in the past want to hear.’ Gabe says this is the core problem of enablement: absorb information in, and give it out when people need it.

42:18 What it's like to be rejected by 40 investors in a row
Gabe says the hardest low point was the A round: at the time there were no star investors on the cap table, David Tisch introduced him to 40 investors, he met Sequoia, Kleiner, Benchmark and others, and all 40 passed. And not the send-a-deck-no-interest kind: it was ‘interesting, meet Gabe’‘like Gabe, talk for an hour’‘come to IC’‘let's grab a meal’‘come back over the weekend’ — and then ‘we've decided not to invest.’ He says that phase had nothing to do with anything except you, like being dumped by 40 girlfriends, each time you fell in love and each time they said it wasn't for you. In the end Thrive didn't invest either; Keith Rabois came about a month after everyone had passed, and Gabe asked Keith back: if this isn't a contrarian bet, why do all your friends say it's a bad idea and none of them believe in me? He sums up three reasons investors didn't invest: they underestimated the finance TAM, the product really was bad at the time, and there weren't enough data points to believe he could chew glass and ship the next version.

item.title: The Rocky Statue Is Not Art, but It Became a Landmark Philadelphia Can't Tear Down
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ninepi-洛奇雕像不是艺术品-却成了费城拆不掉的地标/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ninepi-洛奇雕像不是艺术品-却成了费城拆不掉的地标/
item.description: A bronze made for a movie, rejected by the art commission, moved to a sports arena, left to sit in a warehouse — in the end what saved it wasn't artistic merit but that Philadelphians claimed it. A statue's status is always granted by its audience, not by the experts.
item.content:encoded:
A bronze made for a movie, rejected by the art commission, moved to a sports arena, left to sit in a warehouse — in the end what saved it wasn't artistic merit but that Philadelphians claimed it. A statue's status is always granted by its audience, not by the experts.

Thirty minutes, one complete narrative arc: class, artistic authority, race and monument politics, dense with detail and almost no filler.

4:09 Bronze instead of foam decided its fate
In Rocky III there's a scene: a fictional mayor stands on the museum steps and dedicates a statue to Philadelphia. The production could have had the art department build a prop out of painted plastic and foam and toss it in a dumpster after shooting. Stallone didn't do that — he paid $53,000 to have the artist A. Thomas Schaumburg cast the statue in bronze. Laura Holzman says that choice was crucial: it wasn't made of a material you throw away after filming, it was made of an art material. Stallone went to high school in Philadelphia, called Rocky a ‘euphemism’ for the city, and then offered to donate the 1,800-pound statue to Philadelphia to stand permanently at the top of the steps. Precisely because it was bronze and not foam, the fifty-year fight that followed was even possible.

10:25 The root of the opposition was Philadelphia wanting to be Athens
The museum leadership opposed it most fiercely, and their reasons were far bigger than aesthetics. Philadelphia's glory days had long faded by the early 20th century, and by the 1976 Bicentennial it was the city that could never shake its bad luck: crumbling infrastructure, corrupt local politics. In the 1980s the arts world wanted to remake Philadelphia as a cultural metropolis and restore the title a famous architect had given it — ‘the Athens of the Western world.’ They had bet heavily on the city's most important museum, and they didn't see how a nine-foot-tall, sharply abdominals boxing could help Philadelphia get there. Art commission chairman F. Eugene Dixon Jr. wrote to a colleague that the statue standing temporarily on the steps was fine, but putting it permanently in the courtyard — ‘I hope you're joking.’ In the winter of 1980 the commission voted 6 to 2 against permanent placement; the remaining two votes were to ban it from the steps outright.

12:34 Thousands of signatures couldn't beat eight people with votes
What brought the statue back to Philadelphia from Los Angeles was a grassroots campaign. Local truck driver Art Gorman was one of its biggest champions — Mark Bowden describes him as a straight-talking Philly guy from a blue-collar neighborhood, thinking: who are these self-appointed sophisticates to tell us what we can see on the steps of the art museum? At the end of 1980 he drafted a petition, all in capital letters, knocked on doors for thousands of signatures, and drew a pile of media coverage. The show says it plainly: the story got told as blue-collar Philadelphia versus elite high-culture Philadelphia, a ‘slobs versus snobs’ narrative. But the petition couldn't change the commission's basic position — the snobs were still the ones voting.

13:34 The prop crew bolted the statue into the ground with steel bars
Rocky III opened in May 1982, and the art commission only allowed the statue back on the steps for the premiere; once it was over, it had to go. But the production company simply left it there, the city wouldn't pay to move it, and it was up to the museum to deal with it. Months later the movers finally came and found an obstacle: the statue was bolted to the sidewalk with steel bars driven several feet into the ground — ‘as if the filmmakers intended it to stay there forever.’ In the end the statue was pried loose and hauled five miles away to the Spectrum arena in South Philadelphia, where it stood with other athletes' statues. Most people thought the fight was over, but over the next twenty-five years Stallone repeatedly asked to move it back to the museum, and every time he got the same answer: no.

15:35 One phone call did more than twenty years of aesthetic debate
In 2006 things moved: the mayor was pushing a batch of public-space renovation projects, Stallone was about to release his first Rocky film in 16 years, and the statue was sitting in a warehouse because the city was building a new sports complex. Stallone's friend Jimmy Binns — who appeared in the sequels and is a well-connected Philadelphia lawyer — called the mayor and asked if he'd help get the statue back to the museum. Binns recounted the conversation: he asked the mayor, do those museum trustees invite you to their homes for cocktails on Sundays? The mayor laughed and said no. Binns said, then screw them. The mayor said, all right, screw them. With the mayor behind it, even the Philadelphia Museum of Art started to give ground, and the compromise worked out was: the statue returns to the museum permanently, but not at the top of the steps — a little off to the side at the bottom. The only remaining obstacle was the art commission, which held the final vote.

19:46 By 2006 the debate was no longer about art
In May 2006 the commission announced it might move the statue, setting off a new round of public discussion. City official Harris Baum argued against it on a local NPR call-in show, on the grounds that the Parkway was to be developed into a cultural district like Paris's, ‘but that's not a work of art.’ The response he got was completely different from the 1980s: listeners didn't want to talk about art. Judy said the statue was an image of the blue-collar spirit; Jack, calling from Lansdale, said ideally he'd want it at the top of the steps, but a bunch of pretentious old guys in wigs wouldn't let that happen, and he flat-out called Baum a snob and insulting. Baum was fighting the battle of twenty years earlier. On September 6, 2006, the art commission voted 6 to 2 in favor, and the minutes read: the majority believed the statue's iconic symbolism had earned it a place in the city's identity. Less than a week later the statue was unveiled, fitted with nighttime lighting, and lifted onto a brand-new granite base.

26:14 The real champion's steps are called the Rocky steps
The 2015 Charleston church shooting (nine dead) set off a national reckoning with racist symbols, and the wind reached Philadelphia: the Columbus statue and the statue of former mayor Frank Rizzo — known for violent policing and racist demagoguery — became targets. When Monument Lab asked Philadelphians what kind of monuments they wanted, some began questioning whether Rocky was appropriate: Philadelphia has a real boxing history, and those fighters were mostly Black, including heavyweight champion Joe Frazier, who beat Muhammad Ali in a fight watched by more than 300 million people. The show points out that the two most famous things in the first Rocky training montage — running up the museum steps and punching raw meat — actually came from Frazier's real training routine. Frazier got a statue in 2015, but many Philadelphians feel the twelve-foot bronze falls far short of a real champion: ‘His image isn't on the tour buses, and the steps he ran up are called the Rocky steps.’

28:21 In the reckoning over monuments, Rocky became the city's emotional container
After George Floyd was killed in 2020, Philadelphia's largest Black Lives Matter demonstrations set out from the art museum steps every day, with thousands of protesters gathering right beside the Rocky statue. By then it was already a monument, and by rights it should have faced the same scrutiny — a statue of a fictional white movie character that stole the place of a real Black champion, its days should have been numbered. But no one tore it down; instead they folded it in: someone hung a sign on it reading ‘no justice, no peace,’ early in the pandemic it got a face mask, later a Ukrainian flag, and when the Eagles' Brandon Graham retired, his cleats were hung on it. Paul Farber saw the most contradictory scene: a Black family posing for a photo all raising Black Power fists, and three or four people later, a group of white men in their early twenties raising white power gestures — the two things happening almost simultaneously without conflict.

item.title: Vitamin K Refusal Rates Have Doubled, and Infant Brain Hemorrhage Is Preventable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-tpwky-维生素-k-注射被拒率翻倍-婴儿脑出血本可避免/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-tpwky-维生素-k-注射被拒率翻倍-婴儿脑出血本可避免/
item.description: Every newborn is physiologically deficient in vitamin K at birth, and a single intramuscular injection drops the risk of late bleeding to near zero; but US refusal rates have risen from 3% to 5.8%, and babies whose parents refuse face 81 times the risk of late bleeding.
item.content:encoded:
Every newborn is physiologically deficient in vitamin K at birth, and a single intramuscular injection drops the risk of late bleeding to near zero; but US refusal rates have risen from 3% to 5.8%, and babies whose parents refuse face 81 times the risk of late bleeding.

High information density: it covers both the clinical mechanics of newborn hemorrhage and the history of vitamin K's discovery and how a 1950s overdose scandal destroyed trust. The second half, on who refuses and why communication fails, is the most valuable part.

20:34 Every newborn is born deficient in vitamin K
Vitamin K does not cross the placenta effectively, so even if the mother supplements during pregnancy, the newborn's vitamin K-dependent clotting factors do not rise appreciably. Add an immature gut microbiome and very little endogenous K2 synthesis, and breast milk averaging only about 2.5 micrograms per liter, and a exclusively breastfed infant takes in less than 1 microgram a day for the first six months. The result is that every newborn is at high risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding. This is not an outlier phenomenon; it is the physiological norm.

22:35 Late bleeding often comes with no warning, straight to brain hemorrhage
Vitamin K deficiency bleeding in newborns comes in three types: early, within 24 hours of birth; classic, within the first week; and late, from one week to six months. Late is the most dangerous: about 60% of cases are intracranial hemorrhage, and there is often no warning bleed beforehand, just sudden brain hemorrhage, seizures or unresponsiveness. Mortality ranges from 50% to 60% depending on era and country, with modern figures around 20%. That is why the value of a single preventive shot cannot be measured by "the bleeding probability is low."

25:46 A single intramuscular injection pushes risk to near zero
Since 2003 in the US, and in the vast majority of medical societies and public health agencies worldwide, a single intramuscular vitamin K injection at birth is recommended. It provides stable supply for the first few months, cutting late bleeding risk from 4 to 7 cases per 100,000 live births (some countries report as high as 80) to about 0.4. Infants who receive no prophylaxis have 81 times the risk of late bleeding compared with those who do. Oral regimens also significantly reduce risk, but require multiple doses, are affected by absorption and vomiting, are less effective than injection, and no oral formulation is approved by regulators in the US.

44:27 How a 1950s overdose scandal destroyed trust
In the postwar research climate, informed consent and patient protections had not yet entered the picture, and the logic was "vitamin is harmless and possibly beneficial, so give it to all premature infants." In the mid-1950s Britain gave some premature infants up to 60 milligrams of synthetic vitamin K, after which jaundice, hemolysis and kernicterus rose, and several infants died. The formulation was withdrawn and the dose dropped back to 1 milligram, but confidence had been shaken: of more than 16,000 infants born in Britain in a single week in 1970, only 20% received vitamin K. This history shows the aftershocks of a single overdose incident can last decades.

46:31 The 1990s leukemia scare has never fully cleared
In the early 1990s two British studies linked intramuscular vitamin K to later leukemia risk, and the reaction was swift and strong: some countries switched to recommending oral dosing and reserved injections for the highest-risk infants, and British injection rates fell from 58% in 1988 to 38% in 1993. But both studies had small samples and insufficient controls, and a large body of subsequent research and a WHO working group found no association, with IARC also concluding there was no evidence of carcinogenicity. The problem is that bad news travels fast and good news does not, just like MMR and autism: once doubt is planted, the world never quite recovers.

49:35 Refusal rates have doubled, and the 81-fold risk is badly underestimated
US refusal rates nearly doubled from 2017 to 2024, rising from 3% to 5.8%, with some hospitals reporting higher. Infants whose parents refuse have 81 times the risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a figure that is badly underestimated because the bleeding itself remains rare and communication is inadequate. Research shows most parents, whether they accept or refuse, know vitamin K is related to bleeding, but do not know that this bleeding can cause severe brain injury and a mortality risk above 20%. The information is present, but it is not being effectively conveyed.

50:36 Refusal reasons fall into three categories, and birth attendants matter enormously
Refusal reasons roughly fall into three categories: distrust of medicine, pursuit of "natural birth," and preference for alternative medical lifestyles. Some argue that if infants needed more vitamin K, evolution or God would have provided it; others read a recommendation to supplement vitamin K as "you are not fit to be a mother." Research also finds refusers are more likely to be white, college-educated, over 30, and planning a home or birth-center delivery. The birth attendant's stance is critical: in a New Zealand survey, 100% of doctors thought all infants should receive vitamin K, while only 55% of midwives did, and 26% of those would not give it to their own children; in Canada, infants delivered by midwives were 8 times more likely to have vitamin K refused than those delivered by doctors.

55:46 Doctors are seeing newborns bleed to death for the first time
Some parents who lost a child or whose child suffered brain injury because vitamin K was not given are doing something very brave: saying publicly, "I made this decision, this is the consequence, don't do what I did." At the same time, doctors are seeing newborns bleed to death for the first time in their careers, and they are raising the alarm in their communities. Some researchers and doctors are pushing to establish a national US registry of vitamin K refusal and administration, because vitamin K deficiency bleeding is not a notifiable disease and cases are likely undercounted. In a post-pandemic era when expertise is treated as a dirty word, these preventable injuries and deaths will keep increasing.

item.title: US Strategic Oil Reserve Hits Bottom, and Venezuelan Oil Can't Save It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-indicator-美国战略石油储备见底-委内瑞拉石油救不了它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-indicator-美国战略石油储备见底-委内瑞拉石油救不了它/
item.description: The salt-cavern reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1982, and overuse is dissolving the salt walls and destabilizing the caverns; Venezuelan oil is a different grade and needs $100 billion in infrastructure, and it still runs into the dead end of congressional appropriations.
item.content:encoded:
The salt-cavern reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1982, and overuse is dissolving the salt walls and destabilizing the caverns; Venezuelan oil is a different grade and needs $100 billion in infrastructure, and it still runs into the dead end of congressional appropriations.

Medium information density, but it explains the physical degradation mechanism of the SPR — the part most coverage omits. Suited to anyone watching energy security and macro.

0:00 He promised to fill it, and it fell another 30%
In his inaugural address, Trump promised to fill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve ‘to the top’, but since then the reserve has fallen another 30%. The Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz, a huge share of the world's oil couldn't get out, and the reserve was used as a price buffer to shield Americans from the global supply shortfall. The problem is that the buffer itself is nearly used up. Trump's new answer is Venezuelan oil, which he called ‘the largest oil deal in our nation's history’, saying 65 billion barrels would go to the US. But the question the show pursues is: can Venezuelan oil really save the SPR? And what does this mean for ordinary people's wallets?

2:03 The reserve isn't tanks, it's salt caverns dissolved out of the ground
After the Arab oil embargo against the US in the early 1970s, the US government realized it needed a standby oil supply, and the SPR was born. About 30 countries around the world hold standby reserves — Japan, Germany and Australia all have them — but the American version is unusual. Siddharth Mishra, a petroleum engineering professor at Texas A&M, says the US government decided the most efficient way to store millions of barrels of oil wasn't metal tanks but salt caverns. Engineers pump in huge volumes of water to dissolve underground salt layers and create cavities — these aren't traditional caves you can walk into, they're man-made caverns, single cylinders roughly the size of the Empire State Building or larger. Between Texas and Louisiana, 60 such caverns make up the SPR.

4:10 Overuse is dissolving the caverns themselves
The SPR was first tapped in 1991 for Desert Storm, then for Hurricane Katrina, the 2011 Arab Spring and the 2022 Ukraine war. The 2022 global release saved Americans roughly 17 to 42 cents per gallon. But the reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1982, and it's dropping fast — down 50% over the past six years, with 85% of that attributable to the Ukraine and Iran wars. The risk isn't just about volume: the lower the reserve, the more water needs to be injected, the more room there is for the oil to be contaminated, and refineries don't like contaminated oil, making it harder to sell; contamination also forms sludge that makes rapid extraction harder — and rapid extraction is the entire point of the SPR's existence. As water keeps being injected, the salt layers dissolve, the cavern structures become unstable, and this engineering marvel that once amazed Mishra is being weakened.

5:13 Filling the reserve runs into Congress having to pay
Joseph Mikit, an energy security expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, says the US is not in a position to simply buy oil and fill the reserve. Under the normal mechanism, Congress has to agree to buy oil and bury it underground, and with the fiscal deficit as severe as it is, that's a hard problem. Previous administrations thought up workarounds: under Clinton and George W. Bush there was the royalty-in-kind program — when companies produced oil from federally owned reserves, instead of paying the government in cash they handed over oil directly to go into the SPR. Now the government is looking at more unusual strategies: in April, Energy Secretary Chris Wright proposed drilling for oil beneath military bases, but nothing more was heard; the recent headline plan is Venezuelan oil, with a private company giving the US 20% control of its existing and future oil fields in Venezuela.

6:15 Venezuelan oil is not the same grade as what's in the SPR
A key detail: Venezuelan oil is a completely different type from the oil in the US SPR, so it has to go through some kind of trading mechanism — sell one grade, buy another. Energy security expert Joseph is optimistic about the Venezuela deal, believing such a trade could work. He says the plan needs a lot of mechanisms to line up, but it adds a source of oil that won't cause large-scale market disruption, and it doesn't require the US to get Congress to agree to spend big on filling the SPR at a time of high oil prices and fiscal imbalance. In other words, any plan that doesn't require Congress to buy oil looks great. But the challenge is that getting oil out of the Venezuelan ground is notoriously hard, and after years of underinvestment and corruption it needs enormous infrastructure investment.

7:19 $100 billion, and no one knows who pays
One Latin American energy expert puts the figure at $100 billion over the next decade to restore Venezuelan production to where it was 20 years ago. And it's unclear who foots the bill — oil companies, the US government, or someone else. Arnab Data, a managing director at Employ America focused on energy markets, flatly calls the Venezuela plan ‘a bit of a pipe dream’. His objection: our own domestic and allied production can meet demand, so why support Venezuelan production? Rather than putting $100 billion into another country, coordinating between institutions and untangling Venezuela's political chaos, it would be better to put that money into the SPR. His words: we don't need to go out looking for oil, there's plenty in the fridge, right here.

8:22 The current oil-lending mechanism actually works fine
Arnab thinks the Trump administration's current strategy is working well: the Energy Department lends barrels to oil companies, which promise to return them later, at a premium of up to 24%. He sees this as a well-executed way of delivering to the market, while also signaling to the market that there's demand for US barrels. So here's the split: Joseph is optimistic about the Venezuela deal, seeing it as a source of oil that doesn't disrupt the market and doesn't need congressional appropriations; Arnab thinks it's a pipe dream, that the existing lending mechanism is already sufficient, and that the $100 billion would be better put back into the SPR. The show closes with a reminder: global oil supply keeps falling, another strait is under Houthi control and at risk of closing, and Americans don't know how much longer the SPR can shield them from higher costs.

item.title: Making a Child Perform Isn't Connection, It's Depletion
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-unruffled-让孩子表演不是连接-是在消耗他/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-unruffled-让孩子表演不是连接-是在消耗他/
item.description: Connection isn't getting your child to repeat what he knows to please you — it's observing, receiving, and treating him as a person. Performance connection is fast food: gone the moment it's eaten.
item.content:encoded:
Connection isn't getting your child to repeat what he knows to please you — it's observing, receiving, and treating him as a person. Performance connection is fast food: gone the moment it's eaten.

This episode isn't dense — it's a single-topic parenting podcast. But if you're dealing with relatives pushing your child to perform, or you want to understand what "connection" actually means, it's worth a listen.

1:04 Making a child perform is fast-food connection
A mother writes in that her 17-month-old son can identify shapes and colors, speak in sentences, and name dinosaurs, but his grandmother always makes him "perform" — repeating what he's learned, clapping — and when he won't cooperate she grabs his arm and does it for him, and recently even kicked him in the butt. Janet says this isn't an isolated case: we often think connecting with infants and toddlers means getting them to react to us, to imitate us. But this is "fast-food connection." The child may smile because he's getting attention, but no one is truly seen.

4:08 We're performing too
Connection is two-way: we don't just make the child perform — we're often performing too, rather than being ourselves. In her forthcoming book Baby Person, Janet writes that she used to dance, make funny faces, and try every trick to get a reaction out of babies in order to bond with them. These surface methods left her exhausted, and the payoff was tiny and fleeting — "I made her laugh" is just a moment. She says this isn't deep connection; it's all surface.

6:14 Performance connection teaches a child to be insincere
Janet lists five reasons connection shouldn't be a performance: one, it isn't real connection; two, it teaches the child insincerity — everything we do with our children teaches them something, and this teaches that "connection requires performing rather than being yourself"; three, it wastes energy and effort, and parents can't afford it; four, it doesn't satisfy, and doesn't move the relationship toward trust; five, it subtly belittles the child — why should a child have to perform to hold our attention and interest?

8:19 Charismatic people are charismatic because they're paying attention to you
Janet quotes something she's always remembered: certain people are charismatic to us not because of how they perform or what they put out, but because they're genuinely interested in us and paying attention to us. Children especially need this, because it's harder for them to express themselves proactively and they don't know what to say to connect. They need us to tune in to their subtleties: what they're interested in, what their expressions are saying, who they are.

9:19 Even a parenting expert couldn't connect with her grandchild
Janet read a book by a well-known psychologist regarded as a parenting expert, in which the author — now a grandparent — said she simply couldn't connect with a toddler grandchild and felt the child had no chemistry with her. Janet's immediate read: this grandparent was trying too hard — wanting to initiate play, wanting the child to cooperate, operating rather than connecting. Her method works for every child from infancy on: observe, listen, receive, pay attention.

10:21 Comment on what you see instead of pretending to be interested
The concrete approach: treat the child as a person with depth, talents, interests, and a real point of view worth knowing. Then comment on what you see — "You're looking over there, did you hear a dog?" "You seem really interested in those blocks, I see you lining them up." Not pretending to be interested, but actually becoming interested. Children can tell the difference between "good job" and "wow, that took a while, I saw you thinking about which one goes on top, and the round one rolled down."

12:31 Children can put a grandparent's behavior in context
How do you let go of the fear that "this is bad for my child"? Janet says children are more aware than we think. They know "this is my grandparent, this isn't how my parents are with me, this is just how this person is." So it won't affect how they feel about themselves. Parents have enormous influence, but grandparents are different — even with frequent contact, a child can put it in the context of "my relationship with that person."

14:34 Narrate instead of correcting
Janet advises this mother not to try to teach or correct her own mother, but to connect, reflect, and trust them to handle the relationship themselves. Concretely: if her son does what the grandmother asks, let it go; if he won't and the grandmother kicks him, don't say to the grandmother "you shouldn't do that" — instead say to her son, "Grandma really likes it when you do what she asks, she's really into this" — without sarcasm, just stating what's happening. This is called sportscasting: it helps both the child and the grandmother understand what's going on.

item.title: The Pentagon doesn't lack models — it lacks the chain that puts intelligence on the president's desk
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-五角大楼不缺模型-缺的是把情报送到总统桌上的那条链/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-五角大楼不缺模型-缺的是把情报送到总统桌上的那条链/
item.description: The real miracle of the U-2 wasn't the aircraft — it was procurement reform, the intelligence analysis agencies, and the chain that carried judgment to the president. Today AI has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it, and APIs alone are not enough.
item.content:encoded:
The real miracle of the U-2 wasn't the aircraft — it was procurement reform, the intelligence analysis agencies, and the chain that carried judgment to the president. Today AI has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it, and APIs alone are not enough.

The first half uses the U-2 analogy to lay out the bottleneck in government AI integration; the second half's judgments on procurement incentives, token economics and cybersecurity are worth more, but overall it's a loose interview chat with medium information density.

2:02 The U-2's miracle wasn't the plane, it was the procurement and analysis chain
Garrett says the U-2 story is usually told as a technology breakthrough, but what really mattered was three things: procurement reform that let government and industry work together that way, intelligence analysis being institutionalized (NPIC, which later became NGA), and getting judgment in front of the president and other decision-makers. That, he says, is the ‘miraculous’ part of the story. Today's AI problem is the opposite: the technology comes from the commercial world and moves too fast, and it has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it into systems, workflows and decision processes — so ‘APIs alone are not enough’.

9:06 AI is moving fastest in operations, slowest in business systems
Garrett says the Pentagon and other departments have made visible progress in operational spaces like CJADC2: using AI to build situational awareness across the battlefield, identify targets, and get intelligence quickly to decision-makers at the front. But core business systems — logistics, personnel, finance — have seen the least progress. His personal view is that we should stop dividing systems into ‘mission systems’ and ‘business systems’, because supporting the front line requires clean, well-organized data usable at operational tempo, and those business systems were never built for operational tempo.

10:06 One policy rule blocks the data of twenty thousand logistics troops
He gives a concrete example: some business systems' rules say status only needs to be updated once a week. That's policy — someone wrote it down. But decision-makers now want that data daily, which means going to roughly ten or twenty thousand Army supply sergeants and saying ‘you have to enter it daily, not weekly’. That's ‘a big boat to turn around’, and it has to come with clear value. Worse, the systems the government gave them were bad to begin with — making it hard to enter data while also demanding a big drop in data latency.

14:10 Government has no market competition as a forcing function
The host points out that companies that don't do AI get wiped out, but the Air Force or the national security system won't be ‘competed away’ — that kind of forcing function comes once or twice a century. Garrett agrees, but says we underestimate our ability to manufacture mechanisms. He argues for using personnel policy and leadership as carrot and stick: reward people who take risks and take weird career paths, and let people who don't move fast enough face career stagnation or removal. He says it sounds ‘crude’, but that's the mechanism you have to follow.

19:18 Second-mover advantage: watch others burn money first
Garrett says this time it's the reverse of the U-2 — the technology happens in the commercial world first and then goes into government, so government has second-mover advantage and can see what's working. He cites the lesson of token economics: do you open it up like Uber and let everyone burn tokens without limit, blowing the budget in a quarter, or do you understand token economics first and then deploy to employees? Also, as the federal government, if you do it right you can be a super-sized buyer and negotiate bulk pricing.

23:20 Putting GPUs at the front line first means clearing the liability policy
Garrett says if you put tools in soldiers' hands, you'd be shocked at how innovative and clever they are at using them for their actual jobs — which may mean pushing compute to the edge, putting GPUs in service members' hands. But the obstacle is policy: a logistics officer signs for $500,000 worth of chips, and who's responsible if a chip breaks? He says you have to clear the policy and just say ‘we own this risk’ — if it means some GPUs get broken and money is lost, that's worth it, because capability reaches the edge.

29:26 Intelligence analysis is more tractable than modeling decisions
Garrett thinks using AI to model strategic decisions is very hard, because it needs good data, and the decision process is deliberately murky — you can't get all the private notes, emails and situation-room audio and video. But intelligence analysis is a more tractable project: the intelligence process is structured and rigorous, agencies have their own SOPs and training, there are decades of data, and there are signals of quality, so you can build benchmarks from that. Still, it's only one input to decisions — historically many decision-makers looked at the same intelligence and made completely different decisions.

38:36 Bill by the hour and people will report more hours
Garrett says government buys a lot on hourly rates by person and seniority, and this time and materials structure has a status quo bias. The logic is plain: if the incentive is for companies to report more hours, and there's no hard delivery requirement at the end of those hours, they will report more hours. He says there have been signs of change over the past 12 to 18 months, but looking at public spending data, there's no large-scale shift — most spending is still time and materials. He also mentions that top companies spend 10% of their budget on tokens, while the US government is far below that level.

item.title: Procrastination isn't a willpower problem: you'll fail again next time with the same plan
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-clearerthink-拖延不是意志力问题-下次你还会用同一个计划失败/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-clearerthink-拖延不是意志力问题-下次你还会用同一个计划失败/
item.description: Procrastination is delaying despite knowing it hurts you, and about one in five adults does it chronically. Anxiety, distraction, burnout and perfectionism each need a different fix, but they share one premise: change nothing about the plan and nothing about the result changes.
item.content:encoded:
Procrastination is delaying despite knowing it hurts you, and about one in five adults does it chronically. Anxiety, distraction, burnout and perfectionism each need a different fix, but they share one premise: change nothing about the plan and nothing about the result changes.

It breaks procrastination into types you can actually treat and hands you a concrete toolbox instead of another round of "just be disciplined" platitudes. Medium-to-high information density.

1:16 The definition of procrastination has reluctance baked into it
Itamar's definition is: we put off a task even though we don't intend to put it off, and we know it's bad for us. So "I deliberately decided to do it later and I feel fine about that" is not procrastination. The grey zone is: what if you think delaying is good for you but it's actually harmful? His test is "could you have been expected to know it was better for you." About 20% of adults procrastinate chronically, and among students it's 50%. He stresses that procrastination doesn't only happen to people who don't care — people who are highly conscientious, genuinely productive, and sincerely want to make an impact procrastinate too.

3:27 Procrastination is several types, not one thing
Treating procrastination as a single phenomenon makes two mistakes at once: you fail to see that it happens to people other than students, and you can't deal with it in practice. Because a student who procrastinates from distraction, an executive who procrastinates from burnout, and an artist who procrastinates from perfectionism have different drivers and need different solutions. In his book Itamar distinguishes the anxious type, the pulled-away-by-external-temptation type, the burnout type, and a category he calls zigzaggers — closer to ADHD and impulsivity, switching back and forth between internal rather than external distractions.
