5:00 Anxiety cuts both ways: fear of the task versus fear of the consequences
The mechanism by which anxiety causes procrastination is: doing this hurts, the brain says I don't want to hurt, so you push it away. But anxiety also has an adaptive side — if what you're anxious about isn't the task itself but the consequences of not finishing it, a little anxiety pushes you to act. The key variables are intensity and self-efficacy: a little anxiety may motivate you, a lot of anxiety paralyzes you no matter what it's aimed at; and if you also feel you're incapable of finishing, anxiety turns into paralysis more easily. Itamar adds one caveat: even when anxiety does push you, it's a dangerous source of motivation, because it also brings stress and a worse experience.

9:25 The biggest mistake is believing you'll try harder next time
Itamar says the biggest mistake people make when tackling procrastination is falling into the self-control fallacy: believing that next time, if you just try harder and summon more willpower, you'll get it done. The absurdity is that we watch it fail over and over, and over and over we believe again. The reasons include the bias blind spot (failing to recognize your own biases) and the empathy gap (predicting, in a calm state, what you'll do in a hot emotional state). The real harm of this belief is that it offers a superficially minimal silver bullet, which stops you from looking for what actually works. Spencer's addition: change nothing, and nothing changes.

12:45 Design for your future self as if they were someone else
Spencer's approach: don't assume that the you of two weeks from now will get it done on willpower; instead ask "what would help a person very much like me get this done in two weeks" — set reminders, make social commitments, add rewards. Itamar says this is exactly an illustration of his core claim: procrastination isn't a time management problem, and even excellent time management can fail; what you should do is distance management. Calling yourself by the second or third person, or using your name instead of "I", or asking "what advice would I give a friend", all create psychological distance and help you enter wise reasoning, seeing through the situation and sidestepping bias.

16:13 Anxious type: decatastrophize, or do it anxious
For the anxious procrastinator, Itamar's first choice is to decatastrophize: catastrophizing means overestimating both the probability that something bad happens and the harm it does to you. For example, "there's a typo in my proposal, so the agent will blacklist me, and tell everyone else to blacklist me too." The move is to ask: how likely is this to happen? If it did happen, how bad would the impact be? If it happened, how would I carry on? Spencer offers an almost opposite strategy: notice that this task makes me anxious, sit inside that feeling, feel it, and then do it anyway — he calls it metacognitive awareness. Itamar files it under the umbrella of mindfulness and self-compassion.

21:39 Procrastination is short-term emotional repair, and it reinforces itself
Spencer points out that anxiety creates anxiety: the moment you say "I'm not doing it now", the anxiety usually drops immediately, and you're learning "procrastinating makes me feel better", forming a reinforcement loop. Doing the opposite can unwind it — doing it while anxious functions like an exposure. Itamar says procrastination here is a defense mechanism: because you feel pressure or anxiety about what you should be doing, you push it away to avoid the painful emotion. It makes you feel better in the short term and worse in the long term, because you haven't solved the problem — you've only arranged to face it again and again later, or to face worse consequences.

26:39 The burnout fix is to do less
Itamar admits this is the last thing burned-out people want to hear: if you're burned out because you're doing too much, or doing things that drain you, you probably need to do less and take more deliberate care of yourself — concretely, deciding more deliberately what to do and, more importantly, what not to do. He describes a loop: you're used to performing well, burnout makes your performance drop, so you work even harder, then burn out more, and it gets worse and worse. He calls this "borrowing health and productivity from your future self." He also notes that burnout doesn't come only from hours: reasonable hours with high-pressure, meaningless, or otherwise draining tasks will burn you out just the same.

item.title: The cost of RLHF is mode dropping, not alignment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-latentspace-rlhf-的代价是-mode-dropping-不是对齐/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-latentspace-rlhf-的代价是-mode-dropping-不是对齐/
item.description: RLHF forces models to be extremely conservative to avoid mistakes, poisoning the probability distribution over strings; TypeSafe's Jev takes another path, optimizing only intelligence per dollar.
item.content:encoded:
RLHF forces models to be extremely conservative to avoid mistakes, poisoning the probability distribution over strings; TypeSafe's Jev takes another path, optimizing only intelligence per dollar.

High information density: Diogo goes deep on the trade-offs between RLHF, RLVR and RLCD, for anyone who needs to form a judgment on model training routes.

6:03 The cost of RLHF is mode dropping
Diogo thinks nobody pays attention to RLHF's downsides, especially mode dropping. The mechanism: to generate very long strings without making a mistake, the model has to be extremely conservative, because errors are immediately visible while things that look right but are subtly wrong are very hard to spot; this calibration is "total poison" for the probability distribution over strings. He uses this to explain why Yann LeCun's chart — "LLMs necessarily make errors as sequences get longer" — is mathematically obvious but empirically false: when you cover the distribution you don't get over-penalized by outliers, and it's mode drop that loses the minority classes.

11:12 Refusing to answer is a type error, not a safety problem
Diogo distinguishes safety alignment from capability alignment: the latter is "doing what the user wants," the former is "following someone else's instructions," as with OpenAI and Anthropic. He thinks safety alignment is reasonable for products like ChatGPT and Claude, but in an API it is "nuts," "completely unacceptable" — if a dependency is running in the background, having your software randomly crash because a user sent a weird message is insanity. He opposes adding restrictions at the technical layer, on the grounds that every overfit fractures intelligence a little more, and today's models are already fractured enough.

18:15 Public benchmarks are a substitute for trust
Diogo says he is extremely anti-public benchmarks because they are extremely gameable: in the early days every lab had a team dedicated to collecting data like MMLU to pump up scores, which is essentially "benchmarking with extra steps." He admits intelligence has a je ne sais quoi (good model smell), so people need benchmarks to build trust, but in the long run you can only rely on vibes and trust, until you put the model into a concrete workflow and evaluate it there. He also says that if they wanted to make Jev dumber, they could have shipped that a year and a half ago.

27:34 RLCD is a new North Star, not a new algorithm
Diogo says the term RLHF has been conflated: the original work was Paul Christiano teaching a robot to do a backflip, then it was learning to summarize, and only later instruction following. What he actually calls RLHF is "instruction following as the North Star," having nothing to do with the PPO algorithm — just as DPO and its descendants don't use that paper's algorithm and still count as RLHF. RLCD is the same: a new task direction, programs in the loop, taking the human out of the loop.

40:38 Reliability is a catchall; the North Star is robustness
Diogo defines reliability as a catchall: if AI can't automate something, in the end it's always some kind of reliability problem — maybe type safety, maybe determinism, maybe just that the model is too jagged. He explicitly rejects determinism (same input, same output) as the North Star, thinking it has only slight value for unit tests; what really matters is robustness — similar inputs getting similar outputs. The test is to stuff nonces like UUIDs into the prompt and see whether semantically identical questions get similar answers. He says that when people get burned by AI decisions, that's the layer where it happens.

1:17:12 Reliability is more underrated than speed and cost
Diogo thinks the industry is focusing on the wrong place: "people focus too much on speed and cost and not enough on reliability." His judgment is that reliability is what makes people delighted, what makes them dare to trust. He ties this to TFP growth — he expects TFP growth above 3% within five years, and says that is the mark of an economic revolution, and what the OpenAI charter originally meant to express. He estimates that all current models are still roughly at zero, maybe not even 1%, on valuable work in the world economy.

1:44:10 The optimal dose of RLVR is zero
Diogo says outright that for a model of TypeSafe's shape, the optimal amount of RLVR is zero. His argument is not "RLVR is useless" but that the "pacing the frontier" discussion smuggles in a premise: it assumes everyone must do more RLVR, and RLVR looks dangerous because it lets the model "do anything they want" mid-training — the less you restrict it, the stronger it gets on the outside. So the danger isn't a side effect, it's the design goal. He calls this a "disillusion of responsibility": taking "we must do more RLVR" as an axiom and then deriving the conclusion "we are heading toward a dangerous world."

2:09:13 The KV cache is a tyranny over coding agents
Diogo wants to explore coding agents "free from the tyranny of the KV cache." The KV cache locks you into one model, and for efficiency you must keep appending, so you can't do state management, abstraction, decomposition — normal software practices. From this he explains several phenomena: why routing is hard, why sub-agents don't seem to work, why compaction is a hard problem — because passing state around requires intelligence that is much cheaper than reading state. Directions he imagines include: explicitly annotating state for subtasks, searching for relevant context in a tree of subtasks, parallel sub-agents reading each other's state, and coordinating with smart locks instead of basic-ass locks.

item.title: AI Will Hit an Energy Wall Within Three Years; the Fix Is Building a Computer That Isn't a Computer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-allin-ai-三年内会撞上能源墙-解法是造一台不像计算机的计算机/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-allin-ai-三年内会撞上能源墙-解法是造一台不像计算机的计算机/
item.description: Google alone burns through 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month. At 10 joules per token, that's 12 gigawatts, against roughly 40 gigawatts of total US data center power. Naveen Rao thinks the only way to close that gap is to replace the underlying paradigm of the computer.
item.content:encoded:
Google alone burns through 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month. At 10 joules per token, that's 12 gigawatts, against roughly 40 gigawatts of total US data center power. Naveen Rao thinks the only way to close that gap is to replace the underlying paradigm of the computer.

The first half is the energy math; the second half is his first public reveal of a physical dynamics computer prototype and its measured efficiency numbers — rare hard information. The biology analogy in the middle can be fast-forwarded.

4:45 Energy isn't a cost line, it's the ticket to entry
Naveen's math: Google crosses 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month. At 10 joules per token — a low estimate — that's 12 gigawatts. The US today puts about 40 gigawatts into data centers; the world, under 100 gigawatts. So one company's AI service eats more than a tenth of global data center energy. His call is that the energy ceiling gets hit in about three years. More important, the ranking of scarce resources in a data center has flipped: it used to be floor space, racks, networking gear, GPUs; today it's energy — secure the power contract first, then figure out how to fill it. And energy is 50% of the cost of serving a token; hardware capex and site come after.

7:04 What a squirrel does on 8 milliwatts takes a GPU several watts
A human brain is about 20 watts. Scale linearly by neuron count down to a monkey brain and you get one watt — exactly your phone in your pocket. Further down, mice and bats are in the milliwatt range. A squirrel leaping between branches lands it a thousand times out of a thousand on an 8-milliwatt brain. Meaning your phone's battery could run a hundred-plus squirrel brains. Naveen's conclusion: biology has already built a physical substrate suited to intelligence, and synthetic systems took a different road. The human cortex moves only about 16 billion bits per second; a high-end GPU moves close to 30 trillion bits per second in and out of memory, and inside the chip it's another 10 to 100 times higher. Nearly all the energy goes to moving information, not computing on it.

10:06 Moore's Law stopped; the abstraction layers still charge rent
Transistor counts are still climbing, but frequency stopped scaling long ago, single-thread performance stopped, and now even efficiency no longer improves as process nodes shrink — Naveen says flatly that Moore's Law is basically over. His diagnosis is the abstraction layers: digital is itself an abstraction of the physical world; a transistor actually has intermediate states and is engineered into 0s and 1s. Every layer of abstraction is lossy and ignores the complexity beneath it. So their approach is to wire the physics of the semiconductor directly to the neural network, skipping the layers in between. His intuition pump is flocks of birds and ant colonies: individuals do something extremely simple, and complex behavior emerges at the collective level — the field is called dynamical systems theory.

12:07 Metronomes on a plank sync up on their own
Put several metronomes on a rigid plank that can roll back and forth, and they synchronize to exactly the same phase, simply because each metronome gives the plank a tiny push. That's a purely physical dynamical system. Their question: can such a system be used to compute? The answer is yes — they open-sourced an image generation model called UNO built on a set of such oscillators; it trains and it generates images. Define the system state as the phases of all the oscillators, condition on the output, and generating planes, cars or birds follows different state space trajectories. It's the first demonstration that this class of system can be trained at scale and produce something useful.

14:08 Throwing away connections makes the system easier to train
All-to-all is n squared: 10 elements and 100 connections is fine, 1,000 elements is a million connections — it doesn't scale at all. Their sparsity proposal is to deliberately throw away some connections and see whether the overall behavior can be rescued. The result isn't just that you can throw them away — after throwing them away the system behaves better and is more trainable, and that holds both in simulation and in real physical systems. Naveen calls this the rare case where more efficient, more scalable and better performing all hold at once, a holy grail nobody had cracked for a long time, provided you frame the problem correctly first.

15:09 The first physical dynamics computer has already generated images
This is Naveen's first public reveal: they have built the first physical dynamics computer. The company only formally started in January of this year, with no team at the time; on June 1 they sent the design to tape-out, and the chip is already back in the lab with results — the first images generated by this kind of computer. On efficiency, generating an image takes about 500 nanojoules, versus millijoules for an ordinary GPU; a nanojoule is 10 to the minus 9, several orders of magnitude apart. The reason is that it doesn't move information at all. Architecturally it differs from both CPUs and GPUs: those are von Neumann architectures, with memory and compute separated and data shuttled back and forth; in this machine compute and storage are the same thing, there is no memory interface, and every compute unit is itself a memory.

17:09 4D computing: three spatial dimensions plus one of time
They call this 4D computing: physically, die stacking uses all three dimensions, vertical and planar; the fourth dimension is time in the dynamics. The objective function is intelligence per watt. There is a thermodynamic limit that can never be crossed; animal brains sit only one to two orders of magnitude from it, while today's computing systems are about 10 billion times away. Their plan is to reach the limits of 2D lithography within three and a half years, and the company's overall goal is to beat biology. Naveen expects the result to be a change in form factor: from gigawatt-scale mega data centers toward small data centers scattered everywhere, more local, more adaptive, and supporting billions of robots that dynamically combine to solve problems.

19:12 A thousand times cheaper means a thousand times more consumption
Naveen closes with the Jevons paradox: when the underlying cost of an asset falls, consumption grows by more than the price fell. Halve the price and consumption more than doubles; cut the price to a thousandth and consumption grows more than a thousandfold. So he doesn't think efficiency gains shrink the market — they create the largest market in human history. Chamath then presses on the ecosystem — tape-out, packaging and the rest need a whole set of people to line up. Naveen's answer is a complete product within two years, in the form of an entire rack, sold as a new data center product: tokens in, tokens out over the network, but internally structured completely differently from existing computers.

item.title: Strategic Reserves Are Nearly Drained — the Oil Price Crisis Is Only Now Beginning
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-wsjournal-战略储备快见底-油价危机才真正开始/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-wsjournal-战略储备快见底-油价危机才真正开始/
item.description: Oil hasn't spiraled over the past six months because of three buffers: strategic reserves, sanctioned oil, and China buying less. All three are now being drained, and the real shock is only just about to reach diesel and prices.
item.content:encoded:
Oil hasn't spiraled over the past six months because of three buffers: strategic reserves, sanctioned oil, and China buying less. All three are now being drained, and the real shock is only just about to reach diesel and prices.

Medium information density, but breaking down "why oil hasn't risen" into three buffers and the pace at which they're being exhausted is more useful than reading headlines.

2:03 Close Hormuz and a fifth of the world's oil is gone
The war began with Iran closing the Strait of Hormuz, cutting off roughly 20% of global oil supply outright. This was the move everyone treated as the "nuclear option" — nobody wanted to see it, because it's too bad for every side. Once the strait closed, oil shot from around $70 a barrel to well over $100. But the market didn't spiral from there; it found several buffers that held the price down. The real question isn't "why did it rise" but "why didn't it rise more."

3:09 Three buffers, each less usable than the last
The first is the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve — backup crude stored in salt caverns along the Gulf Coast after the 1970s Arab oil embargo — plus the commercial inventories refiners hold; levels were high before the conflict. The second is sanctioned oil: a large volume of "dark fleet" crude from Iran and Russia drifting at sea, which in March the US temporarily allowed other countries to buy. The third is China — the world's largest oil importer, normally buying about 12 million barrels a day, roughly 10% of global supply, which earlier this year bought about 3 million barrels a day less, effectively giving that oil to others. Together, these three held oil below $100 and the national average gasoline price just under $5.

6:12 Ceasefire talks slapped every analyst in the face
In June the US and Iran began talks and reached a ceasefire, and sentiment flipped 180 degrees instantly: from "extreme crude shortage" to "crude surplus," with analysts predicting oil would fall to $70 or even $60 a barrel. But the peace deal collapsed within weeks, Iran closed the strait again, and Trump declared the ceasefire over. So it was back to the state at the start of the conflict. This episode shows one thing: this price contains a large bet on "the war ends soon," and that bet has repeatedly failed.

8:15 Six months of draining, and the buffers are nearly dry
Commercial inventories have been drawn down, strategic reserves released — and reserves can't be released at will; the government authorized only a specific quantity. The US has taken more than 130 million barrels out of the strategic reserve, leaving about 280 million, which sounds like a lot but is approaching the authorized cap. Worse, this time there's an added refinery crisis: Middle Eastern refineries were struck in the war, and Ukraine, in self-defense, knocked out a large chunk of Russia's refining capacity — and Russia is the world's second-largest diesel exporter. Once a refinery is destroyed, it takes months to restore. So the problem now isn't whether there's crude; it's that there isn't enough refining capacity to produce the fuel the world needs.

9:16 Venezuela can't put out a fire this close
The Trump administration holds up Venezuela as the solution, and its reserves may be the world's largest. But reserves being there doesn't mean production is there: to actually raise output you have to spend money, move rigs, hire people, drill, and ship the barrels out — roughly years and billions of dollars of investment. As for other "miracle solutions," Benoit says there basically aren't any; you can only hope for "small miracles" — like China deciding to raise diesel output, or refinery repairs finishing early. But none of these take effect tomorrow.

10:17 Gas stations haven't blown up yet — diesel blew up first
US consumers haven't yet seen prices spike at the pump; what's actually rising is diesel — the fuel that drives the heavy trucks moving consumer goods from one end of the country to the other. So the question becomes: will companies cut back on deliveries? When do they pass costs on to consumers? Once diesel rises, every kind of business has to factor it into its pricing. This is the real channel through which this shock travels from energy markets into the real economy, and why "gas prices are okay" is a misleading comfort.

12:23 Two paths: absorb it, or pass it on
Companies have only two choices. One is to hold the line and not raise prices: Jim Barber, a third-generation Pennsylvania farmer, has raised his beef price only once in five years — even with the cost of hauling in hay up 15% to 20%, he eats it himself, because he values his relationship with customers and believes the conflict will end soon and that holding on will be rewarded. A farmer's fuel exposure is triple-layered — fertilizer, hauling in hay, shipping his own goods out — so energy costs can be paid three times over or more. The other is to pass it on: Ambix, which makes plastic parts, uses resin, and resin comes from oil; some costs rose 30%, 40%, 50%. At first it resisted raising prices, but as the war dragged on it began passing the 60 cents its suppliers added straight to customers.

15:36 Six-dollar diesel in August, and the shock starts embedding in the economy
When energy prices eased this summer, many businesses had a spell of optimism, thinking maybe they were coming out of it. Then tensions flared again in August, fuel prices rose again, and recently diesel hit $6 a gallon. Owen thinks this is the moment some businesses and economists began to realize "the price shock is truly embedding in the economy." Meanwhile, JPMorgan's commodities analysts said in their latest forecast that they no longer know how to model it — there's no baseline, because they can't see around the corner. On paper many economic indicators are healthy, but consumers feel terrible about prices, and nobody — oil executives, politicians, or CEOs — can say clearly how long this lasts.

item.title: AI Safety Language Is Destroying the Regulatory Debate: It's a Bug, Not a Demon
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-a16z-ai-安全语言正在毁掉监管讨论-那是-bug-不是恶魔/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-a16z-ai-安全语言正在毁掉监管讨论-那是-bug-不是恶魔/
item.description: Calling an AI failure "misalignment" attributes intent and moral judgment to software, leaving Congress and the public unable to understand what actually happened — it should be debugged, reported and fixed like a bug.
item.content:encoded:
Calling an AI failure "misalignment" attributes intent and moral judgment to software, leaving Congress and the public unable to understand what actually happened — it should be debugged, reported and fixed like a bug.

Medium information density, but Sinofsky uses three firsthand histories — the 1983 hacker crackdown, the 1998 virus, and Y2K — to pull "AI safety" back into a software engineering frame. Useful for anyone doing product and policy communication.

0:00 "Misalignment" just means the software has a bug
Sinofsky's core claim: when AI does something we didn't expect, that isn't "misaligned" — it's software not running as intended, i.e. a bug. He says that back when Word ate files and deleted all their contents, nobody thought a demon had possessed Word and made it act against the user's will; and when a spreadsheet miscalculated, nobody circled up to pray to the alignment gods. Calling an AI failure "misalignment" attributes to it properties that don't exist — that it's "trying to do something," that it "made a moral judgment," that it "has rules and principles." And if it's just making decisions based on statistics, that doesn't change the standard that it should do what you want it to do — if the statistics are wrong, that's a bug in the product.

7:07 A self-driving car running a red light is also a bug
Sinofsky uses autonomous driving as an example: if full self-driving runs a red light because it identified a stop sign as a Christmas tree, we wouldn't say it "failed to align with the spirit of the December holidays and road signage" — we'd say it's a bug, and a dangerous one, because that stop sign means something. He points out that both Tesla and Waymo have built in extensive telemetry, diagnostics and extra cameras — things you wouldn't put in a spreadsheet, but would put in life-critical software. And AI models are still at the research-project stage, lacking the tools and telemetry that important software is supposed to have.

8:07 Once telemetry ships, there are more bugs than you can fix
Sinofsky recalls that the software industry spent twenty years with no idea why programs crashed, able only to list crash sites and fix the top ten. Until someone said: why don't we write a program that, when it crashes, tells us over this new thing called the internet? Suddenly there was telemetry, and suddenly there were far more bugs than anyone imagined — going from "we have no bugs, we can ship" to "if we stopped all work, we could fix bugs forever." On that basis he says that when people talk about an AI pause, labs should of course slow down: stop adding new things and go build telemetry, tooling, logging and step-through debugging. He read the bug report OpenAI had just published, and the conclusion was clear: they just don't know.

9:08 Excel wrote "send dogs" to disk
The first version of Excel for Windows in 1987 had a bug: it would write the letters "send dogs" into some Windows settings file on disk. Nobody knew where the phrase came from; everyone scoured the Excel source and couldn't find it. Finally a tester wrote a script that generated charts continuously for days and printed them on an old dot-matrix printer, and found that after about two days it would write send dogs into that location — it depended on how much memory you had, how long it had been running, and which printer and device drivers you used. Sinofsky says we could easily have concluded that "Excel's brain decided to print send dogs," but we didn't — we actually debugged it, and then added telemetry.

13:10 PC software used to claim it was different from mainframes
Sinofsky recalls that IBM people would look at them and say their software was terrible, that Windows was garbage compared to the mainframe software running banks, airlines and power plants. For a long time their answer was "you don't get it, we're different, this is new and cool, we run in 64K not 1MB, we sell for $5,000 not $5 million." But in the end they found the only thing they had to do was grow up: when people started using Excel to decide how planes fly, Word to file briefs with the Supreme Court, PowerPoint to present on the Challenger shuttle disaster, the standard changed. His conclusion: once your tools are used in those settings, you no longer get to use "we're new" as an excuse.

14:10 The virus that cost $12 billion in a day
In March 1998, a virus spread across the internet as a worm. Sinofsky got a call that morning from a reporter gasping "I love you, I love you, I love you." The next day's headline was: $12 billion in damage to the US economy in a single day. He says nobody had previously imagined a bug could cause $12 billion in damage in 12 hours, but it happened. So they held a meeting and decided to pause Outlook development until they understood what had happened. His attitude: the more people use a system, the more damage it can do when something goes wrong, but that's the price of admission, it's what you signed up for — "we're too popular to deal with it" is not an excuse.

16:10 Alignment piles a Google-sized problem on top
Sinofsky points out a concrete problem with alignment: to achieve it, you have to have a huge set of rules defining what alignment is — what may and may not be done, what is safe, what is unfair. And software engineering learned long ago that piling too many constraints on a system makes it stop working, and produces endless unintended side effects. You set one rule, and someone asks "what about this case," so you add another rule. He says this starts to look like Google's job of deciding how to present search results — which took them 20 years and thousands of full-time people, and is very, very hard. And AI labs have signed up for the upgraded version of that problem: they aren't just retrieving results, they're synthesizing them, so they also have to invent a whole pile of things themselves, and no law is going to invent them for them.

17:10 Y2K didn't happen because people did things
Asked whether AI alignment is like Y2K, Sinofsky stresses there's a causal chain here: professionals worried a great deal, then professionals took a great deal of responsibility, and then nothing happened — that's a direct causal link. They rented generators and RVs, moved computers into secure bunkers, and that's what made nothing happen. And there was almost no legislation — there were some odd regulations about Y2K compliance, but most of the rules were drafted by industry itself, by cross-industry coalitions of banks, insurers and others. He thinks OpenAI needs to sit down with all the frontier model players and labs and build a far better reporting mechanism; yesterday's report is a good start, but falls far short of what a third party would need to understand what happened.

item.title: Optimism Is Not a Personality Trait, It's an Explanatory Style You Can Train
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.description: Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself, but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.
item.content:encoded:
Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself, but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.

Seligman himself walks through the full chain from learned helplessness to learned optimism, and in the back half treats agency as a civilisational variable and tries to quantify it — a rare angle.

9:36 The dog doesn't escape because it never learned that escaping works
In Solomon's lab, on day one the dog was strapped into a hammock and given Pavlovian shocks it could not avoid no matter what it did; on day two it was placed in a shuttle box where running to the other side would shut off the shock, and the dog just lay there. Seligman's reading: what the animal actually learned was not "the tone predicts the shock" but "nothing I do matters." That interpretation collided head-on with behaviourism at the time, because it required the animal to be a cognitive subject capable of thinking and of integrating experience across time.

13:50 People can be taught to give up by noise too
Hiroto moved the same design onto humans: on day one, headphones playing an unpleasant noise — one group could not turn it off no matter how they pressed, the other could stop it with a button. On day two they were given a four-foot "human shuttle box": hand on one side and the noise sounds, move it to the other side and it stops. People who had been through uncontrollable noise the day before simply left their hand in place. Seligman stresses that the variable doing the work is not the trauma itself but whether there was control over the trauma — and they ran control experiments to establish this.

19:00 Helplessness became the model for depression
In 1970 depression was not yet a diagnostic category; there was only "manic-depressive illness." By 1975 the American Psychiatric Association's DSM had for the first time split out "unipolar depression," listing nine symptoms: passivity, cognitive difficulty, sadness, anxiety, sleep problems, food losing its taste, numbness, loss of pleasure, thoughts of death. Seligman compared the nine symptoms against the learned-helplessness literature accumulated by then and found the lab could reproduce eight of them; the only one missing was thoughts of death — presumably because the experiments used noise rather than something more severe. The model went on to become the dominant model of depression, and the drugs that broke helplessness in the lab became mainstream antidepressants.

22:19 Five out of eight give up, one in three does not
Across the whole helplessness literature the effect is statistical: on average five out of eight people or eight rats become helpless, and roughly a third do not. From the 1970s Seligman began asking what was different about that third, and it became the turning point of his career. The answer landed on explanatory style: people who explain bad events as permanent ("I'm stupid"), pervasive ("I'm unlovable"), and their own fault become helpless; people who explain them as temporary, local, and not their fault recover quickly.

26:50 West Point's first week predicts who will drop out
The first six weeks at West Point are called Beast Barracks: woken at four in the morning to run ten miles, systematically put through the wringer, with the stated purpose of "breaking them," and about a third of candidates quit. Seligman's team measured explanatory style on day one, and the ones who dropped out were the pessimists. The same pattern showed up in college grades (optimists outperformed their talent, pessimists underperformed it) and in insurance sales: MetLife lost 50% of new hires within a year and 90% within four years; they hired 140 "special forces" recruits whose optimism-scale scores were off the charts, and this cohort outsold the whole company and still had 75% on the job after four years, while the ordinary group was down to 10%.

34:17 Agency breaks down into three beliefs
Seligman defines agency as the opposite of learned helplessness, made up of three parts: efficacy, the belief that you can accomplish a specific goal right here and now; optimism, the belief that you can accomplish it not only now but in the future and the further future; and imagination, the range of possible goals you can picture — the wider the range, the stronger the agency. Full agency is: I can do it now, I can do it in the future, and I can innovate across many different situations.

36:22 The Axial Age's answer may have been "I can do it"
Between 1000 and 500 BC, Greece, the Hebrew world, China, India and Persia all underwent upheaval: the Buddha, Confucius and Socrates appeared, and technology, medicine, art, literature and the first political freedoms erupted together. Seligman's hypothesis is that over those five centuries humanity discovered the concept of agency. The evidence is vocabulary: in the Iliad Achilles does not decide to act on his own, Athena tells him to act; a hundred years later, in the Odyssey, Odysseus is already a wily, resourceful man who makes his own decisions, and the gods begin to exit the stage. By 500 BC every culture had produced a large vocabulary of human agency.

38:30 In the Old Testament the verbs of divine command decline
Seligman took the entire Old Testament and counted agency verbs: broadly, in the Pentateuch God commands and people obey, with only a few exceptions like "choose life"; the further you go, into the Prophets and the Writings, the more words of human agency appear and the fewer of divine agency. You can now have AI score each book for agency, and plotted by date it comes out linear — from the Pentateuch to the Babylonian exile around 300 BC, agency increases, and it correlates linearly with human innovation, population, living standards, political freedom and technology.

item.title: He Never Won Elected Office, Yet He Reshaped All of New York
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-stuffmissed-他从未当选任何公职-却重塑了整座纽约/
