item.description: Robert Moses stacked appointed positions into power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.
item.content:encoded:
Robert Moses stacked appointed positions into power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.

This episode is medium-density on information, but how Moses accumulated power through unelected positions, and the exact words from his 1945 Atlantic Monthly article, are valuable for understanding urban governance and how power operates.

1:01 Never elected, yet he held enormous power
Robert Moses was never elected to any public office in his life, yet he accumulated enormous power through appointment to various government positions. According to Encyclopaedia Britannica, his work includes 35 highways, 12 bridges, numerous parks, Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts, Shea Stadium, many housing projects, two hydroelectric power plants, and the 1964 New York World's Fair. He has been dead 45 years and remains a divisive figure, and his legacy may be argued over for another century or more.

6:10 His mentor taught him not to anger voters
Moses became chief of staff of the New York State Reconstruction Commission in 1919 and learned a great deal from Belle Moskovitz. Moskovitz understood deeply how to maneuver within government to achieve goals without angering those in power. One example: in an early draft of a report, Moses suggested cutting part of the workforce, and Moskovitz reminded him that every one of those people was a voter, that they could not be made angry, and that he had to find a way to cut costs without cutting that many people. This ‘don't anger the voters’ thinking ran through his later government work.

11:11 Parks were the means, highways were the end
When Moses took over the parks commission, most green space plans merely preserved natural wilderness, but he envisioned adding more manicured landscaping and dedicated recreation areas. More importantly, every time he built a new park, he made sure the project included roads connecting the park to highways — that is where the parkway came from. From the start he planned a large state park system for Long Island, all connected by new roads. In just four years in the job, he added 13 parks to Long Island, about 9,700 acres in total, where previously there had been only one park.

13:14 His mother lent him $20,000 to save Jones Beach
Jones Beach was originally just a sandbar on the southern edge of Long Island, almost completely submerged at high tide. Moses wanted to turn it into a great park, and most of the government and the press considered it impractical. He first used large-scale dredging to dig about 40 million cubic yards of sand from the seabed, raising the sandbar from two feet above sea level to twelve feet. But the project nearly died when the money ran out, and Moses did something highly unusual: he borrowed $20,000 from his mother Bella to continue the work. He later confirmed that if his mother had not put up that money, the contractor would not have come back with the equipment to finish. Jones Beach finally opened on August 4, 1925, in a dust storm, and an estimated 1.5 million people visited in its first year.

22:31 His only campaign, and he lost badly
Moses ran for public office only once in his life. In 1934 he ran for governor of New York and was thoroughly defeated by the incumbent Democratic governor, Herbert H. Lehman. Lehman received more than 2.2 million popular votes; Moses got fewer than 1.4 million. The New York Times, reporting Lehman's victory, wrote: ‘Meanwhile, his formidable and combative opponent, Robert Moses, will be free to continue his work as the great parks commissioner.’ After this defeat he never tried to run again, and instead continued to expand his power through appointed positions.

23:33 235 new playgrounds, only one in Harlem
Starting in the 1930s, Moses greatly expanded the city's playgrounds, building 235 new ones. But a pattern began to emerge: he ignored the needs of districts with predominantly non-white populations. Of the 235 playgrounds, only one was in Harlem. In the summer of 1936 he opened 11 new swimming pools: 4 in Manhattan (including one in Harlem and one in West Harlem), 4 in Brooklyn, and 1 each in the Bronx, Queens, and Staten Island. These pools had new filtration and chlorination systems, heating, and underwater lighting, and were considered advanced, but they were also designed to be drained in the cooler months and used for other activities, from shuffleboard to roller skating.

24:35 ‘Tear down the slums, just build a road’
In 1945 Moses published an article in The Atlantic Monthly that opened by describing how slums form: existing buildings become overcrowded, speculators add tenants, and people are packed into tenements like chickens. But the ‘cure’ he offered was this: clearing slums in most cities is accomplished indirectly — not for public, semi-public, or private housing, but for parks, playgrounds, parkways, highways, boulevards, and other public improvements. He boasted that his ‘demolition and construction demon squad’ had torn down more old slums than all the housing experts combined, and that ‘we built nothing but broad highways, lined with landscaping and recreational facilities.’

33:43 Eminent domain is the only salvation
In the article Moses explicitly endorsed the use of eminent domain to acquire land. He wrote that buying large tracts of land at a reasonable price had become impossible, and that in such a situation, ‘eminent domain is the only salvation.’ Eminent domain must be exercised by the city, state, or federal government for private limited-dividend or redevelopment companies. He also criticized unions as ‘a serious obstacle to financing slum clearance,’ accusing them of insisting on retaining hourly wage rights, striking, and ‘resisting invention and improvement in the building field.’ He said this attitude was ‘without justification’ and would not change until a better-educated new generation of union officials appeared.

item.title: Blame Is Not Revenge: A Philosopher Argues We Should Blame Less
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-phibites-责备不是报复-哲学家主张我们该少责备一点/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-phibites-责备不是报复-哲学家主张我们该少责备一点/
item.description: Miranda Fricker argues that retributive blame makes no sense, and that the most valuable blame is "communicative blame" — aimed at getting the other person to genuinely understand the moral significance of what they did, and reaching a shared moral understanding.
item.content:encoded:
Miranda Fricker argues that retributive blame makes no sense, and that the most valuable blame is "communicative blame" — aimed at getting the other person to genuinely understand the moral significance of what they did, and reaching a shared moral understanding.

In 23 minutes it offers a workable moral framework: distinguishing retributive from communicative blame, and explaining why blaming less does not mean abandoning responsibility.

0:04 There is no single definition of blame
Fricker points out that the philosophical literature holds a great many different views of blame: some say it is a hostile emotion, some a reactive attitude, some merely a judgment, some a rupture in a relationship, and some a form of protest. She suspects these views are not talking about the same thing at all. She holds that the object of blame can be any agent — an individual, an institution, or even a collective as large as a nation — as long as it has done something wrong, it is a proper object of blame.

2:05 Retributive blame has no logic to it
Fricker defines retributive blame as: you wronged me, I am at a disadvantage, so I am entitled to even the score by making you suffer a little too — "getting even" is its most apt metaphor. She says she does not believe this logic in interpersonal morality, and does not find it useful. She concedes she does not want to say anything specific about criminal punishment, but admits she is strongly inclined to think the retributive idea there is rather distasteful. She believes genuinely useful alternatives exist.

3:08 Communicative blame wants shared understanding
Fricker holds that the morally most valuable model of blame is one aimed at getting the other person to fully grasp the moral significance of their behaviour. If you blame me for wronging you, perhaps I did not fully understand the moral weight of what I did; you put it into the conversation, and I either come to understand what I did or push back that "it wasn't that serious," and in the end the two of us reach a shared moral understanding of what happened between us. She admits this is an ideal, but one worth pursuing, and calls it "communicative blame."

5:11 Blame is at bottom a judgment of moral wrongdoing
After the functional analysis, Fricker gives her own definition of blame: blame is a judgment of moral wrongdoing, and that judgment is in some sense activated or driven by a disposition suitable for holding someone responsible. She stresses that this is the context of moral blame. The definition is minimalist, and she thinks its advantage is that it can be transplanted across domains — when she studies epistemic blame, for instance, she need not assume the blamer feels any hostility toward the blamed, only that there is an epistemic fault and that the judgment issues from a responsibility-holding stance rather than passive observation.

6:11 An apology must be made to the right person
Fricker points to a key difference between apology and blame: communicative blame can be spread around, and conveying the meaning of blame to a third party can be derived from conveying it to the person concerned — both promote shared moral understanding; but apologising to someone you did not wrong is not an apology at all. Apology is essentially second-personal moral address, and must be done to the right person. She also notes that an apology's reparative power is tied to an ongoing relationship — if a stranger wrongs you at random, there is no need to chase an apology, and we all have to learn to let things go.

9:12 Sincerity is not all-or-nothing
Fricker rejects treating sincerity as all-or-nothing. She holds that in most apology practices a person need only be "sincere enough" to count as apologising, and sincere enough in the right way to be accepted by the particular person being apologised to. She cites the philosopher Jeffrey Helmich's notion of the "apology stance": an apology is a speech act that not only expresses but "enacts" the appropriate sorry inner state. She adds that an overly florid apology is merely irritating, and that apology is a social performance that must fall within the bandwidth of appropriateness to be accepted.

12:15 Responsibility is a social construction, not metaphysics
Faced with the minority view that genes and environment determine everything and people are never responsible, Fricker argues that this line of thought locates the threshold of responsibility in a metaphysical rather than a natural place. She understands responsibility as something that grows out of the practice of human beings living together, for the sake of social coordination and harmony and the construction of a shared moral consciousness. She borrows Peter Strawson's approach: whatever the metaphysics, in everyday life we simply cannot help praising and blaming. She thinks separating metaphysics from the practice of responsibility is itself a way of leading people astray.

19:20 Blaming less is a trainable choice
Fricker says that if blame is a judgment of fault, and the judgment issues from a responsibility-holding moral stance, then we can choose how much human behaviour to bring into this "fault-finding" construction. She gives the example of lateness: some people are highly moralistic about others being late, others are not offended at all. She admits she prefers a world in which everyone is a bit more relaxed about lateness of up to 15 minutes, where it need not be constructed as a matter of respect — it is just "you're a little late," and that is all.

item.title: Chinese open-weight models lead, and distillation explains only one to two months of the gap
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-interconnects-中国开源权重模型领先-蒸馏只解释一两个月差距/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-interconnects-中国开源权重模型领先-蒸馏只解释一两个月差距/
item.description: Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation explains only one to two months of the gap; the real reasons are release cadence and task focus, and US companies are already building products on Chinese models.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation explains only one to two months of the gap; the real reasons are release cadence and task focus, and US companies are already building products on Chinese models.

This is a state-of-open-models briefing written for Congress: high data density, clear judgments, suited to anyone who wants to grasp the US-China open-model landscape quickly.

0:00 Open weights is not the same thing as open source
An open-weight model releases only the weights and a license; an open-source model also releases the training code and data. America's genuinely open-source models are led by non-profits, such as the Allen Institute for AI's Olmo, OpenAthena's Marin, and EleutherAI's Pythia. Nvidia's Nemotron is more open than most open-weight models, having released a large amount of training data, but because it has not released all of it, it still does not count as fully open source. The distinction matters: when people discuss "open source", what they are actually talking about is mostly open weights.

0:00 Chinese models have crossed the agentic capability threshold
GLM-5.2 and Kimi K3 delivered a step change in commercial viability, crossing an agentic capability threshold similar to the one Anthropic's Claude Code crossed in December 2025. Chinese open-weight models overtook the US in these two key areas roughly 18 months ago. On Hugging Face downloads, China took the lead in July 2025, mainly on the back of Alibaba's Qwen. Data from the ATOM project, which the author maintains, shows China's download lead has grown to about 1.6 billion out of a total of 3.2 billion, twice that of the US.

0:00 The benchmark score gap is stark
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, as of September 14, 2026, the top three are Chinese models: Z.ai's GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash score 45 and 42, and Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 scores 44. The US leaders are Thinking Machines' Inkling and Inkling Small, both scoring 26, and Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 23. The top US models were released in June and July 2026, and update less frequently than their Chinese counterparts. Chinese labs are closest on tasks with well-defined demand such as agentic coding, and lag further behind on open-ended scientific tasks such as physics and biology.

0:00 Distillation explains only one to two months of the gap
Distillation is a technique Chinese labs use routinely, training their own models on the outputs of stronger models, but the author estimates that even if distillation were blocked entirely, for instance by deploying KYC tools at Anthropic and OpenAI, the gap between the strongest US models and Chinese open-weight models would widen by only 1-2 months. Distillation matters most in new domains, and it cannot easily produce a comprehensively strong final model. Chinese labs ship faster and have a narrower task distribution, which slightly inflates scores on public benchmarks, because every lab keeps improving and later-released models naturally score higher.

0:00 US companies are building products on Chinese models
Harvey, Cursor and DoorDash use Kimi, Airbnb uses Qwen, Perplexity uses DeepSeek. A large number of young Silicon Valley startups use Chinese models to get a low-cost, flexible option. US startups sign enterprise agreements with Chinese model labs to license products for use, a new form of cross-border technology cooperation the author has not seen in his career. On OpenRouter, the Chinese model share has grown from about 70% to more than 80%, and weekly tokens processed have grown from about 1 trillion in September 2025 to about 80 trillion today. On OpenCode, Chinese models account for about 95% or more of inference volume.

0:00 Academia has already been taken over by Qwen
The author scanned papers in the five most popular ML categories on arXiv (cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.CV, cs.LG, stat.ML). In January 2023, papers mentioning any open model were 2%; by September 2026 the figure reached 50%. In April-May 2023, of about 12,000 new papers, 2,600 mentioned at least one open-model family, 5.5% mentioned Llama and 1% mentioned Chinese models. At Llama's peak in autumn 2024, 23% mentioned Llama and 7.5% mentioned Qwen. Today Llama is still mentioned by about 21% of papers, while Qwen has risen to 30%. Any Chinese open-weight model is mentioned by more than 40% of papers, versus 30% for the US.

0:00 US models get higher adoption at equal capability
Research shows that US models see disproportionately high adoption when capability and scale are comparable. gpt-oss, OpenAI's first open-weight models after ChatGPT, became one of the most widely adopted open-weight models ever. Google's Gemma 4 is one of the few models whose adoption approaches Qwen's most popular small models. Nvidia's Nemotron, despite being more capable at the same scale, has seen only middling adoption. This shows US models have brand and ecosystem advantages, but not enough to reverse the overall trend.

0:00 Open-model risk requires ecosystem-level preparation
The structural challenge of open-weight models is that there is almost no effective way to stop pieces of open-source software from falling into the wrong hands. If access to China's strongest open-weight models were restricted because of the risk, the ones hurt would be US companies. HuggingFace once used a Chinese open-weight model to understand a cyberattack, because closed models refused the request. Managing open-weight model risk tends to come down to ecosystem preparation. Open models are becoming an essential tool for AI diffusion, and continuing to invest in US open models is the best path to staying ahead of these risks.

item.title: Poetry Is Not Democracy's Ornament but Its Pillar
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-mindscape-诗歌不是民主的点缀-而是民主的支柱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-mindscape-诗歌不是民主的点缀-而是民主的支柱/
item.description: Banning books and telling teachers what they can't teach strikes at the root of free expression just like censoring the news; who a collective is and what it values takes shape through language — art is democracy's infrastructure, not its poster.
item.content:encoded:
Banning books and telling teachers what they can't teach strikes at the root of free expression just like censoring the news; who a collective is and what it values takes shape through language — art is democracy's infrastructure, not its poster.

Not a literature class: a working poet who also heads the largest humanities funder in the country explains why close reading, naming and literacy are political capacities; the second half is harder than the opening.

5:32 The poet went to the scene instead of writing reflections
Rukeyser was not a poet who stayed in her study. At 19, while studying at Vassar, she felt she had to go south to sit in on the Scottsboro trial — staying at school simply wasn't an option; in 1936 she went to Spain to see the anti-Olympics mounted against the Berlin Games, and arrived just as the Spanish Civil War broke out; she also went to West Virginia to write about the Hawks Nest mine disaster — Union Carbide dug tunnels without wet drilling and without giving workers protective equipment, the workers were mostly African American, and nearly all died of silicosis, which Alexander says may be the largest corporate industrial accident in American history. The conclusion: writing let more people know what happened, and connected people of different identities on shared human experience.

13:50 Art is a pillar of democracy, not an illustration
She breaks democracy down into a question of language: who a collective is, what it values, which voices it contains — all of it takes shape through language, so without language there is no collective. When we talk about free speech we always fixate on journalism, but artists being censored, books being banned, teachers being told what they may teach — that moves the same foundation. Her wording is hard: art is not democracy's explanatory diagram, art is itself part of democracy — one of its pillars. And poetry doesn't just wave a flag for values; it is the thing itself. You can judge whether a democracy is healthy by whether art can still live in an unfettered space.

33:37 Close reading is critical thinking, and it can be taught
She describes close reading very plainly: a method, a practice, anyone can learn it, and its other name is critical thinking. Its use isn't limited to poetry — you can use it reading the newspaper, reading the propaganda around you, whether that propaganda comes from above or from advertising and very, very powerful culture. Figuring out how someone is working on you is a good thing. And in America many people are nervous about poetry, feeling they ‘aren't supposed to understand it’; her method is concrete: drop your shoulders, read it again, don't just read it on the page, read it aloud, then you read it to me — the same poem read by a different person, and you hear something different every time.

42:37 Misnaming people is an anti-democratic weapon
She says one of the most powerful weapons against democracy is misnaming people, calling people by the wrong name. There's an American saying, calling people out of their names, which means flattening people, using insulting labels, even smearing the behaviour of an entire people as a whole — this is abuse of language, its purpose is to wound and divide, and it is coming from the highest levels of government. She stresses one thing in particular: it has real consequences. Conversely, naming things precisely, saying what you mean, saying who you are, and catching what others say — that itself is the capacity democracy needs.

47:58 Grief has to be put into language before you can hold it
Her husband Fikre died 14 years ago. She wrote a memoir shortly after his death, which surprised even her — she had never imagined writing one or showing it to anyone; it was more a way of landing, of knowing what she was going through: too overwhelming, too unprecedented, and turning some of it into language helped her name the feeling. Writing about him years later was different in kind, became a responsibility: this person was her ‘my person’, who lived a brave, extraordinary, beautiful life and left hundreds of paintings, now shown in museums and galleries. She is wary of herself too: she hopes she isn't wringing this experience dry.

57:30 Writing poetry, you throw away far more than you keep
She doesn't start a poem from ‘I want to write a poem about X’ but from a word, an image, a phrase that resonates there, and she can't say why, so she writes it down again and again. She has a day job — almost all poets do — so the real question is: while you're busy with something else, where do you put the thought down. Fragments accumulate slowly, and when there's time to sit, you ask which piece is still vibrating, still alive. How much do you write versus throw away? Her answer is one word: Most. A serious writer throws away many times what they keep, and that takes a little courage — keep writing even when it's wrong. What really excites her is the editing stage, because ‘the beast is there’, the outline is already visible.

1:02:17 The cost of college is a problem; learning is not
She directly rebuts the claim that the humanities have no prospects: critical thinking, close reading, extracting meaning from complex texts, communicating persuasively, imagining other people's lives, understanding multiple cultures — these are capacities useful in any career. She doesn't deny that the cost of higher education is a real problem that really needs solving, but she puts the emphasis elsewhere: what's more worrying is the attack on the university itself, interference in its mission, and the loud repetition of the claim that ‘the university is not a valuable thing’. Her last line is sharp: creating an undereducated populace serves another purpose.

1:07:22 Those who cannot read are the easiest to control
‘free people read freely’ is a line from the poet and librarian Tracie D. Hall, and Alexander says she borrows it all day long. She reads those five words out of the African American tradition: under slavery, it was a crime for Black people to learn to read and write, and it was equally a crime for a free white person to teach them — what was being controlled was not text but people. So the sentence holds two halves: free people read freely, and, free people are meant to read. If a person cannot read, cannot access a mass of information, they cannot understand their own life, and so lose the capacity to act on an understanding of how external forces work on them. Where literacy is taken away, there is only one logic: this is how you are easier to control.

item.title: Literacy Once Democratised Europe; Now It Is Retreating
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-econtalk-识字率曾让欧洲民主化-如今却在倒退/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-econtalk-识字率曾让欧洲民主化-如今却在倒退/
item.description: Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are pulling public discourse back toward a pre-literate age.
item.content:encoded:
Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are pulling public discourse back toward a pre-literate age.

Medium information density, but two mechanisms are worth hearing: "writing cools discourse" and "bad ideas are easier to whitewash on film"; the later section on pop music and reading is looser.

8:13 Literacy is historically extremely recent and fragile
Marriott stresses that we are so used to literacy that we forget how anomalous it is. By one estimate, in a certain ancient Mesopotamian city-state there may have been only 20 living people who could read and write; literacy in ancient Rome was around 10%. For thousands of years, reading and writing was not a cultural phenomenon but an esoteric code circulating within a wealthy scribal elite — some rulers were literate, some were not. The real turning point was printing: books could be reproduced in quantity, more people could read, and books became more practical; Protestantism then placed enormous emphasis on the written word, pushing more people to become literate in order to read the Bible. These factors fed each other until the "Reading Revolution" historians identify in the mid-to-late 18th century.

11:19 The Reading Revolution really did change the shape of politics
Roberts pushes back: if literacy exploded, why doesn't the world look turned upside down? Marriott's answer is that the spread of literacy has a democratising effect — the more people who can access information and ideas, the more people participate in politics and criticise power. Early 18th-century Europe was ruled by absolute monarchs, and political affairs were essentially court secrets discussed among a small elite; by the late 18th and early 19th century, newspapers appeared, the standing of absolute monarchs declined sharply, France became a republic, the authority of the British monarch was far weaker than at the start of the century, parliamentary debates were reported, and public affairs were no longer discussed only in court. He calls this the great age of democratic revolution and democratic reform, and ties it directly to the spread of literacy.

16:32 Writing forces bad ideas into logical form
Marriott concedes books are imperfect, but argues that the way a book organises information is more rational and more coherent than conversation, video or TikTok. Writing forces you to polish an idea repeatedly, to externalise part of your mind onto the page and then test it; the reader faces a fixed text and can reread and analyse it critically. More crucially, the book limits the means of non-logical persuasion — you cannot bypass argument with charisma, shouting or tears. He uses the Nazis as a counterexample: Hitler's Mein Kampf was unreadable even to the Nazi elite, because Nazism simply does not hold together once it is required to be presented coherently as a written text; yet Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will is treated as an artistic masterpiece, screened in film classes, and regarded as an extremely powerful argument for fascism. Bad ideas are easier to whitewash on a screen than in a book.

25:05 The Republic of Letters filtered out trolls through writing
The 17th- and 18th-century European "Republic of Letters" was a community of thinkers, philosophers and scientists who wrote to each other and ran journals. The economic historian Joel Mokyr rates it extraordinarily highly, saying it is the single cultural fact that explains the Industrial Revolution. Marriott's mechanism is this: if a clever person sits alone in a village, his ideas can only be told to his neighbours, and scientific innovation struggles to accumulate; the spread of literacy let ideas travel further, more and more people joined the conversation, ideas flowed into one central pool, and thought grew more complex. Roberts adds that the key difference is not public versus private but who the participants are — in conversation with Adam Smith, David Hume and Newton, the standard is naturally high; it is a kind of "submission to that which cannot be enforced". Marriott concedes that the literacy barrier itself carries a benign elitism: you cannot burst in and shout like a troll on X, because nobody will pay attention to you.

34:49 The novel gives us a passage into other minds
Marriott believes there is a kind of truth about life that only prose fiction can reach: it lets us see the inside of other people's minds. Reading is an active rather than passive process — you use the words on the page to build images in your head, which is why it is immersive, why it feels like having lived another life. Film cannot do this, because it gives you the external world and cannot enter another mind directly; and writing is precisely the medium we use to express what is in our minds, a mind-to-mind communication. He also notes that oral poetry takes little interest in the subtle differences between human consciousnesses, and that this capacity to "inhabit another mind" appears only in prose fiction. Roberts does not fully agree, arguing that great films can approach it through dialogue, but concedes that film almost never captures the inner activity that is conveyed by more than dialogue.

47:59 The post-literate commentator is more like Homer
Marriott writes that the post-literate commentator does not explain and analyse the world like the print-age public intellectual, but is more like an oral storyteller, weaving strange and unforgettable tales for an enchanted audience. Roberts calls this the deepest insight in the whole piece: faced with the mass of absurd, untenable statements online, people habitually interrogate them with an author's standards — "that isn't logical", "where's the evidence?" — but these people are simply not in that business. Their job is to entertain the audience; truth does not matter, the story that enchants the audience does. Marriott goes further: presenting an argument logically, supplying evidence, driving to a rational conclusion — these are not in fact natural to human communication; in an oral culture, the more effective way to persuade someone is to entertain him, move him, get angry at him. Writing imposes an impersonal, more rational form of communication, and it is not a necessary product of human communication.

53:59 The richness of pop music also feeds off reading
Roberts cites an example from The History of Rock and Roll in 500 Songs: Jagger wrote "Sympathy for the Devil", whose opening is taken directly from Bulgakov's The Master and Margarita — the novel opens with two Russian intellectuals mocking God and belief, after which a suave gentleman appears, they think he is mad, and finally they realise it is Satan. Marriott calls it an "annoyingly good" example and regrets not having put it in the book. He concedes it cannot be pushed too far — it is not that you have to move Penguin Classics into the British Library to join a boy band — but Bob Dylan and Paul McCartney are both obviously heavy readers. He cites research showing that over the past 20 years pop songs have become less complex in both lyrics and melody, partly because the environment favours the simple and the immediate: to go viral on TikTok, a song has to grab you within three or four seconds.

58:17 The future of reading will be deliberate, like fitness
Marriott stresses this is not a new phenomenon: statistics on the decline of serious reading go back to the 1950s and 1960s, television was the beginning of the screen age, and the remote control was the first scroll. Roberts quotes what his father said at the time — books have existed for centuries, television has been a mass medium for only 20 years, let's see if it lasts — and concedes his father should have worried more. Marriott's consolation comes from the analogy with junk food and fitness: McDonald's arrived, many people got fat, but some realised that health could no longer be absorbed naturally from the environment and required deliberate effort, so they started running and going to the gym. He guesses cognitive health will follow the same path: if reading has a future, it will become more deliberate, less "I'm bored at the airport, I'll pick up a book" and more "I value this experience, so I sit down for half an hour to an hour every night". He admits this makes him a little sad, because reading will become more artificial, no longer the unavoidable part of life it once was.

item.title: A Glass of Water Has No Final Truth: Quantum Mechanics Forces Us to Give Up the Single Perspective
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/
item.description: Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not new particles, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is many perspectives that enrich one another but never converge.
item.content:encoded:
Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not new particles, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is many perspectives that enrich one another but never converge.

A four-person roundtable crossing physics, poetry, drama and economics; high density of quotable lines but the argument is loose. Worth listening if you want a few perspectives that can change your judgment; skip it if you want hard information.

2:06 A glass of water has no final version
Rovelli opens with a glass of water the BBC provided: you look from one side, I look from the other, you wear glasses, I see a different colour. This glass of water can be a physical object (mass, velocity, position), it can be temperature and pressure, it can be the chemistry of H2O plus floating bits, it can be the global economy of being bottled in Italy and shipped to England, or it can simply be ‘we want to drink it’. His claim is that these perspectives are all real, none exhausts another, none contradicts another, and there is no ‘ultimate glass of water’. This is anti-Platonic — he does not accept a distinction between a ‘level of appearances’ and a ‘fundamental level’.

6:13 We still have not digested quantum mechanics
Rovelli says what he is describing is not borrowed from philosophy but grown from inside physics. Physicists ran into quantum phenomena; quantum mechanics is an enormous revolution, but ‘we have not yet digested quantum mechanics’ — the newspaper stories about experiments that ‘confirm what I learned in a textbook in the 1970s’ show precisely that we still do not truly believe it. Take quantum mechanics seriously and what it says is this: the Enlightenment dream of ‘describing reality completely, determinately, clearly, independently of an observer’ does not hold. The observer here need not be a human; anything that interacts with something counts.

8:19 The deepest level of reality is not more objective
Rovelli turns it around: the reality at the most basic level physics can reach is in fact not essentially different from the reality Lavinia deals with in poetry or James's characters deal with in economics — both are realities that allow different views, not a reality that is ‘absolutely objective underneath’. So quantum physics is not that hard; it simply has not been digested. The concrete physical phenomena are of course complicated, but poetry is complicated and economics is complicated too.

10:25 Scientists have always used metaphors
Rovelli says the words Lavinia uses could be lifted line by line into his book. What is an electron? ‘It is a grain, a grain of sand, but it is not really a grain of sand.’ Why is an electric field called a field? Because it is ‘a bit like a field in the countryside’. We think through metaphor, by taking old concepts apart and putting a piece of each together into a new concept. The goal is not to arrive at a final, perfect description of reality — a century ago we thought we could, but it does not work — but to gain a better understanding, a better way of navigating reality. He adds a crucial qualification: admitting that everything has a perspective does not mean all perspectives are equivalent, nor that there is no better and worse; it is only that the hope of ‘arriving at the final correct story about reality’ is empty — not unreachable, but meaningless.

12:27 Seeking the ultimate morality is itself wrong
Rovelli turns from ‘complexity’ to ‘value’: if you ask ‘what is the ultimate definition of good and evil, what is universal ethics’, he thinks this is itself a morally and ethically mistaken approach. Our morals and values are powerful, important and indispensable not because they are outside us, but because they are inside us, and therefore equally perspectival. This passage connects directly to James Graham's play — whose very first line is ‘what is a good life’.

15:30 Do not be afraid to learn a jargon
Lavinia Greenlaw argues for embracing jargon: not everyone has to learn it, but if you are genuinely interested in something, do not be afraid to learn its language — a mechanic has to learn the names of parts, a surgeon has to learn the names of parts, and a poet has to as well. It lets you see more clearly, and it lets you see where something has gone wrong. She admits jargon can be exclusionary, but ‘that depends on the context in which you use it’, and ‘you can perform difficulty, poets and poems are probably very good at that, but that is not what difficulty means’. She gives the example of poems on the underground: before everyone was on their phones, people would read a poem first and only then realise they were reading a poem, and that engagement was far more direct and confident than sitting down and being told ‘now you are going to read a poem’.

22:55 Friction is treated as a problem to be solved
James Graham says modern culture has fetishised ‘efficiency’ and strips out every layer of difficulty as friction. He gives a concrete image: emailing himself a script to save it, a prompt pops up — ‘this is a long document, shall I summarise it for you?’ — and his reaction is ‘how rude, I want you to sit inside it and read it’. He connects this back to Bloomsbury and Keynes: meaning is discovered precisely in the friction, in the difficulty, in the process. He also says the collapse of reading is despairing, because reading demands personal investment, and today that investment is treated as a problem to be solved rather than something to be celebrated.

26:05 War refuses to acknowledge complexity
Rovelli uses International Peace Day on 21 September and the words of the UN Secretary-General and the Pope to connect the argument about perspectives to war: war is to a large extent driven by greed and power games, but it always wraps itself in a hypocritical narrative — there is only one truth, only one good, we are the good ones, they are the bad ones, we tell the truth, they tell lies and propaganda. So war is built on a total refusal to be prepared to accept complexity, perspectives, and worldviews different from our own. The host Adam Rutherford immediately offers a counterexample: we also always need simplicity; if you embrace difficulty and act the scholar all day, you may end up achieving nothing and enjoying nothing. Lavinia's response pulls the topic back to rhetoric: language therefore matters more than ever, and poetry and poetics can teach people how to argue.

item.title: Apple has no frontier model of its own, but wants to win again with a foldable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果没有自己的前沿模型-却想靠折叠屏再赢一次/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果没有自己的前沿模型-却想靠折叠屏再赢一次/
item.description: Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the entire event had not one new AI feature; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet is on a foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.
item.content:encoded:
Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the entire event had not one new AI feature; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet is on a foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.

Mark Gurman is the most accurate reporter on Apple, and this episode threads executive turnover, the AI roadmap, the privacy controversy and foldable predictions into one line, with high information density.

5:09 The biggest difference between Ternus and Cook is that he'll make the call
Gurman says the event was almost interchangeable with the Cook era, with the one difference that Ternus opened by laying out a view on AI. The mechanism he gives is management style: you bring an idea to Cook and he keeps probing, in many cases not making a single decision — it's collective decision-making; you go to Ternus and he gives you a decision, gives you an opinion, you may hate the opinion, but he takes a position. Gurman stresses this is exactly the biggest difference between the two men from talking to insiders, and it explains why Ternus talked about AI first thing on stage.

8:20 The 2026 event had not one new AI feature
Gurman points out that Apple held a big product event in September 2026 and launched no notable new AI features; the roughly 15-minute opening just re-narrated the past two years of Apple Intelligence. His explanation: Apple has gone as far on AI as it can and can only tell the best story with the cards it holds; and Apple has no AI-centric device, so it has to prop up the iPhone as its AI device until a killer device appears and it can switch narratives.

13:29 Under Cook, Apple became an institution
Gurman distinguishes the Cook era from the Jobs era: in the Cook era people's relationship with Apple is a relationship with an institution — global, enormous, like IBM; the Jobs era was one new product after another redefining categories. He also corrects the host's read on Vision Pro — every time he writes that Vision Pro is on life support, he gets dozens of reactions close to death-threat level, because some people have built businesses around spatial computing and some consumers paid four thousand dollars for it.

20:45 Apple spent five years swapping out the old guard one by one
Gurman reconstructs the rhythm of the handover: in 2023 Cook began saying at every executive meeting that succession had to be taken seriously; at the time the top ranks either had five hundred million in the bank or were billionaires, and were all around the same age. So they lined up an order and went one by one — at the end of 2024 CFO Luca Maestri retired, replaced by Kevin Parekh; in 2025 COO Jeff Williams retired, succeeded by his deputy; in 2026 the general counsel changed, with Jennifer Newstead poached from Meta; and only at the end of 2026 did Cook hand off to Ternus. Gurman calls this retention strategy Hotel California: you never want to leave.

28:07 The chip chief was kept with a title invented on the spot
Gurman says the second most important person at Apple now is the hardware head, who built Apple Silicon, Apple's key differentiator. In late summer or early autumn last year he went to tell Cook he was quitting, right in the middle of preparations for Ternus to take over. Cook got him to stay and take part in the transition, promising him the title of chief hardware officer — one Apple had never had — once Ternus took over, letting him keep his existing team and also take on Ternus's side of the business. Gurman judges this is not a long-term arrangement and that the man already wants to leave again — he conquered the Mac, ditched Intel and Qualcomm, and Apple has no next goal for him; he may leave within a year or two, at which point the hardware engineering team will have to be split up again, because no successor carries his industry weight.

33:15 Willing to spend tens of billions on modems, but says it needn't own AI
What Gurman finds most absurd is executives saying in interviews over the past year that ‘we never owned search, we don't need to own AI’. He counters: these are two completely different things, and Apple spent tens of billions to own an already commoditised cellular modem, acquiring and fixing Intel's modem business — willing to do that for a modem but unwilling to own AI is ridiculous. The internal idea was originally to partner with Google as a stopgap until it could build its own models, but Gurman says he has seen no evidence that Apple is pushing its own models again, making big AI acquisitions, or paying AI researchers top salaries.

48:53 The watch's always-on transcription stepped on the privacy landmine
Gurman's reaction to the Apple Watch's always-listening feature was ‘I can't believe they did it’. The feature only transcribes, doesn't record or store, and a double tap shows you the last 15 seconds of what someone said to you, without their consent. He says Apple knows the next-generation interface needs some degree of always-on capture, but the societal privacy problem is unsolved: technical white papers, private cloud compute and encryption can't hold back the social backlash. He thinks Apple could have put audio and visual intelligence together next year and told one coherent privacy story; as it is, it's boiling the frog slowly.

57:05 Foldables will become the new normal within a decade
Gurman offers a bold prediction: foldables will become the new normal within a decade. He draws an analogy with smartphone penetration — at the end of 2006 smartphones were about 6% of the market, now 85%, and it crossed half within five or six years; the iPhone itself wasn't the source of that, but it pulled everyone into the smartphone game, and he thinks the iPhone Duo will do the same for the phone market. He also mentions the iPhone's number migration feature, hinting at a future combination of a foldable for work and a smaller, lighter phone for weekends with family.

item.title: The Real Bottleneck in the Treasury Market: Not Size, but Not Enough Intermediaries

item.description: Primary dealers' balance sheets long ago stopped keeping pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Market makers have given way to high-frequency traders, but the latter collectively retreated in March 2020 — that is the core of the Treasury liquidity problem.
item.content:encoded:
Primary dealers' balance sheets long ago stopped keeping pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Market makers have given way to high-frequency traders, but the latter collectively retreated in March 2020 — that is the core of the Treasury liquidity problem.

A front-line operator from the New York Fed explains Treasury market structure, including empirical data from two 2025 papers and the latest TBAC developments. High information density.

11:26 The Treasury market is so big it must attract new buyers
Golay gives the scale: CBO counts $30 trillion in outstanding Treasuries at the end of 2025, projected to grow by another $26 to $27 trillion over the next decade. The market splits into two parts — the cash market (direct buying and selling of Treasuries, partly through inter-dealer broker electronic trading, partly dealer-to-client) and the repo market (borrowing collateralized by Treasuries, mainly intermediated by dealers). A market this large and growing necessarily has to attract different types of investors, including price-sensitive high-frequency traders and hedge funds.

14:31 High-frequency traders went from zero to the main force in electronic markets
Golay calls these firms principal trading firms (PTFs), mostly employing high-frequency strategies and trading on electronic platforms. Twenty years ago they were not in the Treasury market at all; today they may account for the majority of electronic cash market trading. The turning point was the 2014 flash rally — a large yield swing that no one could explain, which led the official sector to truly understand the growth of PTFs in electronic markets and sparked the IAWG's work on market structure and better data.

16:33 Primary dealer balance sheets have not kept up with the growth in outstanding Treasuries
Golay cites a chart from a Darrell Duffie paper: primary dealers' balance sheet capacity for Treasury intermediation has completely failed to keep pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Part of the reason is post-2008 reforms, and part is simply that the stock has grown too fast. The result is that the market has had to attract more price-sensitive investor types. She also corrects a common impression: it is not that PTFs always retreat during volatility; in other volatile periods the official sector has observed PTFs increasing activity. But in March 2020, everyone retreated.

19:42 The essence of all-to-all is bypassing dealer matching
All-to-all trading is literally that: any participant in the Treasury market can trade with any other participant. This is not new in equities, but much of the Treasury market is over-the-counter and dealer-intermediated, so it is not the case there. Golay notes that entering the March 2020 crisis, dealers already had a lot of Treasuries on their balance sheets, and when the selling wave hit there was no intermediation capacity left. If counterparties could be matched without going through a dealer, that might ease things. But she explicitly says that at the time most people were selling, and it is hard to imagine all-to-all perfectly solving that situation — every incremental improvement just helps.

22:51 All-to-all is stuck on the lack of counterparty matching
One of the paper's core findings: in the off-the-run market, if you look at a 15-minute window, there are almost no buyers for the same off-the-run security you want to sell. Extend the window to a day, and the match rate rises to 60% to 70%. Golay mentions possible innovations, such as an end-of-day batch auction, and some institutions already have such capabilities. But to date, no case in this area has truly succeeded at scale. She also notes that expanding central clearing could push the transition to all-to-all, because you would not need bilateral clearing arrangements with every counterparty — just connect to a central counterparty.

29:06 Off-the-run is 97% of outstanding but a liquidity desert
Off-the-run refers to older Treasuries, from those issued three months ago to 29- and 30-year bonds, making up about 97% of outstanding Treasuries. The March 2020 dash for cash selling was mainly off-the-run, and the off-the-run market is dealer-intermediated, with no all-to-all. Golay and colleagues at the Board of Governors and the New York Fed used TRACE data collected by FINRA for empirical work, including transaction-level data that only the official sector can see. The conclusion: the older the Treasury, the worse its liquidity — larger price impact, lower volume, wider bid-ask spreads.

31:15 The cheapest-to-deliver can revive liquidity
Another finding from the paper: when an off-the-run Treasury becomes the cheapest to deliver into a Treasury futures contract, its liquidity improves relative to other off-the-run securities. This suggests that part of the off-the-run problem is trading activity itself — with trading activity, liquidity improves; without it, liquidity deteriorates. On policy implications, Golay mentions that Treasury buybacks can create trading activity around off-the-run securities and improve liquidity; central clearing makes clearing smoother; and as for reducing issuance frequency and increasing individual issue size, the paper does not reach a conclusion, because investors also like the finer granularity of monthly issuance.

36:33 TBAC put the brakes on expanding transparency
At a recent TBAC meeting, some members suggested expanding transparency of Treasury trading data: there is already market-wide aggregate statistics and transaction-level data for on-the-run securities; they suggested considering publishing transaction-level data for Treasury bills and more frequent on-the-run data. But TBAC expressed caution about expanding transparency in other areas, including off-the-run and the TIPS market. Golay says this is interesting because data transparency is exactly what the IAWG has focused on in recent years, and it was listed as a priority in 2021. She personally thinks small incremental transparency is beneficial, but understands that in less liquid markets, releasing too much information can make intermediation very difficult.

item.category: The Gray Area with Sean Illing
item.description: The course isn't in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO on how to extract value from people. The author says students lying isn't an accident — it's what the machine has rewarded all along.
item.content:encoded:
The course isn't in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO on how to extract value from people. The author says students lying isn't an accident — it's what the machine has rewarded all along.

Not a generic Silicon Valley critique — it's a specific investigation with course names, dollar figures and named people; if you care about early-stage investing and talent pipelines, the detail density is high.

5:12 You can raise hundreds of thousands before you have a company
Pre-idea funding was the newest layer of the game when Theo arrived on campus: give an 18-year-old who just got to school a few hundred thousand, even a million dollars, sign a one-page SAFE check, agree that "if you start a company later, come back to us" — otherwise the money never has to be repaid. For a VC that's pocket change; they don't actually believe in these hyped-up teenagers, and they don't need you personally to succeed — they just need one overnight hit. Meanwhile students are encouraged to make enormous promises and then discover, again and again, that nobody follows up: lie, and there are no consequences.

13:22 The secret course teaches extracting value
Stanford has a course that never appears in the catalog, called How to Rule the World, taught by a Silicon Valley CEO who styles himself a professor, admitting only 12 students a year — merely knowing it exists is a status symbol. Its central assignment is extracting value from people, with a strong whiff of the ends justifying the means. One woman Theo interviewed said the course taught her how to lie to VCs to raise money — she later raised millions, dropped out of Stanford, and did it despite having already been caught cheating in a computer science class; months later she put out a glossy launch video for a technology that didn't exist, and Silicon Valley still cheered her on, moved her into a mansion, and invited her back to Stanford to give a talk.

26:46 Ethics isn't a premise; getting caught is what counts
During ethics week in the intro computer science course, the professor described a software defect that killed four people in a radiation therapy machine, and the TA asked who in the room cared about ethics — Theo was the only one who raised his hand. Weeks later a classmate told him he was taking a business ethics course, and "we're all just there to figure out how they got caught." He didn't sense these people felt any need to pretend to care; when Sam Bankman-Fried was under house arrest in the house on the Stanford campus where he grew up, students made pilgrimages, threw parties themed around him, and said they wanted to replicate his success minus the final fall. A colleague's summary of the money that mysteriously vanished at Tree Hacks: it's all just a little bit of fraud.

38:01 The real reason the president fell wasn't the data
Board members who ousted Marc Tessier-Lavigne later told Theo that one of the heaviest reasons they gave was his posture — a highly aggressive public stance when challenged, deny, deny, deny, plus the threatening letters sent by the lawyer he hired, Steve Neal, which embarrassed the university. Theo found no evidence Tessier-Lavigne himself falsified data: the problem was in the labs he oversaw, where subordinates fabricated results in papers he co-authored, including the 2009 paper claiming to have found the cause of Alzheimer's, while internal company results before publication showed its central finding was "at best unreliable." He was asked to retract and refused, dragging it out for a decade. What drove him out was image management, not the data.

39:01 Four days after being ousted, the mansion closed
Four days after the board unanimously removed him, Tessier-Lavigne closed on a 7,600-square-foot mansion in "America's most expensive zip code," valued at over $10 million; eight months later he announced he had raised $1 billion for a new company doing AI biotech. Of the two VCs that led the round, an investor at one messaged Theo two months later to rib him about it, followed by a winking emoji; an investor at the other offered him money to start a company. Theo says it's the most Silicon Valley thing you could imagine: everything can be monetized, even taking down a university president turns into an invitation.

45:44 Duck syndrome: paddling like mad under the surface
Duck syndrome is a term Stanford coined itself: students glide across the surface like ducks, making everything look effortless, while underneath their legs paddle furiously just to stay afloat. Katie Meyer was its best illustration — captain of the women's soccer team, an NCAA champion, headed to law school, didn't drink, didn't smoke, didn't speed. Months before graduation, late on a Friday night, after every student support office had closed, she received a letter: because she had spilled coffee on a football player six months earlier (she said it was an accident, he said it was deliberate), her degree was suspended. That night she took her own life. Twelve schools later paid tribute to her; Stanford was not among them. The women's soccer team she had just led held a mental health night and didn't mention her name.

52:01 A legendary professor's fraud case, and the school says it never heard of it
Stan Cohen was the first geneticist to transplant a gene from one living organism into another, and his 1970s recombinant DNA technique created the model of universities profiting from patents; in its final valid year that patent accounted for 62% of all Stanford patent revenue. In his freshman year Theo found that Cohen had been found liable for fraud by a court: he had pitched investors on a drug target that might cure Huntington's disease, said the drug was already approved to treat another condition, and didn't tell them it had been permanently banned by the FDA in 1976 because it was lethal. He was ultimately ordered to pay $29 million and paid it. Theo asked the university, and the university replied that it had never heard of the case and had no involvement whatsoever — even though Stanford owned the relevant intellectual property and had been subpoenaed in court.

55:04 Raising money is easier than an internship, and that itself is the signal
The saying circulating in Stanford's inner circles is that it's easier to raise money for a startup than to land an internship — Theo says that's absurd, it shouldn't be that way, but that's the reality. He describes the moment as a game of AI musical chairs: everyone is waiting to see who's still standing when the music stops and who's left holding the bag. He isn't worried about cash-flow-positive companies like Meta and Google; he's worried about the companies clinging to the AI narrative that have no technology of their own, no revenue, and no ability to generate revenue — they can't hold on, and they will collapse. But he also cautions that Silicon Valley hasn't held power for long, that it's a very immature power system that hasn't grown guardrails, transparency or accountability, and that one collapse doesn't necessarily mean a reckoning.
